items.title: Sidewalk sleepers: They have nowhere else to stay while a loved one is in the hospital
paragraphs: Balraam Singh, 35, eats breakfast with his wife, Nusaa Davii, and their 7-year-old son, Munna, on the pavement outside Safdarjung Hospital in New Delhi, India. The child is receiving treatment for a heart condition, and the family has been sleeping on the pavement outside the hospital for the past 20 days. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption

DELHI, India — At 2 a.m. on the sidewalk outside one of Delhi's best-known public hospitals, Shabana Kumar gently wakes her husband. They sleep in shifts of about an hour at a time because their 6-year-old son is a patient in the oncology ward, being treated for leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. They are afraid that if they are both asleep, an urgent call could come about their son's condition and they might miss it.
The Kumar family lives more than 600 miles from Delhi in the state of Bihar. Arun, 32, works as a farmer. Shabana, 30, is a homemaker caring for their only son.

They made the trip to Delhi because they could not afford the cost of their child's cancer treatment in Bihar. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, or AIIMS, subsidizes expenses for families in need.

But for many families, there is one challenge they must bear on their own — finding a place to live in Delhi during the days, weeks, even months of treatment. Like the Kumars, families who can't afford to rent lodging often set up a temporary dwelling on the sidewalk.

On a night in August, dozens of families were sleeping on blankets or sheets spread directly on the sidewalk. Some tie mosquito nets to railings to protect themselves and their kids. They keep their bags and other belongings beside them as they sleep.

Families who have loved ones being treated at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi try to get some rest. Thousands of patients and their families travel from across India, sometimes thousands of kilometers, to seek treatment at the hospital. Many who can't afford accommodations sleep on pavement, in subways and in other public spaces near the hospital while waiting for appointments or treatment. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption

During the day, families move between the sidewalk and the hospital for appointments, tests, medicines and consultations. They carry their most important belongings with them while leaving less valuable items at their sleeping spot. One family member often stays behind to keep an eye on their things.

Like the family from Bihar, people who've accompanied a patient may sleep outside while the patient is housed in the hospital. In other cases, the person receiving care is seen during the day but does not have a bed, so they sleep on the sidewalk as well.

At night, the sidewalk dwellers return to the pavement, where a small ecosystem has grown around the families. Women cook rice over makeshift brick stoves. Volunteers distribute food. Nearby shops sell medicines and other necessities. Nearby tea stalls not only serve beverages but let families charge their phones.
Once strangers, they exchange information about doctors, tests and where to find a free meal or, when none is available, an affordable one they can pay for.
Vishnu Singh, 38, serves tea to patients, caregivers and others outside the hospital. Singh runs the stall with his brother, Arjun, and keeps it open 24 hours a day. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption
Vishnu Singh, 38, runs a tea stall outside AIIMS.
"I see poor people sleeping here every day, so many that I cannot even count them," he said.

At AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital, which is associated with Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, we interviewed families who had traveled from across India, often hundreds of miles from home, to seek medical care. The two hospitals stand opposite each other, treating patients with illnesses ranging from cancer and heart conditions to intestinal disorders and other serious ailments.

Some families had been there for a week, others for a month or longer. For many, returning home between hospital visits was impractical, so patients and the relatives accompanying them stayed in Delhi for the duration of their care.
The families we spoke with described their experiences spending days or weeks in Delhi while navigating appointments, tests, consultations and treatment.

A family sleeps inside a subway near the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi, India. Many families who don't have a place to stay sleep in public spaces near the hospital. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption

It is a startling contrast — a hospital that provides critical care, that, according to its annual report, gives subsidies to thousands of poor families for treatment — and that is ringed by folks who traveled great distances to find care for a loved one and who cannot afford a place to stay.
NPR reached out to the hospital by email to ask about the issue of accommodations and the community of sidewalk dwellers. The hospital did not respond.

AIIMS' website notes that its Medical Social Service Unit provides financial assistance for medical treatment and travel costs for some patients coming from outside Delhi. It also states that the unit helps arrange accommodation for out-of-town patients and their family members and caregivers at dharamshalas, traditional charitable lodging facilities affiliated with AIIMS, or other low-cost accommodation.

The website does not say whether AIIMS pays for those accommodations or provides financial assistance specifically for the lodging costs. Shalini Yadav is one of the patients who sleeps on the sidewalk with her parents.

Shalini Yadav, 20, who is seeking treatment at the hospital for an intestinal illness that she's suffered from for five to six years, passes the time reading The God of Sins. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption

Yadav is a second-year college student from Piprat village in Tikamgarh district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India. She had been preparing for the state civil service examination. Her plan was to become a government officer.

Now she is spending her days reading Gunahon Ka Devta (The God of Sins), a famous 1949 Hindi tragic romance novel written by Dharamvir Bharati, on the pavement outside AIIMS, waiting to find out when her treatment will begin and when she can go home.

Yadav says she has been dealing with an intestinal illness for five or six years and has already undergone two operations. Her family had sought treatment elsewhere before relatives and neighbors advised them to travel to Delhi in search of better treatment at AIIMS — a trip of roughly 370 miles. "We thought AIIMS was the best hospital in India," she said. The cost of staying in Delhi was also a burden: Her family could not afford a room and had already spent thousands of rupees on travel and other expenses.
When we interviewed her on Aug. 3, she had been there for about three weeks with her parents, Surendra Singh Yadav, 47, a farmer, and Kalpana Yadav, 45.
"We thought the facilities would be good, the doctors would be good, and everything would happen quickly. We never imagined that we would have to sleep on the road," she said.
For her, the pavement is not just uncomfortable, it is also frightening. During the day, she says, she can manage. At night, she worries about the people around her.
"There are all kinds of people here," she says. "Some are good, but some drink or use drugs. There is shouting and fighting. As a girl, I feel very uncomfortable here at night."
But the family has little choice. They cannot afford a room in Delhi, she says. "We have decided that we have to sleep on the road because there is no other option."

During the day, Yadav goes into the hospital for appointments, tests and checkups, then returns to the pavement while waiting for the next step in her treatment. Everything is on hold — her college education, her hopes of qualifying for a government job, her father's farming work.
"It feels like we are being forced to live like this," she says.

Lakhi Bai, 62, from Ramnagar in Maihar district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India, about 500 miles away, came to Delhi seeking treatment for diabetes and a condition that she says causes numbness and a loss of sensation in parts of her body.

She says she could sometimes sustain an injury without feeling pain. When we met her, she had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about 20 days. During that time, she says, she had been going to different doctors and departments for consultations and tests but had not yet received a treatment plan.
Bai is a farmer and describes herself as a homemaker. She said she has three sons but is no longer in contact with them. She came to Delhi alone.
Lakhi Bai, a 62-year-old farmer who came to the hospital to receive treatment for diabetes, has been sleeping outside the hospital for about 20 days. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption
"I cannot afford to bring someone with me," she says. "If I bring someone, I have to pay for their food and accommodation, too."
It's been a difficult period. "Sometimes I don't even get food," she says. "I sleep with an empty stomach."
Sleeping outside is also stressful. The heat is hard to endure, she said, as is rainwater.
"When it rains, water comes here," she said. "There is nowhere to go."
AIIMS did not respond to requests for comment about her account or the experiences described by other families interviewed for this story.
Bai did not know how much longer she would have to remain in Delhi. "I have no place to stay," she says. "I just pray that I can get the treatment I need and something can be done."
In August, Balraam Singh, 35, a brick-kiln worker from Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a month with his wife and their 7-year-old son, Munna Singh.
Munna has a heart condition that his father describes as a "hole in the heart."
They had come from about 50 miles away seeking further medical evaluation and treatment at Safdarjung Hospital.
"We came with a lot of hope that we would find a doctor and my son would be treated," he says. "But now it feels like we may have to go back without knowing what will happen next.
For Singh, who can earn $5 to $7 a day at the kiln where he works, staying in Delhi means not only a loss of income but the need to spend money on food and other daily needs.

Gulshan Bano, 38, had come to Delhi from Bihar with her 60-year-old mother, Asma Khatoon, and her 6-year-old daughter, Fiza. They had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a week when we met them in August.

Bano says her mother has had a heart condition for several years and was receiving treatment in Bihar. Her mother had undergone checkups and tests there, but the family felt she needed further evaluation and care.

Gulshan Bano, whose mother has heart disease, sits with her 6-year-old daughter, Fiza. They had been staying outside the hospital for the past 10 days while seeking medical treatment for her mother. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption
Relatives also advised them to seek treatment in Delhi, and the family decided to travel for further consultations and tests.
Bano said doctors have told them that her mother has a heart problem and have prescribed medication rather than recommending surgery.
The family returns to Delhi for checkups about every six months. To pay for the trips, Bano works in domestic jobs in Bihar.
"I work for months and save whatever I can, and then I come here," she says. "Whatever little money remains has to be used here."
Bano said her husband does not contribute to her mother's medical expenses and she has little choice but to keep making the journey to Delhi.

A visit can last about a month, Bano said, as the family waits for scheduled consultations, tests and follow-up care. Because they cannot afford other accommodation, they sleep outside the hospital between appointments and tests rather than return home and make another journey to Delhi.
"Where should I go?" she said. "I have to come here because my mother needs treatment."
For families like Bano's, charities and volunteers can provide some of the practical support they need while they wait outside the hospitals.

Rajiv Ranjan, who works with the Delhi-based Donate A Meal Trust, said his organization regularly helps patients and their attendants staying outside AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital by distributing food, clothes and rations.
He said the organization has seen many families remain outside the hospitals while seeking treatment or caring for relatives inside.

"We come here for people who sleep outside while they or their family members are receiving treatment inside the hospital," he says. "They have nowhere else to stay, so we try to help with whatever we can." The group distributes about 100 meals a day, Ranjan says.

"People need shade from the sun, and during the rainy season they need somewhere to stay dry," Ranjan said. "Some of them take shelter under the Delhi Metro, the city's rapid-transit rail system, when it rains."

For Shalini Yadav, the 20-year-old college student from Madhya Pradesh who traveled to Delhi for treatment, the food distributions and other help have become part of life outside the hospital. She said people arrive to help in whatever way they can, but the assistance does not reach everyone.
"Sometimes we get food. When we don't, we buy it nearby. But there are many people here who don't get anything to eat."
Suhana Bano, 47, from Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, has been bringing her 18-year-old son, Mohammad Sameer, to Delhi for treatment for about two years.

Suhana Bano, 47, from Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, has been bringing her 18-year-old son, Mohammad Sameer, to Delhi for medical treatment for about two years. Bano has been staying on the pavement for the past month while waiting for her son's next appointment at the hospital. Sajad Hameed for NPR hide caption

Sameer has irritable bowel syndrome. He was in seventh grade when this digestive ailment forced him to leave school. The family first sought treatment at several hospitals in Bareilly, about 155 miles from Delhi, before traveling to Safdarjung Hospital.
Suhana Bano said the family turned to Delhi after seeking treatment locally, hoping to find the specialized care Sameer needed.

The family travels to Delhi whenever Sameer is due for a consultation or tests. Typically, they stay one to two months, Bano says. While in Delhi, the family sleeps outside Safdarjung because they cannot afford a room.
Aamar Singh, 60, a farmer from Hathras, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside AIIMS for about a week when we met him in April.

His 35-year-old daughter, Neelam, was admitted to the AIIMS intensive care unit with a respiratory problem, he said. His 40-year-old sister, Rashima, stayed outside with him. At night, they sleep alongside stray dogs that also gather on the pavement.
Singh does not know how long his daughter will remain in the ICU after being admitted for treatment and therefore does not know how long he will have to remain outside.
Food is not always available, he said, and some days they go hungry.
"Sometimes you eat, sometimes you don't," he said. "My daughter is inside, so I have to stay here. What else can I do? This is our situation."
So Aamar Singh waits on the pavement for news about his daughter until he can take her home.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Sajad Hameed is an India-based journalist and multimedia storyteller focusing on South Asia. He writes about politics, human rights, health, business, the economy and the impact of climate change, with particular focus on the region's evolving social and political landscape.

Rehan Qayoom Mir is an independent journalist whose work has appeared in outlets including Al Jazeera English, The Guardian, Nikkei Asia, The Progressive, Jacobin and more. He reports from across India and South Asia, with a focus on ground reporting and human-interest stories.

items.title: Weddings are expensive. How about a grocery store cake?
paragraphs: A flight of wedding cake samples at a Publix supermarket in Vestavia Hills, Ala., on Sept. 23. Cake flavors from left to right are red velvet, carrot cake, chocolate and vanilla. Filling flavors from left to right are raspberry, vanilla custard, cookies-and-cream mousse and strawberry. Stephan Bisaha hide caption
Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000.
Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.
"We love Costco, first of all," said Anna Holleran, who got married in California's Bay Area this year — and, yes, picked up her wedding cake from the grocery wholesaler.
"Their cakes are so good," she said. "How can you go wrong?"

Weddings are one of the most expensive days in many people's lives, costing on average about $36,000, according to the wedding-planning website Zola. The Bank of America Institute reports wedding spending among its customers was up 8.5% in May from a year earlier.

Some of that is by choice, with couples deciding to splurge on the venue or chasing the latest TikTok reception trend. But there are less controllable economic factors too, from inflation driving up the price of suits and catering to tariffs bumping up the cost of imported flowers and bridal gowns.

And according to Emily Forrest, head of communications at Zola, one place where couples are willing to trim costs is the cake. About a third of couples surveyed by Zola said they'd consider spending less on cake and dessert.

"When it comes to a wedding, every couple always has to sit down and say, 'Where are we going to save, and where are we going to splurge?'" said Forrest. "And cakes just don't seem to rise to the splurge occasion for a lot of couples."
What couples aren't willing to do is ditch the cake tradition entirely.
"You can't skip the cake!" said Lily Alana Stewart, who got married last year in central Alabama. "Everybody looks forward to a cake at a wedding."
To save money, she ordered her cake from Publix, a grocery chain in the South.

Stewart used baby's breath for decorating the venue, and Publix incorporated that into the cake design. Her co-workers who attended were surprised to learn where the cake came from. "They said, 'Wait, wait, wait. Your wedding cake was from Publix?'" Stewart said. "And they were still mind blown."

While the average wedding cake costs about $5.50 a slice, according to Zola, a slice of Publix cake is about $1.50 cheaper, while still pulling off that classic three-tiered, white-frosted wedding cake look. The chain also offers couples a tasting flight, so they can sample four flavors — including red velvet and carrot — before they order.

The wedding cake business has grown at Publix. The stores around Birmingham, Ala., sell about 50% more than they did before 2020, according to Jeff Brancato, a Publix retail improvement specialist. A chocolate cake with fondant that can serve 94 people costs $388, according to the price guide for the Birmingham area.
"There is definitely big savings when it comes to it," Brancato said.

Still, you do get what you pay for in a grocery store cake, including fewer options than what a specialty baker might offer — like more flavors or more customized decorations. While Publix touts its wedding cake business, Costco doesn't even list its half sheet as a wedding cake. It works out to about 70 cents per slice. (Costco did not return NPR's request for an interview.)
Holleran's priority was saving money where she could. Her wedding was near her home in California wine country — a region that's a destination spot for other couples and where venues are expensive.

Holleran said the culinary details of her cake weren't what mattered. "The real point is that you're sharing a dessert for the first time with somebody that you love," she said. "It's kind of symbolic of all the sweet moments that you're supposed to share in a marriage."

items.title: Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states
paragraphs: President Trump speaks at a campaign rally at Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport in Bullhead City, Ariz., on Oct. 14. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.
"I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump said confidently.

The White House hasn't clarified which 35 places the president was talking about that night. Since then, Trump has campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates. Rather than focus on swing states and swing districts as the president said he would, his travel schedule has taken him to a lot of Republican territory.
Trump's itinerary is both a reflection of where he can help (and where he can't) but also of a shifting landscape where even red state Republicans need a boost.
On the tarmac between rally stops in Arizona and Montana this week, Trump attempted to spin his visits to states he won decisively just two years ago as a matter of gratitude.
"So, I do it to thank them," Trump said. "I also do it because we have some great people there that are running and I want to make sure they win."

He went on to bemoan the drop in Republican turnout in years when he isn't on the ballot, something Trump and his team are trying to counteract with an October campaign rally blitz that has taken him to Ohio (twice), Texas (twice), Oklahoma and even Tennessee.
"What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump mused from stage to wild cheers.

Earlier this week, the president took an eight hour flight to Alaska to campaign for Republicans, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, both of whom face races that are too close for comfort in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.
"This is worth the 8 hours in a plane," Trump said to an adoring crowd. "And don't forget I've got 8 hours going back. Give me credit for that."
In fact, he made two more stops on the way back and spent the night at the Trump hotel in Las Vegas.
The Republican National Committee has announced he'll be campaigning in Kansas Monday, which has a toss-up U.S. Senate race, something few would have anticipated even a month ago.

Republicans are on defense in a lot of states where they've traditionally won without much trouble. Trump's team is picking locations where he can activate the Republican base in places where he's done well in the past.

"Just a lot of excitement, a lot of momentum building up on the ground here," said RNC Chairman Joe Gruters in a call with NPR from a Trump rally in Arizona. "It's turnout, turnout, turnout. How do you get the base to show up? You put the president on the ballot. You put him out there."

Trump frequently implores his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot. It's a novel political strategy that runs counter to the norm for unpopular presidents whose parties face significant midterm headwinds. Trump claims the polls are wrong about his underwater approval rating.

As for Trump's message, it doesn't change much from stop to stop. There are the greatest hits: his past election wins, his One Big Beautiful Bill, and a walk down memory lane from right before he launched the war with Iran when gas prices were cheaper. He teases a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the House and the Senate, an idea he first rolled out at the unconventional Republican midterm convention, but has faced resistance from elected Republicans. On most stops he talks about a specific project or deal he has planned for the state.

On Tuesday, Trump is set to campaign in Greenville, North Carolina. Republican campaign committees have already started canceling ad reservations meant to help Trump's handpicked Republican Senate candidate there, Michael Whatley. It's a sign they see that race as moving out of reach.

There's also a congressional district in Eastern North Carolina that was redrawn to favor Republicans as part of Trump's mid-decade redistricting push. It shouldn't be competitive, but it's now rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.

"I think it's going to backfire on them this year in every way shape and form," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "He's trying to drum up any amount of support that he can at the last minute. But I don't think that North Carolinians are going to fall for it again."

items.title: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
paragraphs: Demonstrators march through the Country Club Plaza shopping district during a "No Kings" protest Saturday, March 28, 2026, in Kansas City, Mo. Charlie Riedel/AP hide caption
No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.

On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections, and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.
The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.

No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.

"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."
There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.

The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls, and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.

Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour.
All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.

Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.

"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."

Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.

Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.

At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.
"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

items.title: Wired headphones are suddenly all the rage, and the best we've tested has £40 off
paragraphs: Wired headphones have seen a resurgence of interest in 2026 as people cotton on to what audiophiles already knew: they usually offer a better listening experience for the money, with superior sound, zero latency and no charging requirements. Wired headphones have taken off so much among the rich and famous, that some have suggested that wires hanging from ears is now a sign of class, despite the fact that you can find professional-quality wired cans for less than the nearest Bluetooth equivalent.

The good news for non celebs is that the Sennheiser 480 Pro is reduced by £40 from £339 to £229 at Wex Photo and video. We've tested and reviewed dozens of headphones and this is our favourite closed-back option so far, as reviewed in our guide to the best wired headphones.

The Sennheiser HD480 Pro only came out in the summer of 2026, but they immediately stood out in the world of closed-back wired headphones. They're very well tuned, incredibly comfortable and they look cool too. While designed for professional studio use, they're also a treat for audiophiles or anyone who wants to discover what makes a neutral wired earphone so special.

The clear, largely uncoloured sound profile evades the issue of overly boomy bass and unrealistic timbre that haunts the closed-back headphone space. Passive noise isolation is well executed and the mature tuning fits all kinds of music at all volume levels.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of expert-curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
paragraphs: The Piper Tomahawk II aircraft took off from Glasgow Airport on Friday afternoon at 16:17.
It stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of Drymen in Stirling.
Earlier the plane had taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46 on Friday morning, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport.
It stayed there until around 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport on Tay before turning round and heading back to Glasgow.
It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight.
Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport.
"This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected."

items.title: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
paragraphs: A roof engulfed in flames is seen during the Norte Fire on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, in San Juan Capistrano, Calif. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.

Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.
"Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse," said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn't had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she's lived in the community, she said.
"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said. "We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."

The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.

It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.

Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.

The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
"The fire is right up on the city," said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
"You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke," Needham said.

Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 118,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

items.title: Swinney insists 'stars are aligning' for Scottish independence
paragraphs: John Swinney will deliver his keynote speech to the SNP conference in Aberdeen
John Swinney will insist that "the stars are aligning" for Scottish independence during his keynote speech to the SNP conference later.
The first minister will tell party members in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in the country's "journey towards statehood".
Swinney will stress that "in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, every first minister now supports our nations' right to self-determination".
He will seek to press the case for another independence referendum in the wake of elections in May which saw the SNP win a record fifth term in government at Holyrood.

The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff last month where they signed an agreement, which is not legally binding, that said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".
Swinney will tell his party's supporters that "one by one, the stars are aligning in our favour".
He will say that if the SNP lost May's Scottish Parliament election, the case for independence "would have been set back decades".
While the SNP won the Holyrood ballot, the party failed to win the overall majority Swinney had set as a target for trying to force a second referendum in the face of Westminster opposition.
Despite that, Swinney will declare that "there is no turning back".
He is expected to say: "The SNP is making the weather.
"And make no mistake – the wind is now firmly in the sails of Scotland's independence movement."
The first minister will go on to claim that the unionist parties at Westminster are "weaker than they have ever been".
Swinney introduced Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth to the conference on Friday
Swinney's address to the SNP conference comes the day after Andy Burnham made his first major speech in Scotland since moving into Downing Street.
The prime minister used that visit to extend an olive branch to Swinney, saying he wanted to work together on giving more power to local communities.
Speaking in Motherwell, the Labour leader said he wanted to "move beyond the old politics of conflict" as he offered to work with the SNP to deepen devolution in Scotland.
Burnham previously told Swinney during a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".
The meeting came after Burnham told MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
Since 2014, successive UK governments have opposed any further referendums.
Scotland previously voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45%.
In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government.

items.title: Olivia Rodrigo’s expectations music video hit with AI allegations
paragraphs: Olivia Rodrigo has finally released the music video for her new song Expectations featuring fellow pop princess Chappell Roan. The playful retro game show-inspired video was met with a shower of praise from fans – that was until some eagle-eyed viewers spotted something awry.

While the music video itself is a masterpiece of storytelling, set and character design, a tiny animated section has been accused of using AI. Having previously denounced the use of AI in her music, the allegations come as a shock for many of Rodrigo's fans.
Olivia Rodrigo - expectations (feat. Chappell Roan) (Official Music Video) - YouTube

The controversial scene in question features cartoon Rodrigo and Roan flying past on a wheel-of-fortune-inspired spaceship. Observant fans were quick to notice that one shot appears to remove one of Chappell's hands, while Olivia appears to have inherited her missing extremity.

Is it the work of AI, or simply a bit of good ol' human error? Either way, fans were dissapointed by the blunder. "Not the AI..." one fan wrote, while another added, "No way, and I just liked a tweet cheering her for not using AI."
where is chappell’s other arm and why does Olivia have three hands 😭 https://t.co/s9S5JDLdH2October 16, 2026

Recently telling The Hollywood Reporter, "I would never use AI in any of my music. Absolutely no,” the AI allegations came as a surprise to many. Some fans came to Olivia's defence, claiming, "This mistake happens in 2d animation all the time," while another wrote, "Honestly, I think the artist might’ve just messed up the colors because honestly it’s the only mistake I saw in those drawings and it’s a minor mistake."
For more design news, check out why Tyla was hit with heated AI allegations over her new animated music video or take a look at Apple Music's new logo that's giving major mixed messages.

items.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
paragraphs: The attacks, which took place while Sir Keir was prime minister, began on 8 May 2025, when a car he had previously owned was found on fire on a street where he used to live in Kentish Town.
Three days later, on 11 May, a fire was discovered at flats linked to Sir Keir in nearby Islington. He had lived there years before.
The next day another fire was discovered at the entrance to Sir Keir's Kentish Town home, which he was renting out to his sister-in-law, Judith Alexander.
She told the trial of billowing black smoke rising up the stairs while she was in the house with her partner and her daughter.
Lavrynovych and Carpiuc were found guilty of conspiring together and "with others" to damage property by fire between 1 April and 13 May 2025.
A BBC investigation revealed the arson attacks were part of an extensive campaign of sabotage, provocation and lies leading all the way to the Russian state.
The handler EL, who directed Lavrynovych, offered Russian citizenship in return for other attacks and glorified President Vladimir Putin.
Evidence identified by the BBC suggested EL was a young Russian diplomat.

items.title: England's 41-match unbeaten run ended by Canada
paragraphs: Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streak
Tries: Bauder, Corrigan, Menin, Seumanutafa Cons: De Goede (2)
Tries: Feaunati, Harrison, Bern Cons: Harrison (3)

England head coach John Mitchell challenged his Red Roses to "find something more" after their 41-match unbeaten streak - dating back almost four years - ended in dramatic fashion as Shoshanah Seumanutafa's late try handed Canada a thrilling 24-21 victory in Toronto.

Canada, who previously snapped England's 39-match winning run with a 26-26 draw in Exeter in September, are the first team to defeat them since November 2022, when they lost to New Zealand in the World Cup final.

Playing in front of 18,621 fans, a record for a standalone women's fixture in North America, the result also marks England's first defeat by Canada since 2016 and their first against their hosts on Canadian soil, having won their previous 11 away matches.

Canada's Savannah Bauder took advantage of Zoe Harrison's yellow card to open the scoring in the 15th minute, but it was England who took a 14-5 half-time lead, hitting back late in the first half through Maddie Feaunati and Harrison, with Laetitia Royer in the sin-bin for the hosts.

Sarah Bern cancelled out a stylish solo try from the hosts' Alysha Corrigan early in the second half to preserve England's nine-point lead before Canada's DaLeaka Menin crashed over for a converted score just after the hour mark to set up a tense finale.

Three minutes from time, Canada mounted an attack from halfway after a fumble put Harrison's clearing kick under pressure, and replacement Seumanutafa charged down the left wing to complete the comeback.

"We're disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance. So we'll stick to our processes," said Mitchell, following his first defeat since being appointed in late 2023.
"I guess [the loss] frees us up and allows us to find more. I know this group has got more in them. Sometimes it requires the context that we've just received to dig deeper and find something more."

The two sides will renew their rivalry in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October (in the early hours of Saturday on UK time) before England conclude their 2026 WXV Global Series against the USA in New Jersey on Friday, 30 October (21:15 GMT).
This result has been coming for England, who showcased vulnerability in their three WXV Global Series home matches in September.

Against Australia, the world champions trailed at half-time for the first time since 2020 before roaring back with seven second-half tries for a 48-15 win. The following week, Canada held them to a draw in Exeter while a nail-biting 26-19 win over New Zealand at Twickenham was secured with the clock in the red.

This time, Canada's defensive resilience in the face of repeated attacks kept the world champions off the scoreboard until the 32nd minute, but England also lacked a clinical touch in their opponents' 22, with multiple opportunities going begging. Notably, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald had an early try chalked off for a knock-on in the grounding.

In defence, multiple penalties afforded Canada the freedom to form free-flowing attacks while it was an individual handling error when delivering the ball to fly-half Harrison which gave the hosts field position to score their match-winning try.
The result places England in uncharted territory, with several players in the squad never having tasted defeat on the international stage - winger Jess Breach was unbeaten in her previous 59 caps.
But for captain Meg Jones, it is no time to panic. England are "still world champions" and her message is simple: "Stick together, look out for each other, and we go again."
She added: "We've got to remember, there's a target on our back continuously. Everyone's got that underdog mentality, that underdog fight.
"We've got to be in a position now where we've got to be the quickest to respond. That's the nature of the game.
"What an amazing achievement for us as a group. I think they will go down in history as one of the best sporting teams.
"We're still world champions, we're still number one, and we'll still keep pushing to be the best we possibly can."
In September, Canada captain Sophie de Goede confessed she still has sleepless nights about her side's World Cup final defeat by England in 2025.

Even after ending the Red Roses' winning run in Exeter, she was frustrated at being denied the opportunity to go for the win, although reluctantly conceding that head coach Kevin Rouet's call to kick the ball dead was the sensible one.
After a historic performance in Toronto, where De Goede's side showcased "the DNA of our team" and "found a way to win", sleep might once again be hard to come by – albeit for far happier reasons.

While several Canadian players play their club rugby in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, the national side – ranked third in the world – does not benefit from the same facilities or depth of talent as the Red Roses, even launching a crowdfunding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.
In the aftermath of their run to the final, the country's government announced a new 775m Canadian dollars (£401m) fund for sport in Canada.
Achieving both an attendance record and victory over England in their first home match since August 2025 demonstrates the growing momentum behind women's rugby in the country.

"It's a little bit more than just the score at the end because we won on so many levels," added scrum-half Justine Pelletier. "Off the field, the crowd, being home. That win at the end on the pitch was just the cherry on [top].
"It was good to beat England but I think for a few years now, we knew that we could beat them. It was just a matter of time and a matter of putting every detail together."
England: Kildunne; Breach, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Matthews, Feaunati.
Replacements: Field, Carson, Muir, Short, Kabeya, Hunt, Rowland, Sing.

items.title: Angry Birds just flapped its way into the Kelly Clarkson feud with a cheeky animated poster design
paragraphs: The internet has been split this week by the heated feud that erupted between singer Kelly Clarkson and Brooklyn novelty shop Art of Play. It's a been a striking example of how brands could benefit from having a clear strategy for how to react when they inadvertently get caught up in the celebrity news cycle.

It might seem sensible at this for anyone else to stay out of it and let them sort it out between themselves, but not Angry Birds 3. The upcoming movie has jumped on the controversy to cheekily remind the world that it's due for release at cinemas in a couple of months.
What Doesn't Kill You Makes You...Angry. The #AngryBirdsMovie3 is only in theatres December 23. https://t.co/QLMjKSNZjjOctober 15, 2026

If you somehow missed the online scuffle of the week, the controversy is basically a “he said, she said” row over a $15,000 mechanical bird, and whether Kelly Clarkson was or wasn't treated like she couldn't afford it. The singer says that when she asked about the bird at Art of Play, a member of staff offered to find her a cheaper alternative. Writing on X, she compared the experience to a scene from Pretty Woman in a post that's received over 11,000 comments.
The shop then responded to complain that it was being hounded by Kelly Clarkson fans and claimed that the bird, called Molly, hadn't been for sale in the first place.

Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone “yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.” That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it ✅ And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t.October 11, 2026

It's not an obvious branding opportunity, but Angry Birds 3 quickly saw the potential. In the animation above posted on the same platform, Chuck, AKA Yellow Bird, is cast in the role of Molly. He doesn't take sides, instead sitting back to watch others being angry for a change, but the animated poster design pokes fun at Molly's price tag, pointing out that we can see Chuck for the price of a movie ticket.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
paragraphs: NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.

Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.

The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in the NHS of a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”

According to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”

Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.

Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson, saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.

Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.

But two parliamentary select committees have urged the government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.

“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”

Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.

“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.
Palantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.

“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministers stating that it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”

It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.

Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHS England has, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.

The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this week urged ministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.

Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.”

A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

items.title: Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie
paragraphs: Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it.

Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie.
The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures.
An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing".
Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100.
Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment.
From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK.
The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours.
However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits".
Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit.
"There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.
"We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit."
It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs.
According to the UK Government's official website, external, the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate.
There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health.
However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection.
"The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation.
"We're effectively opening up more space for wild birds."

items.title: Pope's health should not be taken 'for granted', says top Vatican diplomat
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV's health should not be taken "for granted", a British senior Vatican official told the BBC.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, said the news of the Pope's ill health was "a bit of a game changer", adding "it's going to make things a bit different".
The Pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.
Speaking on Tuesday after the Pope's operation was announced, but before his cancer diagnosis, Archbishop Gallagher said: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted."
The 71-year-old had surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

Speaking to Radio 4's the Sunday Programme, due to air this weekend, the Archbishop said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair.
"And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out."

Asked how it will make things different going forward, the Archbishop said church figures might have assumed "that he was not quite like the rest of us who are very aware of our vulnerabilities and the ageing process".
He went on: "But lots of us have been through similar experiences at different times in our lives, and we've got through them, and so we hope it's going to be the same case with Pope Leo.
"I am concerned. I think we've got to ask the question: how was it discovered? What happened?"
The Vatican has said the Pope is showing steady improvement in hospital, and he was expected to lead Sunday prayers.
They had stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited at the Vatican, overlooking crowds in St Peter's Square but has sometimes been given from a hospital window by previous popes when necessary.
No date has been given for Pope Leo's hospital discharge, but recovery was expected to take around a week.
Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
Leo himself announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.
Archbishop Gallagher, who is from Liverpool, also said he expected the Pope to visit the UK at some point.
"We have exchanged a little bit," he said. "He's just beginning to think about what he might do in 2027, but it's still very much at the examining the possibilities (stage)".
He would "bring a spirit of renewed hope", said the Archbishop, after the Pope received a rapturous welcome in France and Spain earlier this year.
"But these things do take quite a lot of planning, and so you don't just do it overnight."
You can hear more of Archbishop Gallagher's interview on The Sunday Programme on Radio 4 at 0710

items.title: The Influencer Project to Melanie C: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
paragraphs: The Influencer Project Out now When your career involves constantly posting footage of everything you do to social media, it makes things a cakewalk for stalkers. And lo, the influencer-in-peril horror subgenre was born. British social media star Chiara King plays herself in this chilling iteration, set in Copenhagen.

Naza Out now The ongoing genocide in Gaza has proven an urgent subject for documentaries and drama alike. Here, directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the four film-makers behind the 2025 Oscar winner No Other Land) construct a doc made up of interviews with Israeli Intelligence Corps agents, who map out the details of targeted airstrikes in civilian areas.
