Maybe all three? – in which scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) has one hour to find a way to escape before his oxygen runs out. Also starring Josh Brolin (sadly not as the whale).

Street Fighter Out now This reboot marks the third live-action movie based on the hit video game to make it to the big screen, and features Jason Momoa as Blanka, 50 Cent as Balrog, and Callina Liang as Chun-Li. Ready… set… fight! Catherine Bray

Melanie C 18 to 24 October; tour starts Dublin The seemingly indefatigable Melanie C, whose dancefloor-focused ninth solo album Sweat peaked at No 3 earlier in the year, takes her solo oeuvre for a spin around a collection of mid-sized venues. As well as the raft of recent bangers, there should be space for some Northern Star-era pop gems, too. Michael Cragg

J Cole 19 October to 2 November; tour starts London The US rapper heads out on his first solo headline tour in five years in support of seventh, and apparently final album, The Fall-Off. A star-studded, 24-track behemoth, it’s quite the swansong, so chances are these arena shows will carry a similar sense of celebratory closure. MC

Mingus Big Band Ronnie Scott’s, London, 19 to 24 October Charles Mingus, one of the most soulfully creative jazz composers, died in 1979, but the powerful legacy band bearing his name has cherished his repertoire for three decades. The classy lineup includes saxists Wayne Escoffery and Craig Handy, trumpter Alex Sipiagin, and uncannily Mingus-echoing bassist Boris Kozlov. John Fordham

Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Liverpool Philharmonic Hall, 17 October Rising-star conductor Adam Hickox takes to the podium for the world premiere of a new clarinet concerto by Gavin Higgins, performed by outgoing RLPO artist in residence Mark Simpson. The programme culminates in Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring – still thrilling, more than a century after its own premiere provoked a riot. Flora Willson

Sturtevant Raven Row, London, to 20 December Sturtevant was the ultimate appropriator, a satirical copycat who had been mimicking the work of other artists since the 1960s. This first UK institutional show since her death in 2014 is a celebration of her radical take on conceptualism.

Hokusai: 36 Views of Mount Fuji Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, 13 October to 17 January Hokusai’s iconic depiction of Mount Fuji, one of the most famous images in the history of art, wasn’t a one-off. It was part of a series, and this exhibition brings the full set together.

Joy Gregory Arnolfini, Bristol, 17 October to 7 February A celebration of four decades of experimental photography by this leading voice in Black and feminist art, working across historic photographic processes and digital manipulation.

Larry Achiampong Karst, Plymouth, to 12 December Using the visual language of science fiction, this British Ghanaian artist tackles big ideas of colonialism, class, diaspora and displacement in this continuation of his ambitious film project. Eddy Frankel

Olga Koch Where Else?, Margate, 15 October; touring to 4 December Not all standups ooze confidence like Koch – and not all have such good reason to. In her meticulously crafted new show Fat Tom Cruise, the Russian-British comedian (and PhD student) explores the masculinity crisis via routines delivered with vim, vigour and flair. Rachel Aroesti

Some Woman National Theatre: Dorfman, London, to 21 November Anne-Marie Duff stars as an overlooked woman who, after a troubling encounter on a train platform, decides to take a stand in this new play from Helen Edmundson. Miriam Gillinson

Northern Ballet: Cinderella Nottingham Theatre Royal, Friday to 24 October; touring to 15 December A new Cinderella for Northern Ballet. Created by choreographer Michael Pink for Milwaukee Ballet, this is the show’s UK premiere, with all the trappings – pumpkin carriage, fairy godmother, comic stepsisters – as well as a great live Prokofiev score. Lyndsey Winship

Lanny Bristol Old Vic, to 7 November Max Porter’s acclaimed novel is adapted for the stage by Bea Roberts, with a cast drawn largely from the south-west. It’s a blurred and beguiling tale about a young boy who goes missing: is it foul play, the work of an ancient shape-shifting figure or something else? MG

It Gets Worse Channel 4, 15 October, 10pm Leo Reich has created the first good gen Z hangout comedy with this London-set tale of three university friends struggling to self-actualise in their mid-20s. From Lena Dunham to Zadie Smith, celebrity cameos abound – but Reich’s winningly bratty protagonist is the real star attraction.

The Audacity HBO Max, 15 October Writer Jonathan Glatzer (Succession, Better Call Saul) mines frantic comedy from the dark heart of Silicon Valley in a series about a megalomaniacal tech boss (Billy Magnussen). Industry’s Sarah Goldberg plays his therapist, Motherland’s Lucy Punch is his wife and Zach Galifianakis guests as another unhinged billionaire.

The New Stanford Prison Experiment Netflix, 14 October The 1971 psychological study which saw male college students randomly split into guards and prisoners in a mock jail remains one of the most fascinating and notorious of all time. Will Netflix’s new reality show version have the same results – and, crucially, the same grim appeal?

Last One Laughing: Halloween Prime Video, 16 October The spectacular success of our version of the Japanese gameshow means it’s already entered seasonal spin-off territory. Phil Wang and Reece Shearsmith (plus old faves Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper) are among the comics trying desperately not to laugh or – spooky twist alert! – scream in this latest edition. RA

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Switch 2; out 15 October Take up boxing, bowling, archery, basketball, tennis, skating and more in this latest game in the fine controller-waggling lineage of Wii Sports. Parents of competitive siblings: remember to use the controller straps to stop a Joy-Con from flying through a window.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 PC, Switch 2, PS5, Xbox; out Friday Activision’s theatre of war goes on tour to Korea, where an invasion threatens the stability of the rest of the world. The multiplayer offers the usual cornucopia of ways to play soldiers, where the campaign follows a Korean private and returning character Captain Price, on the run after an assassination. Keza MacDonald

Rachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too Soon Out now Lyrically influenced by a mid-20s existential crisis, the second album by London singer-songwriter Chinouriri sweetens those fears with vibrant musical touches. On Broken Chair and One Song Away from Crying she dabbles in bubbling 80s synthpop, while the murkier Make Believe grows slowly overcast.

Angèle – Instinct Out now Five years after her second album, Nonante-Cinq, the Belgian superstar returns with more gleaming dance-pop. With production from French knob twiddlers Justice and SebastiAn, plus assistance from Caroline Polachek on the slinky Love Triangle, it’s a play for the big leagues.

Florrie – Magic for a While Out now As part of production hothouse Xenomania, Florrie played drums on hits by Kylie and Girls Aloud. Since stepping up to the mic she’s released her own collection of decadent bops, with this second album expanding into indie pop (The Times) and pensive balladry (Catch You If You Fall).

Fontaines DC – Dopamine Chamber Out now After hitting their creative and commercial stride on 2024’s Grammy-nominated Romance, the Irish rock experimentalists are back with this swaggering fifth album. As with Romance it’s been produced by James Ford, who peppers the undulating Tongue with twitchy electronic effects. MC

The LRB Podcast Podcast Intellectuals’ favourite the London Review of Books makes the big questions of our time slightly more digestible in this audio series. Writers, thinkers and experts discuss everything from the worth of criticism to the German far right.

TED-Ed: Public Speaking 101 YouTube This ongoing and insightful series of lectures on public speaking is sure to give even the shyest person confidence to talk to a crowd. The most recent episode covers succinct ways to explain complex ideas.

Illuminated: Faithless BBC Sounds, out now Journalist May Robson’s expertly reported and deeply moving documentary follows four people who were raised in religious devotion and who have since chosen to leave their faith. Testimony comes from former Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormons and others. Ammar Kalia

items.title: Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)
paragraphs: I have an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress.

On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”. Men were portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining.

It is odd that a quarter of the way through the 21st century images of men crying – see the “weeping Frenchman” during the second world war and Paul Gascoigne’s tears during the 1990 World Cup – could still be seen as remarkable. Judith Butler describes masculinity as a phantasm, a haunting fiction of invulnerability and toughness that is all the more potent because it’s such a lie. We know this, but we’ve probably all had a part in enforcing it, knowingly or obliviously. Boys are still told they shouldn’t be sensitive, that it’s somehow shameful.

These photographs are proof that masculinity has strong connotations, histories and counter-histories; a lot of baggage. We stand in some relation to that baggage however we choose to express ourselves, and an image can either reinforce or challenge those associations.

Anyone with half a mind must feel a certain amount of pity for a man who feels the need to be depicted in his finery, or in a manner that expresses his prowess or authority – see Karen Knorr’s photographs satirising the privileged postures of men in gentlemen’s clubs – but we’re still surrounded by them, like it or not.

Despite the wonderful range here, it’s interesting how normatively hench many of the men depicted are, from Eugen Sandow, the father of bodybuilding, to Arnie to Hulk Hogan. There’s an absence of the body type enjoyed by roughly 80% of men: basically OK, a bit lumpy, sporadically hairy. We might run a 3k every couple of weeks and feel so pleased with ourselves that we down a bottle of wine and a box of cheese straws the same night.

To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men. Of course, the super-jacked male form is ubiquitous in film and television now, from Hollywood movies (where you expect it) to depressing ITV crime dramas (where you’d hope for a few more noodle arms and football-shaped tummies). Even the bang-average is barely represented; I feel like cheering when an even slightly flabby man takes his top off.

If there’s no body positivity movement for average men, that’s because men’s bodies are less likely to be scrutinised and judged. Certainly we don’t talk about body image much unless it’s in the context of the gym. It has only occurred to me in my 40s that I can marginally improve my appearance through exercise (I’m still not fully convinced and suspect I’m wearing myself out for no reason). We can say, “What do you bench?” but can’t say, “I’m feeling insecure about my jowls today.”

There’s a powerful defiance to the camp and the performative, of casually putting on a dress or a sarong as a straight man, already aware of the tedious reactions and thinking: “Yeah, and what of it?” There’s also a terrible self-consciousness to masculinity. I find the giant fake Warhammer-figurine shoulders of American football kits absolutely adorable. I’d feel the same about dictators on horseback if they weren’t dictators.

Depictions of queer masculinity offer an alternative here, from Leigh Bowery’s magnificently confrontational surrealist portraits to Rotimi Fani-Kayode’s beautiful, sculptural compositions of black queer men. Deliberately rougher round the edges, Sunil Gupta’s Exiles series depicts the underground (then illegal) culture of gay male life in India in the 80s: a furtive glance, a shy smile, the position of a cigarette, a palpable sense of risk.

The current resurgence of the crassest form of strongman masculinity feels overwhelming; a dictatorship of the most dysfunctional, damaged, spiteful elements of the male ego, emotionally dysregulated and outright evil. It’s pervasive in the manosphere, but also in government and political administrations. I’ve heard it described as a death-rattle before it finally goes extinct. That may be wishful thinking.

So many current manifestations of masculinity feel beneath contempt, but maybe they’re not. Maybe we should loudly express our contempt for them and hopefully speed their decline. Every significant photograph that enters the collective unconsciousness shifts our reality a little – the power of an image to either bolster or subvert machismo is still profound.

“He made no effort to seem overpowering,” wrote a Gay Times correspondent of Arnold Schwarzenegger in 1978, “but, rather, radiated a mild – nay – sunny, disposition.” In the 1970s, Schwarzenegger turned body-building from a niche subculture into a national obsession. He combined an exaggeratedly masculine body with a sense that he was secure in himself. “He accepts the inevitable attention of gay men as a compliment,” concluded Gay Times.

Robert Mapplethorpe took this portrait of Schwarzenegger in 1976, a year before the release of Pumping Iron, the hit docudrama that led to his Hollywood stardom. Mapplethorpe, who was celebrated for his images of queer and S&M subcultures, was particularly fond of this photograph, using it for postcards and party invitations. “Hot Dirty Man,” went the text over Schwarzenegger’s torso on one invitation from 1979. “You are invited to … ” FB

“When Marlon Brando appeared on stage in a torn, sweaty T-shirt,” wrote Gore Vidal in 1985, “there was an earthquake.” Before Brando’s breakout performance in A Streetcar Named Desire in 1947, Hollywood leading men had been “nothing but a suit of clothes”, Vidal argued. Brando made it OK for a man to be a sex object.

Many of the actor’s performances eschewed the buttoned-up vision of masculinity in the films of the 1930s and 1940s. He was emotional, violent and physical. “I’d never seen anything as visceral,” wrote the critic Pauline Kael, remembering her first glimpse of Brando on stage in the late 1940s. FB

“Great success here,” wrote Oscar Wilde of the American speaking tour on which this photograph was taken. “Nothing like it since Dickens, they tell me.” Though the 27-year-old had not yet written famous works such as The Importance of Being Earnest and The Picture of Dorian Gray, he was already a society sensation. His tightly controlled performance of a queer, urbane form of masculinity made him famous, but came with great risks. He was later imprisoned for gross indecency with men, and polite society turned on him – perhaps prefigured by newspaper digs at the time about the “effeminate” figure in this portrait. FB

You may not recognise him now, but Sessue Hayakawa was one of Hollywood’s first heart-throbs. Born in Japan, he moved to the US in early adulthood and broke out as a major matinée idol with a star-making turn as the villainous lead in Cecil B DeMille’s The Cheat (1915). He was then one of LA’s highest-paid actors. One photographer recalled Hayakawa arriving at a premiere to a horde of female fans who “spread their fur coats at his feet” so he could avoid stepping in a puddle.

As an Asian leading man, Hayakawa had to put up with a lot of racialised typecasting, and anti-miscegenation laws meant his characters never got the girl; when anti-Japanese sentiment rose in the 1920s, his star faded. He did get a late-career comeback, however, with his Oscar-nominated role as the tyrannical Colonel Saito in 1957’s The Bridge on the River Kwai. GS

Nuba mountain communities in the Kordofan region of Sudan have faced violence from outsiders for centuries, from British colonial authorities to the Khartoum central government. Against this backdrop, a renowned tradition of wrestling tournaments has developed.

This image by Magnum co-founder George Rodger, of a wrestler hoisted on a supporter’s shoulders, brought global, and unwelcome, attention to the area. Former Nazi photographer Leni Riefenstahl produced controversial and exoticising work there. “When they found out what was going on, people felt exploited,” said Sudanese professor Guma Kunda Komey. FB

It’s estimated that around one in four women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence by a male partner. Since the early 1980s, the photojournalist Donna Ferrato has dedicated her career to documenting the devastating impacts of these relationships.

This photo is from Ferrato’s 1991 book Living With the Enemy, which includes texts based on conversations with victims and perpetrators. Over the course of the project, she spent time in women’s shelters as well as riding in police cars and staying in people’s homes. Here, an eight-year-old boy, Diamond, shouts at his father as he is being arrested at their home in Minneapolis: “I hate you for hitting my mother.”

“I’d never seen a child stand up to his abusive father,” Ferrato later recalled. “That blew my mind. The mom hadn’t called the cops – the boy called the cops. He had just shown the police where his father had hidden the screwdriver.” GS

“The most masculine president in the American memory,” according to one recent biographer of Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt. He is pictured here on horseback when he was a lieutenant colonel in an army unit known as the Rough Riders.

His carefully crafted butch image was, on closer inspection, a jumble of contradictions. Raised in extreme wealth, he was fond of being photographed in suspiciously pristine working-class clothing. And, plagued by physical infirmities since childhood, he was sensitive to any hint of weakness. FB

Karen Knorr’s languid photograph, part of a series of 26 images she took in gentlemen’s clubs in Mayfair, London, captures how comfortable certain men feel luxuriating in hereditary privilege – “an archetypal image of aristocratic power”, in Knorr’s words.

Each photograph is paired with a satirical text written by Knorr, who was inspired by parliamentary speeches and books about the British empire. “I wanted to make work that used irony and parody to explore attitudes prevalent amongst the English establishment in the 1980s,” she said. FB

Russian president Vladimir Putin has a penchant for staging topless photo ops – always while partaking in a macho outdoor activity such as horse-riding or hunting. “It is easy to laugh at,” says Ruth Ben-Ghiat, author of a book on the political figure of the strongman from Mussolini (who also liked to pose shirtless) to the present. “But the use of masculinity as an authoritarian tool is deadly serious. Strongmen use their bodies to proclaim themselves the defenders of the nation, and yet they often pose as victims as well.” GS

“A vital element has been added to the well-planned and generously financed campaign to make Senator Jack Kennedy president of the United States,” reported the North American Newspaper Alliance in 1957: the Kennedys were expecting their first child, Caroline.

A year later, Life magazine staff photographer Ed Clark visited the couple’s family home in Georgetown. Clark later recalled that when asked if he could take a photo of the senator with the baby, “Jackie said no, that she was upstairs asleep. But Jack bounded up the stairs, and I followed.”

Jackie ended up asking for 75 copies of “that marvellous picture” to give to family and friends. And after JFK became president in 1961, the framed photo was hung in the Oval Office. His identity as a father of small children had become a key part of his public image as a novel breed of male politician: the youthful and vigorous leader of – to borrow his well-known phrase – “a new generation of Americans”. GS

This famous shot of a naked aeroplane gunner was captured by Horace Bristol, who was part of a group of photographers recruited to promote US naval aviation during the second world war. The aircraft had been sent to rescue a US marine pilot shot down while attacking Japanese forces at Rabaul Bay in the Pacific.

“One of our crew stripped off his clothes and jumped in … He couldn’t have swum very well wearing his boots and clothes,” Bristol later recalled. “As soon as we could, we took off.” Though the soldier has never been identified, his image quickly became a symbol of male valour and heroism in wartime. GS

“He was a dandy and a great eccentric,” remembered Leigh Bowery’s friend Donald Urquart in 2004, “in the tradition of Curricle Coates, Bunny Roger, Barbara Cartland, Edith Sitwell, and Quentin Crisp.” As a performance artist and “club kid” of the 1980s, Bowery’s intricately constructed – and sometimes controversial – outfits and costumes exploded traditional ideas of what a man could look like and what he could do.

In one famous performance, he birthed his friend and later wife, Nicola Bateman, out of a “vagina”, with an umbilical string of sausages trailing behind. Another was seen by painter Lucian Freud, who immediately asked Bowery to sit for him.
Bowery died in 1994 at 33 of an Aids-related illness. “I miss him,” friend and film-maker John Maybury said last year. “He was like a kinetic beacon, vibrating.” FB

Adrian Street went by many nicknames, including “the Exotic one”, “the Sadist in Sequins” and “the queen bitch of pro wrestling”. His catchphrase was, “Imagine what I could do to you,” finished with a suggestive, moaning, “Mmm …”

In the 70s, the Welsh former coalminer became famous for his taunting, butch, queer-coded persona. For a profile in a national tabloid in 1974, he arranged this striking photograph – much reprinted over the years – down his former pit with his miner father, who had disapproved of his career.

“That look, even though it’s outrageous, he would have said it was super-masculine,” says artist Jeremy Deller, who made a film with Street before his death in 2023. “It’s a challenge, isn’t it? You’re challenging other people as well as society, so you have to back it up.” FB

“It’s fake violence, a parody,” said William Klein of his 1954 photograph. “I asked the boy to point the gun at me and look tough. He did, and then we both laughed.” Klein saw the image as a “double self-portrait”; he himself was a mix of “the street kid trying to look tough, and the timid good little boy on the right”.
Klein saw it as playful, but the twisted face of the child retains a threatening power. FB

This photograph – actually a still from a newsreel – was first published in Life magazine in 1941, to illustrate the fall of France after the Nazi invasion. As the Germans advanced, the French government decided to send the historic regimental flags of its armies to safety in Africa. Before they were put on ships out of Marseille, a parade was held through the streets of the town. It was here that cameraman Marcel de Renzis caught footage of a French citizen called Jerôme Barzetti weeping as they passed by.

The image is often cited as a rare example of public tears from a man, as taboos around male emotional expression have softened in recent years. A 2016 study found that modern men cry in public more than twice as often as their fathers. Barzetti’s tears, however, fit into a long history of martial crying, with roots in Homeric epics. According to one count, men are depicted weeping in the Odyssey more than 30 times. FB

“The most wonderful specimen of man I have ever seen” is how a Harvard professor described Eugen Sandow upon taking his measurements in the 1890s. By then, the Prussian-born athlete was a global fitness star. Today, he is remembered as the father of modern bodybuilding, having organised the world’s first major “physique” competition in London in 1901. “He’s Arnold Schwarzenegger before Arnold Schwarzenegger,” says sports historian Conor Heffernan.

As Heffernan explains, Sandow’s “lean and muscular physique” – still aspirational now – had previously been more associated with farmers and sailors than the perfect man. Images such as this helped to reinforce what modern bodybuilders refer to as the “Grecian ideal”: a physical type based on statues from the ancient world. (Although appearances can be deceiving, as Heffernan points out: the dumbbell Sandow is lifting is probably empty.) GS

In Ralph Ellison’s novel Invisible Man, the unnamed narrator, an African-American man, hides out in a basement in New York, which he lights with 1,369 bulbs. “Before that I lived in the darkness into which I was chased, but now I see. I’ve illuminated the blackness of my invisibility – and vice versa,” he says, before telling the story of a life that had, until then, been defined by ideas projected on to him due to his race and gender.

Gordon Parks collaborated with Ellison on A Man Becomes Invisible, a photo essay published in Life magazine to promote the book. The striking images recreate key scenes from the narrative; this one shows the final passage, in which the protagonist (played by John Bates, an actor friend of Ellison’s) emerges from his underground retreat through a manhole – a reclamation of his place in society. GS

“You can show two men killing each other at three in the afternoon in any country in the world on public television,” said photographer Wolfgang Tillmans in an interview in 2022. “But you can’t show two men kissing each other.” Ghetto was a cult London venue of the noughties; at a club night there called The Cock, Tillmans captured a tender, passionate moment between two men. When the photograph was exhibited in Washington DC in 2007, one visitor reacted by slashing it with a key. It’s since become a symbol of solidarity and resistance: after the shooting at Orlando’s gay nightclub Pulse in 2016, many posted Tillmans’ photograph as a defiant act of protest. FB

In this photograph, David Bowie is captured pushing a pram with his baby, Zowie, alongside then wife Angie. Laura King, a historian of modern Britain, explains its significance: “In the decades after the second world war, there was a real movement towards what I call family-oriented masculinity. Men often weren’t doing anything like what women were doing in terms of looking after children, but fatherhood was very much aligned with masculinity.” Pushing a pram became a way to signal your identity as an involved family man.
Bowie – the famously gender-bending icon – wasn’t exactly a typical dad of his time. “I don’t feel very paternal,” he told an interviewer in 1976. GS
“Ballet is woman,” proclaimed the choreographer George Balanchine. The idea that it’s a dance form for girls persists today, especially in cultures where machismo is dominant.

Against this backdrop, Uruguayan photographer Santiago Barreiro documents the diversity of men’s ballet in Latin America. For Barreiro, his subjects offer an example of how traditional gender roles – which he has observed as deeply ingrained in Latin societies – can be deconstructed through art.

This portrait depicts Juan Pablo Rodríguez, a Colombian-born choreographer and principal soloist with the Ballet Nacional del Perú. Rodríguez told Barreiro that he sees freedom of expression as an act of resistance. GS

Hugh Hefner’s urbane, sex-obsessed vision of masculinity “became central to what it meant to be a modern man” in the 1960s, says historian Amber Batura. Hefner would spin Playboy magazine – first published in 1953 thanks to a loan from his mother, among others – into a global empire of clubs, staffed by women wearing distinctive “bunny” uniforms.

Like Ian Fleming’s James Bond, Hefner modelled a fantasy of masculinity “as gratifying, masterly play”, in the writer Esther Allen’s words, “in which women were seen as a sort of consumer product”. As Hefner put it himself in 1992: “Much of my life has been like an adolescent dream of an adult life.” FB

“Black men from the third world have not previously revealed either to their own peoples or to the west a certain shocking fact,” wrote the Nigerian photographer Rotimi Fani-Kayode in 1988. “They can desire each other.”

After training with the US photographer Robert Mapplethorpe in New York, Fani-Kayode moved to London and produced a stunning body of work from his Brixton home studio, before his death from Aids-related complications in 1989.

Mark Sealy, co-editor of a new book of Fani-Kayode’s work released this month, calls it a “radical transformation of Black male subjectivity”, made at a time when “the Black male subject was wrapped up in violent hostility via the press as muggers and bad guys”. Fani-Kayode’s work presented a subversive and playful vision of queer Black masculinity “at the height of Aids, in a very, very homophobic society”. FB

“The virtue of all-in wrestling is that it is the spectacle of excess,” wrote Roland Barthes; wrestlers are performers in a pantomime of rivalry and aggression. This photo depicts one of the most celebrated bouts of all time: the hotly anticipated face-off between Hulk Hogan and André the Giant (also known as Fezzik from The Princess Bride) at WrestleMania III in 1987. Pro wrestling had boomed in popularity and the stakes were raised by a much-publicised feud between the superstars, who were actually good friends. Hogan defeated a 520-pound (37 stone) André with his legendary “bodyslam that was heard around the world”. GS

Over the course of his 50-year career, Martin Parr repeatedly trained his camera on the football stadium – though, as a committed chronicler of ordinary British life, he was less interested in the players and more in the fans. In this photograph from 2012, we witness a moment of unbridled euphoria for the supporters of Wolverhampton Wanderers, who have just scored in a home match at Molineux stadium.

“[Football fandom is] a way of people accessing emotions. It’s very tribal,” Parr said when interviewed in 2022. “It’s an important aspect of creating your own identity. Especially for men; it’s a very welcome way of letting your emotions go.”

There is a dark side, too; recent statistics show that racist and homophobic abuse are on the rise at matches, and there was once again a spike in domestic violence reports during this year’s World Cup. GS

The actor Billy Porter is known for his audacious, gender-fluid red carpet fashion. “This look was interesting because it’s not drag,” he told Vogue of this gown, which he famously wore to the Oscars. “I’m not a drag queen. I’m a man in a dress.” Inspired by a Renoir painting, and made at short notice in over a week of 18-hour days by designer Christian Siriano, Porter’s tuxedo dress garnered huge attention, coming just a month after he wore a bright pink cape to the Globes, which in his words “changed everything for me”. The dress was later displayed in the Victoria and Albert Museum, and has its own (extensive) Wikipedia page. FB

“I decided to shoot pictures of men who made comments to me on the street,” Anderson wrote of her 1973 series titled Fully Automated Nikon (Object/Objection/Objectivity). The artist displayed the images with white strips over catcallers’ eyes, granting them anonymity while also symbolically taking away their ability to objectify her. GS

“Growing up in Morocco, we were definitely not scared of colour,” Moroccan-British photographer Hassan Hajjaj has said. His playful portraits blend north African textiles with markers of global consumerism; his sitters often wear clothes designed by him.

This image was part of Hajjaj’s recent My London Rockstars series featuring portraits of artists in the capital, including Our Motherland Collective, a skateboarding crew that has transformed into an arts group.

“The people in the pictures come from all different parts of the world, and when you start putting them next to each other, it becomes a positive image,” Hajjaj has said of his work that explores identity and multiculturalism. If his photos make a young person think, “Oh I can be that person,” or, “I can be the person taking that picture,” he says, “that’s the greatest feeling you can have as an artist”. FB

“I had a personal motivation to establish an Indian gay presence in art history,” says the artist and photographer Sunil Gupta, who was born in New Delhi in 1953; he later settled in London in the 1970s. “It was hard for me to be postmodern because I had no references. So I decided to make the references.” He wanted to “visualise” the experience of gay men in Delhi.

Initially, “nobody wanted to be in the picture” – homosexuality in India wasn’t decriminalised until 2018. Eventually, Gupta was introduced to a network of gay men who agreed to model for the project Exiles (1986–87). The accompanying texts came from interviews he’d conducted at cruising sites around the city. GS

This year marks the 40th anniversary of one of the bestselling posters of all time: a photograph of a hunky man cradling a baby. Paul Rodriguez, art director of the poster retailer Athena, conceived the idea and recruited photographer Spencer Rowell. The image tapped into the archetype of masculinity that emerged in western culture in the 1980s: the New Man, who rejected sexist ideas around domesticity.
The model is Adam Perry, who later claimed to have leveraged the poster’s fame to sleep with more than 3,000 women – not quite a New Man, after all. GS

“Ever since that picture of a pregnant man was sprung on an astonished nation,” wrote a Daily Mirror columnist in 1970, “we men haven’t been able to stop wondering what would happen if we really did become pregnant.”
The public information poster, dreamed up by ad company Cramer Saatchi, caused a storm when it was released, aimed at increasing the “sexual responsibility of the male”.
Photographer Alan Brooking, now 98, remembers an extended search for the perfect model – a man in possession of “the subtle kind of embarrassment that one might expect in that situation”. FB

“It is like a resistance movement for peace,” journalist and photographer Justin Makangara says of the sapeurs. “They are fighting with clothes.” The sapeurs of the twin Congolese capitals of Brazzaville and Kinshasa have become famous for their style.

Until recently, many regarded the sapeurs as “foolish, hooligans, idiot people” for spending so much money on flashy clothes. Recently, however, Makangara has seen a change in their public perception. Most sapeurs – like Celestin Moundounga, the 48-year-old technician here – hold down respectable jobs and are “responsible to the needs of their families”. And as the civil war grinds on in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, their way of life suggests that “even in conflict, we can try to be in joy”. FB

It was the 1998 World Cup in France, a peak moment for British lad culture. Then David Beckham was photographed wearing a Jean Paul Gaultier wrap. The Sun ran the photo alongside the headline “Beckham has got his Posh frock on”.

The footballer has stood by the look. “Sarongs are great,” he said in 2014. “I would still wear it now.” Today his bold outfit is recognised for cementing Beckham’s role as the poster boy for a new type of heterosexual male ideal: the fashion-forward metrosexual of the 2000s. GS

Thomas Dworzak was on a photographic assignment covering the fall of the Taliban when he stumbled on a set of highly stylised studio portraits of soldiers of the former regime in a photo shop. The fighters had probably died before they could pick them up.

“I was very surprised, of course,” he says. The Taliban had famously banned all photography of living beings. He bought the prints – the beginning of a collection eventually published in the 2003 photobook Taliban.

In the secretly commissioned portraits, the fighters pose against pastel-coloured and scenic backdrops and hold props such as flowers and guns. Here, two men clasp hands. The unmistakably “camp aesthetic”, Dworzak explains, was “not specific to the Taliban” – such images can be found across the region. But they also couldn’t be further from what we expect a militant soldier to look like. GS

The sight of a man with a baby strapped to him was too much for Piers Morgan in 2018, who posted this picture with the hashtag #emasculatedBond. Men responded in their thousands with photographs of themselves similarly “emasculated” – including wrestling star Adam Copeland holding his child while dressed as Elsa from Frozen. “Any man who wastes time quantifying masculinity,” tweeted actor Chris Evans at the time, “is terrified on the inside.” FB

The clashes that arise between differing factions of masculinity could be summed up by this photograph of a brawl between mods and rockers in Brighton in 1964. That summer, long-standing tensions between the competing youth subcultures erupted in a series of confrontations during bank holiday weekends in seaside towns across the south of England.

It’s now thought that the extent of the fighting was overplayed at the time – a moral panic stirred up by the establishment about the youth of the day. But the rivalry was real enough. The rockers, who rode high-speed customised motorcycles known as “cafe racers”, mockingly compared the Italian scooters of the “sissy” mods to their “mums’ hairdryers”. As one mod put it to a BBC interviewer at the time: “You can’t just stand and let a load of kids take the mick out of you, can you?” GS

Hells Angels – the motorcycle gang founded in California – haunted the US psyche in the 1960s. They modelled a rebellious, hyper-masculine image, but were also – for the time – provocatively homoerotic, frequently giving each other “a sloppy wet kiss”, in writer Hunter S Thompson’s words. “It blows their minds,” said one Hells Angel of the effect on “squares” – “especially the tongue bit”. FB

An interest in “performing masculinity” – which she first explored in San Francisco’s butch lesbian community in the 1990s – eventually led photographer Catherine Opie to high school football. Her portraits of star players, taken just after practice, show “adolescent boys beginning to form and perform for the first time an image-ideal of manhood”, in the words of one critic.

Opie also linked the series to the various wars that the US was involved in at the time. “So many young men were having to make very interesting choices between sports scholarships and becoming a soldier,” she has said. “It was actually very emotional.” FB

Historically, pubs and other drinking places were considered a “masculine republic”, somewhere for the menfolk to gather while their wives stayed at home. The notion of the watering hole as an almost exclusively male space – with notable exceptions granted to barmaids, landladies and loose women – is summed up in this image of an establishment in the working-class Gorbals district of Glasgow in 1968.

German-born Schadeberg, best-known for his portraits of life in South Africa under apartheid, had been sent to the Gorbals to document an area in rapid transition: the old tenements were being pulled down and replaced by modernist housing. GS
“I had let down the fans, my team-mates, the manager, everybody,” remembered Paul Gascoigne in 2020. “I cried because I thought it was the end of my career.”

In 1990, 23-year-old Gazza had already captured the hearts of the public for his skill in the World Cup. When he burst into tears after receiving a yellow card for tackling a West German player, the nation erupted with a mixture of sympathy and, eventually, mockery. Today, public male tears are a relatively uncontroversial part of major sports tournaments, with everyone from Tiger Woods to Roger Federer having a good sob. FB

items.title: This week we revealed the Stirling Prize winner
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen, we reported on the Lion Green Road housing scheme in Croydon winning the Stirling Prize.
Designed by local studio Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, the project was named the UK's best new building at a ceremony in London.
Commissioned by Croydon Council, the development contains 157 homes spread across five blocks that are connected by a series of shared green spaces.
Following the win, we discussed the project and its place within the wider Stirling Prize winners on our podcast, Dezeen Weekly.
This week also saw car brand Tesla unveil its flying Roadster at an event in Texas, where the vehicle flipped off a ramp and briefly flew.
The demonstration used compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claimed will enable it to make the world's quickest production car.
In design news, technology brand Apple unveiled HomeView, a device that consolidates the functions of its app products and home-management software into one device.
The seven-inch screen, which can also stand on a base with an integrated speaker, was designed to function as a centralised location for home controls.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a rammed-earth visitor centre for the Twelve Apostles in Australia, a monolithic concrete home in India and a cricket pavilion in Dulwich.

items.title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
paragraphs: Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.

In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.

Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.

“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”

After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”

If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.

Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.

“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.

“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”

The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.

Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.

Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.

“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”

She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”

The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.

In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.

“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.

In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.

Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.

As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.

Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”

The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.

“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

items.title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
paragraphs: Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth", after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed the expansion.
Speaking from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings in Bangkok, Healey said that airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades.
His predecessor Rachel Reeves had put Heathrow expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain is open for business.
But Burnham has been more sceptical about the case, telling the BBC it was "a matter for London and Londoners".
It follows a warning earlier this week from Heathrow's chief executive, who said that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".
Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades, with the project facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners.
Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".
Asked about the project last month, Burnham suggested it is an argument for London to decide.
"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.
"The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department. We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow," Healey told reporters.
The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Thomas Woldbye, the airport's chief executive, said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.
He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".
"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.
The project, which has an estimated price tag of £33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

items.title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
paragraphs: A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.
Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.
They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April, 2024.
Their bodies were found days later in a cliff-top well with gunshot wounds to the heads.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.
Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.
The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.
Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.
The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.
Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.
He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for all sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

items.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.

In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.

It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.
The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The law took aim at Russian's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.

Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.
The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.

The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".
Last week, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow.
US allies criticised the move, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

items.title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
paragraphs: Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off where the rainforest's future is a key issue.

Left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

On 25 October, Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

Satellite data shows that in the year up to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.
The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.
Why the Amazon rainforest is so important | What in the World podcast
Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.
During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, AFP news agency reported, citing official data.

Lula reversed Jair Bolsonaro's policies and saw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.
Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.

But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.
Brazil's Environment Minister, Joao Paulo Capobianco, described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".
It is a "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
It shows that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

items.title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
paragraphs: When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.
At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.
In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.

Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.
It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.

This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.

The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.

Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".

It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.

But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

items.title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
paragraphs: US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight travelling to New York.

A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting ​multiple sclerosis (MS), the statement read.
The statement says that Blair, 54, has a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".
The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board.

In a statement to the BBC, Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York "has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline". They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.

The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement notes that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".

It adds that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.
The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary, and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying, or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.
She described Blair's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and noted that she still lives with pain daily.

"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," the statement said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported, and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."

The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.
The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail.
With additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder.

items.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
paragraphs: ByChris Fawkes, Sarah Keith-Lucas, Matt Taylor
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.
Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.
This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.
However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El Niño strengthens in the Pacific.

As autumn sets in and the nights get longer temperatures around polar regions start to fall. This causes a greater contrast with the warmer tropics which can fire up a more potent jet stream - the fast moving, narrow band of fast winds high in the atmosphere.
The jet stream is largely responsible for developing and delivering our stormier pressure systems.
Typically in autumn the jet stream would be a regular visitor to the skies above the UK, steering wet and windy weather towards us.

However, so far this season it has often been sitting to the north or north-west of the UK. This has meant south or south-westerly winds bringing warmer than normal conditions and high pressure having more of an influence leading to reduced rainfall for many.
So far this autumn the jet stream has been largely to the north-west of the UK, steering stormy low pressure systems away
These weather patterns have therefore meant only occasional bouts of stronger winds across the north-west of the UK, with little disruption.
The heaviest of the rain has also been focused across Scotland and Northern Ireland while parts of England and Wales have continued to be much drier than normal.
Parts of Herefordshire for instance have only received a tenth of the rainfall they would normally have seen by mid-October so far this month.

Some of the biggest impacts of the dry weather have been across the southern England where exceptionally low reservoir levels have prompted the Environment Agency to declare "severe drought" in some areas.
A change in the position of that jet stream and its strength is expected through the coming week.
This will allow deeper low pressure systems to affect more parts of the UK marking a shift to a more widespread wetter and windier weather.
Forecasts will need to be monitored closely as there is potential later in the week that we could see our first spell of widely disruptive weather this season.
There are also longer term signals for increased rainfall and storminess later in autumn and early winter in the UK.

The Met Office's current three month outlook covering October, November and December forecasts a double the normal chance of wetter weather and 1.3 times the normal chance of windier weather which is consistent with the type of patterns seen with previous El Niño events.
Storms are most often named when potentially damaging winds are forecast, but can also be named for flooding rain or disruptive snow.
They were first named to help bring public attention to episodes of severe weather, to help people prepare to avoid the worst impacts by planning ahead.
In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location.
The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group which started naming storms in 2015.
Weather systems are named by the the UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann and Netherland's KNMI based on expected weather impacts as well as how likely those are.
The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.
It is not unusual to still be awaiting the arrival of the first storm at this time of year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

items.title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
paragraphs: Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.
Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister, Mathias Cormann, is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.
“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.
“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”
Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities.
He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.
But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

items.title: Evacuation orders as fast-moving California wildfire burns homes
paragraphs: Evacuation orders in California are in effect due to a rapidly growing wildfire that has already burned six homes in the southern Los Angeles area.
The Norte Fire erupted on Friday in Orange County and quickly grew to 465 acres by the evening. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze.
Officials say the fierce Santa Ana winds will blow until Saturday, bringing further risk of more conflagrations.

The US National Weather Service (NWS) has issued a red flag warning for several California counties due to strong, gusty winds combined with low humidity and dry vegetation that create critical wildfire spread conditions.
The Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

In an update on Friday evening, Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said that six homes had either been damaged or destroyed by the Norte Fire, and one firefighter had been injured from heat exhaustion.
"We continue to engage in the firefight, and have additional resources coming," he said.
Footage posted online showed blazes tearing through homes in the communities of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.
The Bryson Fire, burning in the affluent coastal city of Malibu in Los Angeles county, has also sparked evacuation orders throughout the Santa Monica mountains and has grown to 147 acres.
More than 400 firefighters have been fighting the blaze.

items.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
paragraphs: Leigh-Anne offered to make Miranda's "dreams come true" by teaching her a Little Mix dance move
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.
The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.
Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.
The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.
Sleepy time at The Celebrity Traitors castle
If one of the faithful succumbs to the traitors' soporific tactics and yawns as well, they will be put to sleep for good.
We must wait until next Thursday to find out who, if anyone, is murdered in plain sight. That was what passed as a nail-biting cliffhanger this week.
There was, thankfully, some more animated action elsewhere in Friday's episode.
After Thursday saw King Kenny recruited by the traitors - that episode ending with his deliciously evil laugh - the YouTuber and former aspiring boxer brought fresh and fiendish energy to the turret.
"This threesome's going to be different," mama traitor Maya Jama predicted. "There's a new vibrance."
James Acaster, her reluctant fellow traitor, was also happy with their choice of ally.
"As predicted, Kenny's taken to this like a duck to water," the comedian said, visibly relieved. "He's the opposite of me. So relaxed. He's a natural born traitor."
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked
Kenny is relishing the role, barely able to disguise his pleasure as Miranda Hart confided to him over breakfast that "you're my main faithful".
The self-declared modern-day Miss Marple warned Kenny to be on the lookout for anyone acting differently, reasoning that "if you're suddenly a traitor, you're going to be a bit on high alert".
In the show's diary room, he said: "The first taste of being on the other side - it does feel good, because you have the power.
"I'm good at staying calm because as a boxer you have to have a poker face. You can't let the other people know that you're intimidated."
