items.title: Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says
paragraphs: Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.

items.title: UN special rapporteur warns North Korea’s human rights situation has worsened
paragraphs: United Nations Special Rapporteur Elizabeth Salmón has issued a stark warning regarding the worsening human rights situation in North Korea, highlighting an alarming expansion in the scope and application of the death penalty as a tool for social, political, and ideological control.

In an interview with VOA, Salmón discussed her newly submitted report to the U.N. General Assembly, which focuses on the right-to-life violations occurring in North Korea, including the expansive use of the death penalty, preventable deaths in state custody, and the lack of protection for North Korean military personnel deployed to fight Ukraine alongside Russian troops.

“It addresses arbitrary deprivation of life—including the death penalty and deaths in custody—as well as the state’s obligation to protect the lives of military personnel,” she told VOA. “This report is scheduled to be submitted to the Third Committee of the U.N. General Assembly,” she added. Special rapporteurs traditionally present their reports during the committee sessions held in New York from October through November.
In her annual report to the UN General Assembly, Salmón documented that North Korea has expanded capital punishment far beyond intentional murder to include ‘non-violent and sociopolitical offenses’.

New additions and amendments recently approved to the North Korean Constitution by the Supreme People’s Assembly, have raised the number of capital crimes under the Criminal Law from 8 to 16, while seven standalone statutes now authorize the death penalty. Among these are laws penalizing ‘the consumption and distribution of foreign media, speaking or writing in South Korean-style speech, drug-related offenses, and non-compliance with emergency epidemic or disaster regulations."

"Information received by the special rapporteur indicates that the enjoyment of the right to life continues to face grave challenges in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea," Salmón stated in her report, referring to North Korea by its formal name. She emphasized that executions carried out for offenses failing to meet the international threshold of "most serious crimes"—reserved strictly for intentional killing—constitute “arbitrary deprivation of life and may amount to crimes against humanity.”

The report further highlighted severe gender dimensions and human rights violations against women, noting cases where she tracked 11 women who defected to China, were forcibly repatriated, and subsequently faced severe penalties—with two reportedly executed and the rest imprisoned.
Salmón reiterated that victims of human trafficking “must not be criminalized or punished.”

“Even if these women are viewed as undocumented migrants, we must respect our human rights obligations regarding their safety and survival,” she told VOA. “I wanted to make the international community aware that the situation for North Korean women—especially those sentenced to death—is extremely dire.”

She also raised grave concerns over deaths in custody caused by torture, overwork, and starvation, as well as the deployment of roughly 14,000 North Korean troops to the armed conflict between Russia and Ukraine, where over 2,000 soldiers have reportedly been killed and young adolescents face intense pressure to sacrifice their lives.

“In my latest report, I emphasized that the lives of these soldiers must be protected and that they must be provided with the necessary information, training, and equipment,” she said in her VOA interview. “There is also some very concerning news: young high school students are beginning to believe that they must die for their country. This is highly abnormal. Children must be protected.”

Addressing her ongoing monitoring work, Salmón told VOA hat there is currently insufficient information regarding the safety, protection, and human rights conditions of the two North Korean prisoners of war recently transferred from Ukraine to South Korea.She underscored the critical need to protect their privacy and ensure they are not exposed to public curiosity, warning that public exposure could endanger their families remaining in North Korea. Furthermore, she stressed the absolute applicability of the principle of non-refoulement to ensure individuals are not sent to places where they face torture or abuse.

She also emphasized that human rights issues must remain a core component of any future diplomatic engagement or summits—such as potential talks between the United States and North Korea—stressing that viewing human rights as an obstacle to peace has consistently proven ineffective.

items.title: NGO tells VOA millions of Ukrainian children affected by deportation, occupation and displacement abroad since start of Russia war
paragraphs: Ukraine has seen its child population decline by millions since Moscow launched its war on Ukraine in 2014, due to deportation, occupation, displacement abroad and direct war casualties, Mykola Kuleba, founder and head of Save Ukraine, told VOA.
Kuleba's NGO, Save Ukraine, rescues children from Russia and Russian-controlled territories.

Russia’s full-scale invasion that began in 2022 triggered the largest displacement crisis in Europe since World War II. Although many Ukrainians have returned home, more than five million remain abroad, according to UNHCR, most of them in Europe, many of them children.
An estimated 1.5 million Ukrainian children remain in territories under Russian control.

According to Ukraine`s Children of War portal, as of October 16, 2026, Ukrainian authorities have recorded 20,651 children as deported or forcibly displaced and 2,689 as returned. These figures reflect documented cases, not necessarily the full number of children affected. Also, as of mid-October, 762 children have been killed and 2,952 injured in the war, while 2,362 remain missing, according to Ukrainian authorities.

Ukrainian children under Russian control are subjected to indoctrination and militarization aimed at molding them into future Russian soldiers, Kuleba says, which includes those forcibly transferred to Russia.
Russian officials claim that Russia is not stealing Ukrainian children but saving them.

However, Article 78 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions sets strict conditions for evacuating children to a foreign country during an armed conflict. Such evacuations must be temporary and justified by compelling reasons related to the children’s safety, health or medical needs, and require the written consent of their parents, legal guardians or other persons responsible for their care. The article also requires the authorities arranging the evacuation and where appropriate, the receiving country’s authorities, to create an individual record for each child and send it to the International Committee of the Red Cross to help facilitate the child’s return to their family and country.

In March, the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concluded that Russian authorities committed “the crimes against humanity of deportation and forcible transfer, as well as of enforced disappearance of children.”

The commission found that the actions were a part of a policy conceived at the highest level and systematically executed. Only 20 percent of the children in the cases of forcible transfer investigated by the commission have been returned.

Through missions whose operational details it keeps confidential, Save Ukraine says it has rescued more than 1,800 children, according to the organization’s website. Its work forms a part of a broader effort coordinated by Ukraine president’s initiative Bring Kids Back UA, which also includes the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children with 52 members – countries and international organizations – five other Ukrainian NGOs, and the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights.
The efforts of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump have also helped to reunite 34 children with their families, according to an August 17 White House statement.

“When Moscow completely denies the abductions and refuses to return the children, the efforts of the first lady of the United States are very helpful in bringing these children home,” Kuleba told VOA in a recent interview.
He said that every passing day makes the return of children more difficult.

“Russian propaganda shapes the information environment in which people live and often turns families and children into adherents of the Russian Empire. They begin to fear Ukraine and believe that there are supposedly Nazis in Ukraine, and that the West has joined forces with the Nazis to destroy Russia,” he said.
Children are also subjected to military training intended to prepare them for future combat, Kuleba said.

A 2025 investigation by Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, identified at least 210 facilities in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territory to which children from Ukraine had been taken. The researchers found evidence of militarization in at least 18 percent of these facilities.

“Children who return tell us that Russian military personnel come to their schools to teach them how to handle weapons and provide tactical medical training," the children's activist said. "Starting at around age 14, many are taken to the military camps in Russia, where three-week programs teach them how to throw grenades and blow up tanks. One 15-year-old girl who was taken to one of these camps showed me how to set up a tripwire with a grenade. She also described how other children practiced parachuting. They are genuinely being prepared for combat.”

Some children that Save Ukraine was trying to bring back have been sent to the frontlines and even died, Kuleba told VOA. He warned that Russia`s policies pose a threat beyond Ukraine because children are being raised to hate not only Ukraine but also the United States and other Western countries.
After children return, Save Ukraine helps them reintegrate into Ukrainian society. The organization operates rehabilitation centers across Ukraine, with a reported capacity of 800 beds.

items.title: Iraq's cabinet completion raises Iranian influence concerns, but offers PM chance to curb militias
paragraphs: The completion of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's Cabinet has renewed concerns about the continued influence of Iran-backed Shiite groups in Baghdad, particularly following the appointment of a senior militia leader and U.S.-designated terrorist as deputy prime minister. But some political observers say the appointments could offer al-Zaidi an opportunity to consolidate his authority and gradually bring armed factions under government control.

The debate reflects competing assessments of whether accommodating Iran-aligned political forces will further entrench their influence in Iraq's government or provide al-Zaidi with the political leverage needed to reduce their power.

Iraq's parliament on Thursday approved more than a dozen Cabinet appointments, completing the formation of al-Zaidi's government five months after it took office. Several key positions had remained vacant amid political disputes and concerns about Iranian influence.

Lawmakers approved Nayef al-Shammari as defense minister and Yasir al-Maliki as interior minister. They also appointed Laith al-Khazali, a senior leader of the Iran-backed Shiite militia Asaib Ahl al-Haq, as a deputy prime minister.

The United States designated Asaib Ahl al-Haq a foreign terrorist organization in 2020 and named al-Khazali and his brother, Qais, as specially designated global terrorists. Washington has accused the group of carrying out attacks against American and coalition forces.

The appointment has raised concerns, though, that Iran-backed armed groups continue to wield considerable influence over Iraq's political institutions, despite efforts to strengthen the authority of the central government.

Republican Rep. Joe Wilson condemned al-Khazali's appointment on social media platform X, describing him as a “designated terrorist and Iranian puppet” and calling for an end to Tehran's influence in Iraq.

“He is no better than ISIS, maybe even worse,” Wilson said of al-Khazali, using an acronym for the Islamic State terror group. “It is outrageous but sadly not shocking that he has been appointed deputy PM of Iraq.”

Despite those concerns, the United States has reaffirmed its support for Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi, emphasizing the importance of Iraqi sovereignty and curbing the influence of Iran-backed armed groups.

“As President Trump made clear when he hosted Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s historic July 14 visit, the United States strongly supports his vision to ensure a brighter future for all Iraqis,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA in a statement.
The spokesperson said Washington's goal remains a sovereign and secure Iraq capable of preventing attacks from its territory and maintaining strong relations with the U.S.

“Iran is an untrustworthy actor with a long history of using Iraqi militias to steal resources from the Iraqi people and threaten Iraq’s sovereignty,” the spokesperson said, emphasizing that U.S. efforts to promote regional stability focus on strengthening national sovereignty and economic prosperity.
Pragmatic approach to Iran-backed groups?

Former U.S. diplomat Joey Hood says the Trump administration may be willing to give al-Zaidi greater flexibility in dealing with Iran-backed militias, rather than opposing political arrangements that bring some of their leaders into government.

Hood told VOA that Trump and his special envoy to Iraq, Tom Barrack, appeared to favor an approach centered on economic partnerships rather than military operations or direct intervention in Baghdad's political decisions.
“They do not appear to be interested in micromanaging how the prime minister gains primacy over the Iranian-backed militias, unlike some previous U.S. administrations,” Hood told VOA.
He said Washington could adopt a wait-and-see approach, allowing al-Zaidi to use figures such as al-Khazali to bring less cooperative armed factions under control.
“If al-Zaidi succeeds in using al-Khazali and others to squeeze the uncooperative groups, he will have found an Iraqi solution to this problem,” the former U.S. diplomat said.

Hood said such an approach would place greater responsibility on al-Zaidi to demonstrate that political accommodation can translate into stronger government authority over armed groups, rather than allowing those groups to consolidate their influence from within the state.

The former ambassador to Tunisia cautioned that the ultimate test of al-Zaidi's strategy would be whether Iran-backed groups could continue exploiting Iraqis, influencing political decisions and launching attacks against Iraqi citizens and neighboring countries.
Political compromises raise spending concerns

Following the parliamentary vote to approve his cabinet, al-Zaidi pledged swift action to implement his government's priorities, promising continued efforts to deliver on commitments to the Iraqi people.

Beyond the question of Iranian influence, the cabinet expansion has also prompted criticism that the new Iraqi prime minister is creating government positions to accommodate competing political forces at the expense of Iraq's public finances.
Before Thursday's parliamentary session, a number of lawmakers protested and boycotted the proceedings, opposing the creation of several deputy prime ministerial positions and new ministries.
The lawmakers argued that the additional posts reflected the distribution of government positions according to political party quotas, at a time when Iraq should instead be reducing public spending.
Ghalib Aldaamy, a Baghdad-based academic and political researcher, told VOA that many Iraqis opposed the creation of new ministries and senior government positions.

Instead, he said, there had been expectations that the government would merge some ministries and abolish other institutions to streamline government bureaucracy and reduce pressure on the national budget.

items.title: X suspends 13,000 accounts linked to China, Russia and Iran
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Social media platform X says it has suspended more than 13,000 accounts involved in suspected foreign influence operations linked to China, Russia and Iran that targeted U.S. political discourse ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

In a statement posted on October 14, the platform said the networks used inauthentic accounts to post and amplify political content targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.

X said its safety team uses a variety of detection methods to identify and address activity that violates the platform's rules, building on security measures that operate around the clock throughout the year.

“Free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and we are proud that X is the global town square where these debates happen,” the social media platform said. “Our job is to keep that conversation authentic, open, and safe.”
X said its authenticity policy plays a key role in efforts to combat spam networks and influence operations that use coordinated inauthentic behavior to undermine the integrity of the platform.
The company did not publicly provide evidence supporting its findings or specifying how many of the suspended accounts were linked to each country.

X also highlighted what it calls its civic integrity policy, which addresses misleading content that could affect participation in elections or other civic processes. The policy covers information that could confuse voters about how, when or where to participate, as well as content intended to discourage participation.

The platform said users can report potentially misleading content under the “Civic Integrity” category in its in-app reporting system. The company said its efforts to address election-related violations would continue through Election Day and beyond.
X is not the only platform to raise concerns about alleged Chinese influence operations.

On June 10, OpenAI said it had disrupted two online influence operations linked to China. The operations used ChatGPT to generate social media posts, comments and images in an apparent effort to shape U.S. debates over artificial intelligence, data centers, tariffs and technology policy.

OpenAI said in its report that the accounts used its models to support covert influence operations while concealing their origins and intentions. However, the company said the operations appeared to have limited impact, with no evidence that the content generated substantial authentic engagement or spread widely beyond the accounts involved.
President Donald Trump also has accused China of attempting to interfere in U.S. elections.

In a prime-time address in July, Trump warned that U.S. election infrastructure was vulnerable to foreign attacks, and he specifically accused China of trying to interfere in the 2020 presidential election. He did not provide evidence, though, that the election had been disrupted or that votes had been incorrectly counted.
Despite his warnings, the president did not publicly raise the issue of alleged Chinese election interference during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington last month.

items.title: Afghan women farmers call for international support
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
Women farmers in Afghanistan are calling on the international community for support.

Mumtaz Yousufzai, founder of the Union of Female Farmers in Afghanistan, told VOA that agriculture is the largest sector employing women, with 80 percent of women in rural areas working in the sector.
“In rural Afghanistan, women farmers are working alongside men in the fields, but these women need support,” she added.

On the International Day of Rural Women, observed annually on Oct. 15 to recognize the contributions of rural women worldwide, the United Nations called for women farmers’ “unpaid care work” to be “recognized, reduced, and redistributed.”
Despite restrictions on women in Afghanistan, Yousufzai said that agriculture remains one of the few sectors in which women continue to play a significant role.

Under the Taliban in Afghanistan, women are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, attending secondary schools and universities and traveling a long distance without a close male relative.
However, women are allowed to work in private businesses and work in rural farms and agriculture production.
About 74 percent of Afghanistan’s population live in rural areas, where agriculture is the main source of earning a livelihood.
According to a 2024 World Bank report, agriculture accounts for roughly 34 percent of Afghanistan’s GDP. This includes cultivation of crops and livestock production, forestry, and fishing.

But experts say Afghanistan has been facing “a severe and interconnected” climate and humanitarian crisis. It is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries and is facing worsening acute food insecurity and malnutrition.
Raqiba, who goes by her first name, is a gardener in the De Sabz area of Kabul province.
She told VOA that farmers and gardeners face numerous challenges, including a shortage of irrigation water, limited markets for their products, and a lack of financial support.
“We call on the international community to help rural Afghan women farmers. We need help and support,” said Raqiba.

items.title: UN says Taliban arrest at least 443 for alleged violations of strict rules, including hijab, prayer, music
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

The United Nations says the Taliban have arrested at least 443 people primarily for alleged violations of their strict hijab rules, trimming beards, cutting hair, failure to attend congregational prayers at the mosque or listening to music.

A new United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) report released Thursday, covering a period of three months from July 1 to Sept. 30, also documented 97 incidents of ill-treatment of Afghan women and men by the Taliban’s Ministry of Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice.

The Taliban’s law on the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, known as the “morality law,” imposes punishments on violations of the Afghan Islamist group's strict interpretation of Islam, including enforcing dress codes and certain hairstyles.
“The law gives the Taliban’s morality inspectors extensive power to arbitrarily detain and punish individuals, including physically,” said the U.N. Human Rights Commission in a statement in 2024.
Last week, UNAMA said that it verified the arrest or detention of 52 women and girls for several hours in Herat and Kabul, from July to September, over violations of the Taliban’s dress code.
“Women were detained for not wearing a chador, having visible hair, wearing colorful scarves or makeup, or being in public without a mahram,” the statement noted.
After returning to power in 2021, the Taliban imposed repressive restrictions on women, including requiring women to cover their bodies from head to toe in loose clothing.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees imposing restrictions on women and girls.

These decrees are “institutionalizing discrimination and stripping them [women and girls] of their fundamental rights – with profound consequences for their lives and their communities,” said a new U.N. Women report, calling the women’s situation in the country, “the world’s most severe women’s rights crisis.”

In a virtual hearing on September 23, Asif Mahmood, chair of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, said the Taliban continue their “repressive crackdown against those who violated or are perceived to have violated the group’s narrow interpretations of Sunni Islam.”
Mahmood noted that Afghan women and girls continue to bear the brunt of the Taliban’s religious decrees.

Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have imposed restrictions on women and girls in Afghanistan, including barring them from secondary and university education, long-distance travel without a male relative, and access to public spaces.

items.title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
paragraphs: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.

But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.

Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.
The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).
However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.

Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.

These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.

The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.

The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.

The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.

It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.

The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country.

Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.

The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.
Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible.
“However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”

items.title: 'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation
paragraphs: An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him.

The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts.
The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years".
The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations.

The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026.
As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published.

At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals".
The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case.

Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known.

A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual.

The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

items.title: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
paragraphs: For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.

Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still feels underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.

But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.

Drance says the big reason was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”
The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.

The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.

She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.

Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”

Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.

Drance says setup and ease of use were a big focus. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.

Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”

The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.

Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.
“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”

According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.

The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.
At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.

Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.

However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.

As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.
With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

items.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
paragraphs: Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."
Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) held a press conference with parents in September around the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.
Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoyment
Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.
Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media ban
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.
Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feeds

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

items.title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
paragraphs: No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.

They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.

Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.

According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.

Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.

China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.

While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.

Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

items.title: Katie Zacharia is 'transitioning out' as press secretary, White House says
paragraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump is followed by White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia (L) as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on October 13, 2026 in Washington, DC. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption

Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman who officially started Monday and is out by Friday.

Zacharia's first briefing was Tuesday morning where she faced scrutiny both over her performance – during which she delivered a lengthy and halting opening statement read from notes and called on only three reporters – and her legal credentials.
President Trump on Friday cast doubt on the future of Zacharia, saying he had a discussion with her just before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia.

"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'," he told reporters. "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily. And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want."
He said he was leaving the decision up to her but advised her "you should reconsider" serving in the position.

The 41-year-old graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law and self-described attorney had stepped in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.
Much of the scrutiny of Zacharia focused on her credentials as an attorney. While standing with Trump, she was asked by reporters where she passed the bar exam.

"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered, an apparent reference to what she has described on her LinkedIn page as a period of time from 2011 through 2013 spent working for a prominent Beijing-based law firm called Zhon Lun.

NPR asked the White House to clarify whether Zacharia is a licensed attorney in the U.S. In a statement provided to NPR, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.

items.title: Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
paragraphs: For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images hide caption

For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. The doctor's group, known as ACOG, recommends hormone replacement therapy alongside certain antidepressants, nonhormonal medicines, and other treatments to address symptoms like hot flashes, insomnia and mood swings.

"What's changing is the breadth of options that we now have … And the benefit of that is that we are better equipped to be able to take an individualized approach for patients," said Catherine Cansino, MD, MPH, an obstetrician/gynecologist, chair of ACOG's Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines and co-author of the new guidance.
The guidance, released Thursday, focuses on specific menopausal symptoms and underscores that the safety of hormone replacement therapy is now "well-established," Cansino said.
In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative suggested that hormone replacement therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.

However, as researchers revisited that data years later, they noticed certain limitations, (including that a majority of participants were 60 years or older) making it difficult to generalize the findings to younger women experiencing menopause or perimenopause.
With more and better quality studies, physicians are able to review the evidence and make better-informed recommendations, Cansino said.

"Hormone therapy is probably the best option for symptomatic, newly menopausal women within 10 years of the final menstrual period or before the age of 60," said Robert Kauffman, MD, MSCP, a co-author of the guidelines, during a press briefing on Thursday.

In addition to hormone replacement therapy, the guidelines highlight new nonhormonal options for treating menopausal symptoms, including the drug fezolinetant, brand name Veozah, which the Food and Drug Administration approved to treat hot flashes in 2023 and elinzanetant, brand name Lynkuet, which was approved in 2025.
"What's so exciting about these treatment options is they were specifically studied based on the understanding that we have of the physiology of thermoregulation and sleep," Cansino said.
The medications work by blocking certain chemical messengers in the part of the brain that regulates body temperature and manages sleep/wake cycles, according to the guidance.

About 2 million women begin menopause each year. The average age of a woman experiencing menopause is 49.9 years, according to the guidelines. However, symptoms of menopause can begin years before a woman's final menstrual period.

The new recommendations support the use of systemic hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, with a combination of estrogen and progestogen in women with a uterus who have no contraindications to hormones.

Reasons to avoid hormone therapy include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, and current or past histories of certain gynecologic cancers, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or a known or suspected pregnancy.

The reason progestogen is recommended in women with a uterus is because estrogen can stimulate growth of the uterine lining and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Progestogen therapy helps mitigate that risk, Cansino explained.
Around half a million women have hysterectomies each year, and for women without a uterus, ACOG recommends estrogen alone.

As an alternative to estrogen-progestogen therapy, ACOG also recommends a pill, sold under the brand name Duavee, that combines estrogen and a drug called bazedoxifene. Bazedoxifene is a "selective estrogen receptor modulator," which blocks the estrogen from working in certain areas of the body, such as breast tissue, while mimicking estrogen's benefit for bone density, for instance.

Another drug recommended in the new guideline is gabapentin, an anticonvulsant typically used to treat seizures. It can also manage menopause symptoms for people who can't tolerate hormones or the other new medicines.

Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise, clinical hypnosis, and acupuncture can all improve some symptoms, ACOG says, however the guidelines also note that the evidence for these interventions is weaker than the evidence for HRT.
Still, patients may have their own preferences and goals, Cansino said.

"I live in California, and I have a practice where many patients don't necessarily want pharmacologic therapy," Cansino said. So, she tends to have a lot of conversations about non-pharmacologic treatment options with her patients.
"A healthy diet and regular physical exercise is going to go a long way. So let's start with that," and then discuss what other interventions to add to the regimen, she said.
Asked, in a follow-up email, whether Cansino recommended one medication or tool over another, she warned against "over-simplifying treatment based on tiers."
Just like with contraception, she noted that patients may choose a certain method, knowing that it's less effective. "As long as they understand the pros and cons, such a decision is perfectly OK."
Meanwhile, demand for HRT is already rising. Last year, the FDA scrapped the "black-box warning" on labels for certain estrogen therapies.
In recent months, estrogen products like transdermal patches have been hard for pharmacies to keep in stock.

"I think the shortage of transdermal estrogen therapy highlights the fact that we have all of this attention about hormone therapy, and not necessarily enough about other treatment options," Cansino told NPR.
She also stressed the need for patients to talk to trusted clinicians about the pros and cons of treatments and to avoid having "tunnel vision" about a single option.
The level of care that OB/GYNs provide by helping individual patients find the right treatment is one of the most important aspects of the new guidance, Cansino said.
"There's a lot of misinformation out there and exaggerated claims about hormone therapy, and so some people end up taking risks when they shouldn't," she added.

items.title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moved to low-security facility in Pennsylvania
paragraphs: Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.
The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons.

"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".
Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.

Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.

The move comes about two weeks after NBC News, external reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC.
"It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees, told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there."

NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028.

Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".
The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports.

"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.
FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.

The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.
