items.title: ‘Incredibly healing’: artist Tony Albert receives more than 2,000 public donations of racist Aboriginalia
paragraphs: Five months ago Indigenous artist Tony Albert made a public request for donations of Aboriginalia – souvenirs, homewares and other objects depicting Aboriginal people and designs, often as caricatures, that were created and sold by non-Indigenous people.

It was a request that accompanied his career-spanning Not a Souvenir exhibition at the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) in Sydney, which featured 4,400 objects from the artist’s own collection – one he started in the 1980s as a child.
Now, in the exhibition’s closing days, the MCA is packaging and shipping 2,000 more items donated by the public to Albert’s studio in Brisbane.

“I have been genuinely overwhelmed by the generosity and response,” says Albert via email from Paris, where he is on a month-long artist residency. The 45-year-old, who has family connections to the Girramay, Kuku Yalanji and Yidindji peoples, has been personally in touch with the people who brought stuff in.

“What has moved me most is not simply the number of objects donated, but the personal stories and conversations that have accompanied them,” he says. “There is something incredibly powerful and healing about people wanting to confront this history and entrusting me with these objects, so that together we can give them new meaning.”

Carolyn Ienna, a 63-year-old Wiradjuri artist and activist from Sydney, dropped off a painted image of an Aboriginal man with a spear last week. They found it in a council pickup collection over a decade ago.

“I’d look at it and feel sad, but I didn’t have a name for it,” says Ienna. “I didn’t know what Aboriginalia was.” When they discovered it, it felt like the previous owners were “throwing away an Aboriginal person”.
“I don’t think [people] understand the complexities of not only the trauma of colonisation, and how different Aboriginal people may see this Aboriginalia, but also the propaganda of it,” says Ienna.
One of the aims of Albert’s Aboriginalia call-out is to take items like this out of circulation; another is to reappropriate them through his practice.
Lesley Pepper, who travelled from Dunedin in New Zealand to see the exhibition, dropped off a set of serviettes, placemats and four porcelain plates that she has had for “30 or 40 years”.

“They were probably purchased here in New Zealand, in op-shops,” says the 67-year-old. “I have a Māori background, and when I first bought them I felt that I was bringing them home, as a sign of respect.”
One of her plates depicts a young Aboriginal woman, which Pepper says reminded her of herself. “[The woman] was probably never asked if her image could be used,” she says, remorsefully.

It wasn’t an easy decision to give away pieces she had cherished for decades, but “when Tony said he wants to get them out of circulation, I thought ‘yep OK’, they have to come down. If that’s what he’s asking, that’s what you do.”

Items have been delivered to the MCA every day of the exhibition, says assistant curator Antares Wells. “Yesterday we received a donation of a nearly one-metre-tall figurine depicting an Aboriginal man with a spear,” she says. “One donation alone had 120 plates, cups and saucers depicting Aboriginalia, another had 200 beer coasters.”

Unpacking items has been a more positive experience than Wells initially imagined. “When we launched the appeal, we didn’t know what the response would be from the Australian public – and in this political and cultural climate the first thing I personally thought was I really hope that we’re not exposing Tony to hate mail,” she says.
“But I haven’t seen one piece of hate mail and I think that has actually been incredibly inspiring and very powerful.”
Kathryn Hopps, who lives in Canberra, made a detour to Sydney on the way back from visiting family to hand in a pair of silky Australiana scarves she had inherited from her grandmother.

“They were classic 1970s and 80s Australian souvenirs with kangaroos and wattle and Uluru, and pictures of Aboriginal people and designs all mixed in together,” says the 46-year-old. “I immediately recognised that this was not something I wanted to wear … I don’t think my grandma had any idea.

“The only reason I held on to them is because I thought they should be in a museum,” she says. “We can learn from these things, which is why I was delighted to find out about Tony Albert’s exhibition and the opportunity to donate … It felt like a significant thing to do.”

Though the MCA’s donation boxes will be removed after the exhibition closes on 19 October, Wells says the gallery will “gratefully accept” any further Aboriginalia, which will then be passed on to Albert.

Collecting has been integral to Albert’s life and artistic practice since he was young, he says. “I don’t think that will ever change, but what continues to evolve is my understanding of these objects and the possibilities they hold for telling stories, challenging perceptions and creating something meaningful from a difficult history.”
A donated object that really stood out for him is a 1930s ceramic shaving mug in the shape of a caricature of an Aboriginal man’s face.

“I find it astonishing that someone would have wanted this object sitting in their bathroom, and used it as part of their everyday routine,” he says. “These objects are actually incredibly rare and quite valuable, but what fascinates me most is what they reveal about the way Aboriginal people have been represented and how casually these images became part of Australian domestic life.”
Tony Albert: Not a Souvenir is on at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney until 19 October 2026

items.title: The strange business of Roman Abramovich– level 1
paragraphs: Roman Abramovich is a rich man from Russia. He owns Chelsea Football Club some time ago.

A new report shows that he uses fake papers to hide his money and pay less tax. Advisers help him hide big boats, planes, and expensive houses. These things cost hundreds of millions of dollars. Because he is a close friend of Russia’s president, many countries stop him from doing business there. Now, his big boats are in Turkey.
Experts say that hiding money with fake papers is a crime. Abramovich says that he does nothing wrong. He only does what his advisers tell him to do.
Difficult words: hide (to put something in a place where others cannot see or find it), tax (money which you must pay to the government), crime (an illegal action).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The strange business of Roman Abramovich– level 2
paragraphs: A new investigation shows how Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich hid his great wealth to avoid paying taxes.

Secret documents show that companies in Cyprus wrote fake and backdated papers for him. These papers helped hide over 600 million dollars worth of luxury items, including yachts, private planes, and expensive houses. The advisers also changed bank records, so Abramovich wouldn’t have to pay millions in taxes.

Today, Abramovich faces strict sanctions in many countries because of his close relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He can no longer do business in Britain, and his large superyachts are now parked in Turkey. Experts say changing official financial records to avoid taxes is against the law. Abramovich denies doing anything wrong and says he only followed advice from his financial team.

Difficult words: avoid (to stay away from something or prevent something bad from happening), backdate (to put an earlier date on an official document), advice (an opinion given to help someone decide what to do).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The strange business of Roman Abramovich– level 3
paragraphs: A new investigation has revealed that former Chelsea FC owner Roman Abramovich used fake, backdated financial documents to hide his wealth and avoid paying taxes.

The leak shows that Cyprus-based financial firms, along with major global accounting advisers, helped rewrite company records to secret away over 600 million dollars in luxury assets, including superyachts, private jets, and luxury homes. These firms also changed bank records to help the Russian oligarch avoid paying millions of dollars in local taxes on a 2 billion dollar fortune.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine, Abramovich has faced heavy international sanctions over his close ties to Vladimir Putin, which forced him to move his massive superyachts to safe waters in Turkey. While legal experts argue that these fake records amount to clear tax fraud that should face criminal prosecution, Abramovich’s legal team strongly denies any wrongdoing and insists he simply followed professional financial advice.

Difficult words: secret away (to hide or place something in a secret location so others cannot find or see it), oligarch (a very rich and powerful business leader who often has strong connections to political leaders), fraud (the crime of tricking people or changing information to illegally get money or power).

items.title: Are you triggered by GTA 6's giant Paris advert?
paragraphs: GTA 6 is now big enough to swallow entire buildings, but the huge ad wrapped around one of the Les Mercuriales towers in Bagnolet, Paris, has a design problem. The guns have been removed from the illustration, even though the game and series famously feature lots of guns.

The banner recreates Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI cover art, with Lucia and Jason front and centre and joins the growing marketing campaign that started in earnest with yesterday's GTA 6 launch trailer. Look closely, though, and two weapons have vanished: the pistol Lucia holds in the original, and an assault rifle in another panel. Kotaku spotted the changes after fans started comparing the finished banner with the official image (X user Rockstar Mags had been following the ad's creation and took photos).

On paper, removing a gun from an image sounds like a five-minute job. In practice, it leaves Lucia with no pistol and no hand to hold it, and the character in the lower image with an arm thrust into thin air, as if they’ve just spotted a particularly interesting cloud, so a canny zoom has solved the problem.

But these guns aren’t background clutter for GTA 6; Rockstar’s art centres on its characters, their poses, and what they’re holding, and the weapons give those silhouettes attitude and tell us a little about who they are and what we can expect from the game. Take them out and the balance tips, leaving gestures that no longer quite make sense. It's a similar, though perhaps less dramatic, edit that made Amazon's shockingly bad James Bond posters so appalling by removing Bond's famous pistol.

La fresque de Paris sur les tours Mercuriales est quasiment terminée ! La seconde fresque sur les côtes des tours a officiellement débutée ! 🔥 Merci à Théodore (mebta56) pour les photos ! https://t.co/uJumfdV8vcOctober 14, 2026

It’s a handy reminder of how tricky it is to adapt key art for different spaces. An image designed for game boxes, websites, and trailers won’t always hold up when blown up across the side of a building, especially when bits have to be cut out because locals don't want a 30ft gun staring down at them as they pop out for a croissant.

Other GTA 6 murals in the US reportedly keep their weapons, so this looks like a Paris-only tweak for the local area, which also shows how aware Rockstar is of the impact its campaign can have. I get the feeling Rockstar doesn't want to start culture-war fires this time and wants people to focus on the game.

That said, it’s a strange compromise for a game defined by crime, chaos and bad behaviour. A gun-free GTA is a bit like advertising a racing game without the cars, or James Bond without a Walther PPK. And once you’ve spotted those empty hands, you can’t stop looking for them.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
paragraphs: A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.
But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

items.title: Zelenskyy defends himself after Trump’s claim he is more difficult to deal with than Putin – Europe live
paragraphs: Zelenskyy gets asked about Trump’s comments that he is more difficult to deal with than Putin (11:09).
He says that in his meetings with Trump he always found topics for discussion and decisions.
“I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests,” he says, responding to Russian attacks.
“And no matter how Russia would like to limit all of our rights, it’s clear that we do have a right to defend ourselves.”

He says Putin “does not seek negotiations in any format,” but only “playing these games of words.” “He does not want the war to end,” he says, saying Putin’s actions are a “parody” of efforts to end the war.

He says that’s why he cannot accept any diesel deals with the US, because they will then be followed by gas agreements or other attempts to lift sanctions on Russia or its frozen assets, banking system, chemical industry, certain Russian individuals.
“If I don’t stand up to this, if I don’t defend it, who else will do this diplomatically?”

Zelenskyy got asked by Sky News if he feels he’s being treated as a scapegoat for Trump’s domestic problems ahead of the tricky midterm elections.
In response, he pauses for 15 seconds, and eventually smiles before saying:
And the press conference immediately wraps up after that.

Asked again if he’s feeling some pressure among European leaders or fearing potential changes in European politics with big elections coming up next year, he says that he “feels full support from Europe now.”
“Europe is very united and it’s cognisant of all of the risks,” he says.
He says the war clearly shows “major risks for Europe” as he recalls recent incidents in Bulgaria, Germany, Poland, Romania.
“Europe understands as long as Ukraine stands, there will be fewer escalation with Russia,” he says.
He says Russia’s demands are not about Donbas or any part of its territory, but about “our country’s existence.”
“We’re now standing and fighting. What’s the alternative? Annihilation.”
He says Putin “wants to destroy us,” and “does not respect our sovereignty and territorial integrity.”
“So you really trust that he needs only a part of our country?”
He also warns that any further progress in Ukraine could also trigger a wave of Ukrainian migrants in Europe.
Zelenskyy says that he often hears from Trump that he just wants to “stop the killings.”

“Yes, [but] Russia is killing us, on our territory. They came on our land and further pushing further. They don’t want to stop. They even don’t want to freeze [the conflict], as you see. And what will be after that? On what borders will he [stop]?”
Visibly frustrated, he says that more than 1,000 drones were sent to Ukraine yesterday, but the American side “said that it’s difficult to speak with Zelenskyy.”
Zelenskyy gets asked about Trump’s comments that he is more difficult to deal with than Putin (11:09).
He says that in his meetings with Trump he always found topics for discussion and decisions.
“I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests,” he says, responding to Russian attacks.
“And no matter how Russia would like to limit all of our rights, it’s clear that we do have a right to defend ourselves.”

He says Putin “does not seek negotiations in any format,” but only “playing these games of words.” “He does not want the war to end,” he says, saying Putin’s actions are a “parody” of efforts to end the war.

He says that’s why he cannot accept any diesel deals with the US, because they will then be followed by gas agreements or other attempts to lift sanctions on Russia or its frozen assets, banking system, chemical industry, certain Russian individuals.
“If I don’t stand up to this, if I don’t defend it, who else will do this diplomatically?”
Asked about his relationship with Hungary’s Magyar (13:08), Zelenskyy says it was “a very good meeting” on the economy, logistics, energy.
He says he is “not against” meeting the Hungarian PM in Budapest next.
Zelenskyy gets asked if he heard any criticism from fellow leaders to his response to the US deal with Russia on diesel.
He says he “heard … only support,” and he is “grateful to them for this.”
He says the diesel deal caught Ukraine by surprise, and he believes Ukraine “should be aware of these things.”
He says despite all of that Ukraine is ready to support an energy ceasefire, but “it all depends on Russia and they do not want it.”
“And if there is no energy ceasefire, give us anti-ballistic missiles so that I can protect my energy facilities – … not too many, but for the period … of the diesel deal.”
He says Ukrainian negotiators are in touch with their US counterparts, and “in the coming days, they will arrange a meeting at a certain level,” and they will keep discussing it.
Zelenskyy gets directly asked if Ukraine is hitting refineries in Russia.
He says he “usually don’t communicate” the details of Ukraine’s military operations, but says “the main rule of our operations is to respond.”
Earlier he said Europe is “making certain steps” to have its own track in peace negotiations, but he didn’t offer more details on that.
Zelenskyy says that Ukraine’s requests for further help ahead of this winter cover “the bare minimum” needed.
He says it’s unclear what Ukraine could get, but he is confident that European countries have enough interceptors to share and “go through this winter.”
He also says the focus is on producing a new anti-ballistic system and make it “quicker to produce, cheaper to produce” and then share with the rest of Europe.
Zelenskyy then gets asked about media reports that Ukraine is running out of Patriot interceptors and its reliance on Starlink.
He acknowledges that Ukraine is “not a priority destination” for deliveries funded by Europe, but thanks for all help it can get.
“We are picking them up where we can: one or two here, five there, ten there, arranging all of this and bringing them to Ukraine,” he says.
On Starlink, he says Ukraine “is working with some countries, including France” on additional capabilities.
Zelenskyy also addresses the issue of intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
He says “many countries are sharing their intel with us, … dozens of countries.”
But he then gets asked again for a straight clarification on what is the status of both Starlink (or its military version, Starshield) and US intel.

On Starlink, he says “certain speed levels are needed” for its military to work properly – not for “deep strikes inside Russia,” but for its defence operations, particularly against Russian jet-powered drones.
“This is why it was a very dangerous and unpleasant surprise,” he says.

“Starlink was not turned off, but the speed limits were lowered … and we were incapable of shooting down some Shahed drones, and were no longer able to use one of the tools to protect our population,” he says.
Jet-powered Shaheds move at 400 km/h, and the speed limits were reduced to 70 km/h, he says.
He says the technology is also used for “mid-range strikes against military targets,” and for logistics deliveries.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities. Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
The briefing kicks off with Zelenskyy getting a question about Russian frozen assets and Belgium’s opposition to the issue.

He says by thanking Belgium for hosting the summit and for his meetings with PM de Wever and the Belgian king, Philippe. Ukraine expects additional F-16 from Belgium to be delivered by the end of the year.
Turning to frozen assets, he says “of course” he is raising this issue again.
He says Ukraine “would want to receive these funds in a certain format” and wants them to be safeguarded from Russia, “because we know very clearly that they want to bring these assets back.”
Zelenskyy is finally here to brief the media after his EU talks in Brussels.
I will bring you all the key lines here, but you can also watch along here:
We are still waiting for Zelenskyy to show up to his press conference, but in the meantime we have just heard from Hungary’s Péter Magyar after his first meeting with the Ukrainian president.

The pair have a long list of tricky topics to discuss given Hungary’s tense relations with Ukraine under the previous government of Viktor Orbán, including the issue of minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine, which is critical to Kyiv’s ambitions of joining the EU.
But the noises coming from that meeting are positive.

In a statement after the talks, Magyar welcomed the Ukrainian parliament’s adoption of a new law on minority education as “a first step towards restoring mutual trust,” and the two sides will “continue consultations … at the ministerial level.”
“We agreed that it is in the interest of both countries to place their political and economic relations on a new foundation,” he said.
In sharp contrast to his predecessor, Magyar also declared his strong solidarity with Zelenskyy “in the face of inhumane Russian aggression against his country.”
“Hungary stands ready to provide assistance, through all available diplomatic means, towards achieving an immediate ceasefire and a lasting peace,” he said.
Back to Brussels, we are expecting to hear from Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy shortly, as he is about to deliver a press conference after his talks with EU leaders.
I will bring you all the key lines here when he steps up to the podium.

Separately, Italy is struggling with technical issues affecting the data transmission network for air traffic control, with lengthy delays at airports across the country affecting thousands of passengers.
Transport minister Matteo Salvini is “monitoring” the situation closely, his ministry said, with particular focus on ensuring the safety of operations, La Repubblica reported.
The air navigation operator ENAV ruled out any “malicious activity,” and said the disruption was due to technical issues with the system managed by telecom operator TIM, Corriere della Sera said.
Italy and Spain are reported to be close to dropping temporary border controls, introduced after the migration crisis in Ceuta in late August.

The move, reported in the Italian and Spanish press, was reportedly discussed on the sidelines of the ongoing EU summit in Brussels, with Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez and Italian PM Giorgia Meloni meeting on Thursday night.

The current thinking includes Italy extending its measures for seven days to align their expiry date with the Spanish restriction, when both would get lifted simultaneously on 22 October, El País reported.
Italy first suspended Schengen arrangements with Spain in late July, much to criticism from Spain.
In their doorstep comments, EU leaders also called for Europe to do more on reducing Ukraine’s dependence on the US Starlink satellite communications system.
The bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe did not have a readily available alternative to technology controlled by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, AFP reported.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” Kallas said before the talks.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back,” Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters.
Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed with French president Emmanuel Macron “how we, as Europeans, can provide more of these kinds of services in the not too distant future”.
Bloomberg reported that the European Union will look to fast-track antitrust approvals for a rival European project.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he discussed financial support for Ukraine with the presidents of the European Commission and European Council on the margins of the EU summit in Brussels.
“I had a good meeting with the President of the European Council, António Costa @eucopresident, and the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen @vonderleyen.

Right now, there are no signals from Russia that it is ready to end its war. The signals it is sending point to something entirely different and certainly do not bring peace any closer. After overnight Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, Russia carried out a horrific strike on Kharkiv this morning. Two people have already been reported killed. My condolences to their families and loved ones. Seventeen others were injured. Russia also struck a shopping mall in Rivne and energy facilities in four regions.

European leadership is needed to ensure that people’s lives are sufficiently protected from this Russian terror. We appreciate that everything we agree on is implemented promptly. Today, we discussed further assistance, first and foremost for our energy and air defense needs. We talked about support for our financial resilience, including for next year, and coordinated our work on the European integration track. It is important that new negotiating clusters were opened this week. We are working to open the remaining two by the end of the year. Thank you, António! Thank you, Ursula! Thank you, EU!”

items.title: Street Fighter movie is 'made by fans for fans' - but can it KO the critics?
paragraphs: Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.
First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.
The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.
Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.
But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.
BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.
The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.
The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.
Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.
The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs.
"It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat.
"And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."
He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail.
Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.
His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look.
"I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says.
"My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'".
Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.
Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula.
"I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says.
"I think we could feel it when we first read the script."

items.title: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event
paragraphs: Elon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”.

The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters.

A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land.
Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time.
“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event.

Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.”
“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”.
In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles.

However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and is priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”.

After the event, a Tesla reservation website for expressing interest in the two-seater Roadster 2 showed that a “performance” version of the vehicle would require a £50,000 deposit. A “thrust” version would require a $250,000 deposit.
Meanwhile, a one-seater “rocket” variant with “full flight system” was labelled as being available only by invitation. The car company added that flying it was not permitted on public roads.

items.title: Sweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at Frieze
paragraphs: The raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.

Yuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.

Finally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.

It might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazzard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.

The urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.

There is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.

My love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.

There are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.

You eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.

There’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.

items.title: Hokusai on high, Bruges goes Bosch and Tate’s Turbine Hall has a blast – the week in art
paragraphs: Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji Perhaps the most celebrated and charismatic body of work in the history of Japanese art is shown in its entirety. Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, 20 October to 17 January

Pre-Raphaelites: Art and Poetry The woozy visions of Millais, Rossetti and the rest are profoundly literary, shows this exhibition of the ever-popular Victorian art movement. Laing Art Gallery, Newcastle, 17 October to 13 February
Michael Landy Landy’s drawings are painfully and beautifully honest. Here he muses on the nature of ruin. Soane Museum, London, until 17 January
Middlesex Hospital Blues Derek Jarman’s Blue and its revolutionary meditation on illness are explored by Tilda Swinton and others. Fitzrovia Chapel, London, until 18 November
Ancient Landscape, Modern Times Rolling hills and chalk horses were evocatively depicted in early 20th century British art, this exhibition claims. Holburne Museum, Bath, until 10 January

Tarek Atoui’s entrancing Turbine Hall installation at Tate Modern is an interconnected musical machine you can lose yourself in for hours. The artist teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear – managing to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. Read the five-star review.

The Virgin and Child in a Landscape, 1520s, by Albert Cornelis and Associates Behind the melancholic Madonna and lively Christ child in this Renaissance painting is a fantasy version of the city of Bruges in a blue landscape that is nothing like the Flemish city’s actual setting. The city’s towers are depictions of the real towers of Bruges, the medieval powerhouse of industry and commerce where Albert Cornelis worked. But he or a helper have turned Bruges into a twinkling, dreamlike place beside a vast, placid sea inlet, loomed over by huge mountains: an imagined, alluring landscape inspired by the science-fiction utopias of Hieronymus Bosch, as well as the surreal vistas of Joachim Patinir. It may even owe something to the melting blue mountains and seas in Leonardo da Vinci’s altarpieces, for this painting was apparently made for the Italian market and has the name of an early Italian owner on the back. It’s a lovely, little known example of the way 16th-century artists could combine religious imagery with romantic, bizarre musings in their freely painted landscapes. National Gallery, London

items.title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis
paragraphs: For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September.

Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.”

London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations.
Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire.

The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost.

Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides.

The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.

In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.

The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said.
TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic.

For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road.

Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat.

As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets.

That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene.

City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday.

Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.”

Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.”

Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern.
“People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.”

Abdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day.

“But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.”

A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, and urged the government to tax autonomous vehicles to help pay for the social consequences and economic losses.

The GMB union has demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.”

The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.”

An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in.
“We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.”

Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections.

Wayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel.

“There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.”

A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.

items.title: Sydney Sweeney’s racy ad sparked a Gen Z culture war – and Powerade just piled in
paragraphs: Novig's 'Just Sports' ad shows Sydney Sweeney in a sports kit, strategically covering her naked body to sell a sports prediction market app – come on, admit it, you've all searched for it. It joins Pepsi's 'Wild Cherry' and Callaway's Obsession parody as ads that got us thinking 2026 is the year of the cancelled ad, and like her American Eagle campaign from last year, Sydney Sweeney has been torn apart for this new racy commercial.

However, Powerade's response, the 'Never Just Sports' campaign, adds one word and turns the whole furore into a different debate about women in sport. The Ogilvy-made campaign has been running on digital screens in New York's Times Square, directly opposite the Novig billboard, with images of women swimming and clearing the high jump, and it never mentions Sweeney or Novig; it just nicks the phrase, changes it just enough to make a difference and trusts you to remember the original – but it's also right there next to Sweeney, so it's not hard.

What interests me more than who has the better line or how clever Coca-Cola feels right now is why an ad with a Hollywood actor in a cheeky pose ended up as a row about how women are shown in sport at all, whether we really are returning to 'ads' old dirty tricks', and whether Millennials and Gen Z read the same pictures differently, because I suspect the answer is messier than one lot being offended and the other shrugging.

Novig's idea is commercially clear: it wants to stand out as a sports-only prediction market app, unlike platforms that let you trade on politics and world affairs. Its CEO says Sweeney helped develop the campaign's creative, and that it's an eye-catching way into something few people care about (I mean, really?). The gag is that she's wearing "just sports", footballs and other kit doing the job of clothes, a play on words that's as subtle as "good jeans".

Just like American Eagle's slogan, it worked for what was needed at the time, with plenty of attention both good and bad, and Novig reporting a rise in activity on its platform: it claims first-time depositors rose more than 218% in the 20 days around the 9 September launch, and the Instagram reel passed 37 million views in four days. (Honestly, if you, like me, never felt clear on what a naked Sweeney and Novig were selling, I'd argue that alone could have driven the search.)

By contrast, Powerade's athletes skip the Austin Powers prancing-around-his-love-pad routine and use their bodies for sport. The physicality remains, shown as the result of training and competition, with no '90s lads mag revival.

Yet the bad-ad-versus-good-ad framing is too easy, because women can be glamorous without undermining what they've achieved; Serena Williams and Naomi Osaka have done just that in their careers. So what are these ads actually saying, beyond getting people to look? And who comes out on top?

The easy answer is Millennials raised on lad mags and tabloids against a Gen Z fluent in social media and the language of representation, but plenty of Millennials hate sexualised advertising, plenty of Gen Z see Sweeney confidently making her own choices (she's Gen Z herself), and a fair few probably think it's ordinary attention-seeking marketing, so you can't pin a view on a whole generation.

Millennials watched brands move from traditional ads to blogs, Facebook, and YouTube, and saw influencers take over, while Gen Z grew up with influencer celebrities selling them everything from games to makeup, with brand deals and staged images all muddled together. Gen Z has its own cues for knowing when they’re being sold to (the #ad tag, the suspiciously candid photo), plus the vocabulary to call it out on the spot. Which is how the same billboard can be a knowing joke with one lot and the oldest trick with another.

So we're in a place where one person sees Sweeney owning her image and getting paid on her own terms, while another sees the old shortcut of using an attractive woman to grab attention, and both can be right, since she can have agency over her image while a brand still uses it to sell something. Powerade is selling too, using a live row to position itself alongside female sports achievement, and it's playing the same attention-grabbing game.

We've been having the same debate since tobacco ads became a thing in the 1870s, and I'm old enough to remember Madonna making a career out of it, from Material Girl to the Sex book. So what's changed?

Sweeney's American Eagle 'Great Jeans' campaign had already been through this, with arguments about beauty standards, race, genetics and political identity, because the "genes" pun plus a blonde, blue-eyed actor led some people to read it as being about far more than denim, and it showed how an ad can pick up a meaning its makers never intended and can't control once the internet gets hold of it. Adweek's Weissbrot called it a return of “male gaze” advertising, and many people read it as the end of the brand-purpose decade.

In many ways, that's what American Eagle can teach us about branding in the 2020s, because the Novig row is really about how women are presented in ads, here in sports, and whether sexualised imagery undermines female athletes, and whether criticising the ad is an attack on Sweeney's right to make her own choices. When Madonna did it, the provocation at least started a conversation; now polarisation turns everything into a shouting match.

Female athletes have criticised it, from Ariarne Titmus to Felicity Palmateer and Gracie Kramer; Novig has defended it and kept promoting it, and Powerade elbowed its way in with a polar opposite view, one that, let's be honest, is happy to play off the furore too, only from a different angle: women powering through the water and lifting the weight.

Powerade's timing has an obvious commercial angle: it chose to wade into a mess, make a point without building awareness from scratch, and the one-word swap hands journalists like me a simple way to describe the idea and write about how clever it all is.

But Powerade has a history of campaigns focused on mental and physical well-being, hard work, and training, which gives this context beyond a swipe at a rival brand. The response has landed with at least some of the people it's aimed at, too: a female athlete working in marketing wrote in PRWeek that many women in sport, herself included, greatly appreciated it.

A reactive ad like Powerade's still has to be judged as advertising, so it's fair to ask whether it gives female athletes a real platform, changes how people see their achievements, or just gets remembered as a clever troll to another saucy Sydney Sweeney campaign. The same goes for any brand taking a stand, because people are wary of companies that adopt a cause only when it becomes useful.

Powerade could have issued a statement or run a montage of sporting achievements, but instead it took a phrase with a public meaning and flipped it, short enough for a bold ad and with a second life for anyone who's seen Sweeney's butt on a billboard and Novig's pun. For brands, an empowerment slogan, a provocative image or a well-timed reply only gets you so far; what lasts is whatever holds up once the joke or shock wears off.
Will Gen Z and Millennials agree on what that is? Probably not. As a Gen X, I've seen it all before too. Move on.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Sex was 'huge preoccupation for Russell Brand', ex-flatmate tells trial
paragraphs: Warning - this report contains graphic content
A former flatmate of Russell Brand has told a jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer.
Andrew Dobson, who was in Bournemouth where Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, has been giving evidence on the fourth day of the trial.
Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial at Southwark Crown Court - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.
On Friday, the jury heard from witnesses associated with the complainant who gave evidence on Thursday.
The woman alleged Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999, after they met while she was attending the Labour Party conference.
Dobson told the court on Friday he first met Brand around 1999, and wrote music for a fringe event Brand was part of at the conference.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous.
Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical".
"I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term."
Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand.
He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand.
The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members.
The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard.

Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried".
The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?"
Dobson replied: "I can't recall anything specific that was said. I only remember the atmosphere and panicked, urgent. Feeling tense and confusing."
He went on to tell the jury there had been an "abrupt change of atmosphere" from what had been a "fun week" to an "abrupt change of tone".
Under cross-examination by Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, it was put to Dobson that in his witness statement he said that Russell Brand was one of few men he knew that women would swoon over.
Dobson replied: "He was certainly charismatic".
Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.
The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

items.title: Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
paragraphs: Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India, with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site.
The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events.

Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings.
"The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen.

"The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added.

Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape.
Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community.
Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating.
"The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said.

"An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building."

The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building.
This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles.
"The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said.
Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof.

Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research, while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara.

items.title: What is behind the success of dark skies festival?
paragraphs: The Exmoor Dark Skies festival celebrates its 10th anniversary in 2026
Stargazers and astronomers are preparing to enjoy a festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky.
The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival is being held from 16 October to 1 November and this year is its 10th anniversary.
Taking in villages and towns surrounding Exmoor National Park, the event offers walks, talks and shows - putting the dark, clear, night sky into full focus.
But what is the event all about - and what is behind its success over the past decade?
The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve.
Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution.
Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it."
There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows.
Photographers and astronomers can enjoy clear views of the stars during the festival
Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting".
"In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations.
"You can see the Milky Way - it really is fantastic."
Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop.
Locations such as Wimbleball Lake are big draws
The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season.
In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book".
The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park.
Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down.
"We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend."
The growing popularity of the festival meant that many events sold out before the opening day.

items.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
paragraphs: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

items.title: Issy Wood: Self-Portraits review – suffocatingly revealing works from the ultimate zillennial painter
paragraphs: It might feel like Issy Wood is staring right back at you, glaring out of every canvas, making hard, uncomfortable, unflinching eye contact. But she’s not. The young British painter is staring at herself, lost in soul-searching rumination. You’ve just walked in at the wrong time.

This display at the National Portrait Gallery – the first in a new series of presentations looking at contemporary artists’ use of portraiture – is Wood’s first big public foray into capturing her own face. She’s painted self-portraits before, but never at this scale, never this big and personal. For years now, her focus has mainly been on external stimuli: Diet Coke cans, antiques, clocks, ceramics, leather coats. The stuff of midnight doomscrolling, obsessive research, fetishistic desire. Seeing her close-cropped, soft-focus approach to everyday ephemera over the years has been like spying on someone’s internet tabs, peeking into the diary of a bored, sad, overtired, caffeine-wired young overachiever.

She never really needed to paint her face because her work was always so obviously personal and diaristic. But she’s done it anyway, and the results are tense and heightened. She’s taken the same close-cropped, fuzzy, angular compositional approach, but now it’s all skin and lips and tears. She sips a Diet Coke while doing a goopy, wet face mask in one enormous painting, squidges her cheek against a mirror in another, doubling her twisted reflection. She bleeds from her cheek and eyebrow in some smaller works, leans forlornly against her guitar in others. One painting catches her mid-sob, blurry-eyed and disconsolate.

Every painting here is her looking back at herself, lost in navel-gazing, self-pitying introspection. Two pictures of her as a kid are full of smiles and giggles, but they just make you realise how miserable the rest of the images are, and how miserable she must be. And that’s not a bad thing in art terms (but probably not great on a personal level) because it makes for some really good paintings. They’re weird, suffocating, intimate things, like you’ve been allowed into her weakest moments, like you’re interrupting her mid-weep. You feel like you have to back out of the gallery quietly to let her get on with it.

This makes it all sound bleaker and more maudlin than it is. There’s a humour to the work, a bit of silliness at points. In one painting, she’s framing her face with plastic stick-on monster fingers, like she knows this is all a bit overblown.

It’s surprising that she’s not had more major institutional attention, because she’s not just good, she’s quietly important. A whole load of close-cropped, dark, woozy imitators have come out in her wake. She’s a market darling, and I think we’ll look back on her in a couple of decades as the ultimate zillennial painter.

Few artists manage to capture the crushing, endless, tedious anxiety, the malaise and ennui of the contemporary western condition like Issy Wood. This is the art of the bored, the medicated, the perpetually online, the depressed overachiever who feels like no matter what they do, they’ll never be happy. And as uncomfortable as it is, the mirror she’s squashing her face against here actually reflects us back on ourselves too.

items.title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen
paragraphs: A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.

The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.

For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.

Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”

While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”

This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.

Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”

Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.

Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.

Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.

He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”

That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”

His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.

“Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.

She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

items.title: Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize
paragraphs: A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh, designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026.
Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world's best new building outside the UK.
Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees.
"Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond," said RIBA president Christ Williamson.

"By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change."

It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year's prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London.
Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited, Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements.
Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems.

Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles.

Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers' families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room.

A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community.

"The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike," said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain.

"Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country," he continued.

"The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own."

The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that "demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context".

Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+.
Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year's International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium.
The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920's garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space.
In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an "inclusive and sustainable" social housing project in Barcelona.
