items.title: Designers are cringing at Tate McRae’s new single cover
paragraphs: Singer Tate McRae has released a teaser for her new single Housewife, and while the moody superyacht setting has sparked fan theories, there's one detail designers can't ignore. The font.

Featuring one of the most iconic typefaces of all time, the design has surprised creatives thanks to its unexpected appearance on the single's branding. But while some are clutching their metaphorical pearls, others see the controversial font choice as a return to form for the pop music design world.
So what typographical sin has ol' Tate committed? She's used an ultra light Helvetica font. I know, the horror.

"She will pay for her crimes," one X user wrote, while another joked, "It's grotesque tbh." While one critic claimed "Tate McRae has NO REASON to be using an ultra light Helvetica font," others gestured to album covers of the early 2000s, like Britney's I Love Rock 'N' Roll, and Madonna's Bedtime Stories. Remember those? Exactly... that's why we don't use ultra light Helvetica, folks.
For more music news check out why Kpop group IVE's new album cover felt so unsettling or take a look at Phoebe Bridgers' 'internet-free' album campaign.

items.title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors
paragraphs: A Nazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape.

For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language.

But let’s zoom out for a moment because playing Penguin Colony is more straightforward than this description suggests. First and foremost, it is a semiopen world exploration game in which you direct a penguin to the same unearthly entity that the Nazis are chasing. You hop, swim and glide about tummy-first, chewing up miles of frozen wasteland like an indefatigable snowboarder. Tapping a button next to another penguin lets you swap into its body. Some of these, like the rockhopper penguin, are nimble movers, capable of jumping especially high. Fluffy penguin chicks, meanwhile, can squeeze through tiny gaps.

At first, the game’s polar levels are straightforward: snow drifts and ice floes peppered with the remnants of human habitation such as fishing huts. But your surroundings quickly grow stranger: supersized stone labyrinths whose architectural splendour evokes Dark Souls, alien-looking obelisks and abyssal crevasses. Everything in the world is rendered in jagged, low-poly graphics, looming from the screen like a hallucinated PlayStation 2 game.
As you navigate these spaces, a deep-voiced narrator relays the expedition of a scientist from decades before. It’s clear he is driven by the same hubris and racism as his Nazi successors.

The layering of space, time and narrative is terrifically unsettling. At one point, having just hopped my way through a challenging platform section, I came across a Nazi cannibal feasting on his fellow soldier as a researcher delivered yet another verbose pontification on his God-given right to plunder Earth’s southernmost tip. At times, jarring cuts to archive footage and what seem to be Indigenous art interrupt the low-poly action. My head was often spinning, trying to reconcile all these conflicting, contrapuntal elements. Better, I found, to let go and soak up the unnerving, discordant whole.

Penguin Colony is a little uneven technically: I experienced a small number of audio glitches and, at times, bugs with the controls. Yet this does not overly detract from an experience that builds to an incendiary conclusion: a takedown of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism while also, intriguingly, inviting the player to see the world in newly reenchanted terms.

This latter point is made with aplomb at the game’s end: a spectacular cosmological map that details everything you discovered on that playthrough. More tantalisingly, it shows you all the things you missed. This reveal is liable to induce a feeling of vertigo and wonder: Penguin Colony, one of 2026’s boldest, most original games, is far bigger than it first lets on. To access all of its secrets and excavate all of its meaning, one must think and act less like a human mainlining towards their objective. On the contrary, you must embrace the spirit of a renegade penguin, waddling carefree towards whatever piques your interest: atrocity, beauty and all.

items.title: This 3D artist explores fractured identities in a striking ZBrush sculpt
paragraphs: Skander Mallouki is a 3D character and props artist based in Tunisia who loves bouncing between vibrant stylisation and detailed realism. Heavily inspired by game design and fantasy, he uses brings his storytelling to life through digital sculpting, using ZBrush, 3ds Max and Substance Painter (see our guides to the best 3D modelling software and the best laptops for 3D modelling).
Below, he talks us through four examples of his work.
“This creature contest entry was a specific challenge for me to switch to realism, leveraging my professional skills in texturing and dramatic, mood-driven lighting.”
“I aimed for a natural flow within a highly stylised look, paying special attention to the hair shapes while maintaining a rapid, decisive sculpting process.”
“This piece focuses on complex metal panelling, precise armour modeling, and glowing emissives. I wanted to balance futuristic cybernetics with an ornate, regal silhouette.”
“Inspired by Ev Ganin’s concept, this piece explores character identity. I focused on telling a deep story while keeping my process streamlined through sculpting and hand-painting in ZBrush.”
You can see more of Skander’s work on his ArtStation profile

items.title: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations
paragraphs: Greens leader David Shoebridge has denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.

The Nine newspapers reported on Friday afternoon the existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.
Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.
In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.
“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.
“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”
The WA Greens confirmed the existence of the document and said it was created in response to allegations first made against the senator in 2016.
“The Greens WA responded to allegations about Jordon Steele-John in 2016. The allegations were not substantiated and the named persons have never lodged a formal complaint,” the statement said.
“Reference has been made to an internal document that has been provided to the media. This document outlines the management of communications about this matter.”

Steele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.

The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.

Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service (PWSS), which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.

The PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission (IPSC).
Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.
The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.

A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”
Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.
“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.

“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”

items.title: Apple Music’s ‘miserable’ new logo is giving mixed messages
paragraphs: Apple has been going through quite the metamorphosis as of late after releasing the Gen Z-ified MacBook Neo and embracing a playful new brand direction. But it seems its signature minimalism isn't going away completely.

With the new iOS 27.2 update, Apple debuted a new icon for Apple Music, which caused quite a stir among users. Monochromatic and confusingly basic, the new logo design feels like a regression to Apple's minimalist roots, but not all fans are on board.
Nobody: Absolutely nobody: Apple: *rebrands Apple Music* https://t.co/RNdcI4u3n2October 13, 2026

The new design is essentially a black-and-white version of the previous music note logo, with slightly bolder lines. Completely flat and admittedly a little characterless, the new look confused fans who believed Apple was on the road to embracing a quirkier look. With the recent leak of the new Apple Music wordmark, it appeared the brand was waving goodbye to minimalism, but now I'm not so sure. Talk about mixed messages...

"This ain’t it chief," one X user wrote. "The new Apple Music branding is miserable how do you sap a thing of all of its colour like this and think it's okay?" another added. "My best guess is that they want to turn Apple Music into more of a brand to compete with Spotify, and this new mark will allow artists to provide the color and emphasis in billboard ads," one X user theorised.
For more Apple news, check out the chaotic Apple HomeView advert that's proving to be stressful for viewers or take a look at Apple's perfect iPhone Duo TikToks that nail foldable phone marketing.

items.title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
paragraphs: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.

The Queensland coroner’s court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.

The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.
Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.

But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.

The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).
The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.

“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.

“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.
“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”
She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.

But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.
The case worker agreed that she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.

Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.
On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.
“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.
On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.
The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he would leave her.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

items.title: Pornography with strangulation and incest to be banned in England and Wales next month
paragraphs: Pornography that depicts strangulation and incestuous relationships will be banned in England and Wales from early November, the government has announced.
The content will be outlawed from 6 November after cross-party pressure prompted ministers to announce new legislation earlier this year.
Online pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, sex between people who are related or pretending to be related, or when somebody is pretending to be a child under 16, will be illegal.

The justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said: “This isn’t about criminalising harmless sexual preferences. But porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people.
“Content that normalises, or even glorifies, violence against women is dangerous and can blur the line with what is acceptable in real life.”
The Conservative peer Gabby Bertin made the recommendations in her review into pornography regulation which reported in 2025.

Her report found pornography that shows women being choked can have “devastating” real-world consequences. It highlighted “disturbing” role-play, including incest and adults portraying children. Both will be banned.
The report said there had been a “total absence of government scrutiny” of the pornography industry.
Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence in its own right, but it is not illegal to show it online.
Reacting to the announcement, Lady Bertin said: “It is very good news these offences will come into force, and not a moment too soon.

“This change in law alongside better enforcement and stronger regulation will send the unequivocal signal not only to the companies that host and facilitate porn but also to wider society that extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable.”
The End Violence Against Women Coalition campaign group welcomed the ban, urging ministers to ensure it is enforced.

Its interim director, Janaya Walker, said: “This is an important step towards tackling the normalisation of violence against women and girls, and the result of years of campaigning by EVAW and other experts who have raised concerns about the impact of violent pornography.
“Strangulation can cause serious, lasting harm and even death, yet its widespread portrayal in pornography risks normalising this violence in sexual relationships, particularly among young people.

“The introduction of this offence is an important recognition of the harm caused by violent pornography and the need to hold an industry accountable for content that depicts and profits from violence against women and girls.
“The government must now ensure the ban is effectively enforced, and update the Online Safety Act so that online platforms are required to remove this content.”

items.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
paragraphs: Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.

The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.

Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.

The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.

Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.

Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.

SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.

The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.

Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.

Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”

Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”

Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”

Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”

Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”

Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.
This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

items.title: Quote of the Day by LAIKA’s Nelson Lowry: "When the challenges are that raw, you just make mistakes, and you learn from them"
paragraphs: Nelson Lowry has designed sets for LAIKA for years, and Wildwood still gave him problems he couldn’t solve on the first try. The new stop-motion animation from the studio behind Kubo and the Two Strings and Coraline has been a labour of love, taking seven years, with Lowry's team building four years of one battle scene and a massive 132 physical sets. So you'd expect to accept that, on a massive film project like this, you have to get things wrong to get them right.

Speaking to journalists, including The Nerds of Colour, he explained that the film’s storyboards and constantly moving camera meant the sets couldn’t always make physical sense. One example was a battlefield shot where a character on one side sees someone on the other, who in real life would be smaller than a pixel. His team mocked up options, tested them in camera, and got many of them wrong because the problems were so unconventional. They kept going until it worked. He’s done this a long time, he said, but with challenges that raw, “you just make mistakes, and you learn from them.”

What can we learn from Lowry? Most of us only see the finished version of a painting or project: the polished portfolio, the behind-the-scenes reel where everything looks smooth. Lowry’s story is the part those leave out. If your current illustration, animation, or design isn’t working, it may be at the stage where the first attempt failed and the second hasn’t happened yet.

If LAIKA's artists can spend seven years making characters move millimetres at a time, making mistakes, learning, moving on and improving, then maybe the rest of us can cut ourselves a bit of slack, too. You can see every inch of that work at the Design Museum exhibition, too.
Source: Mike Manalo, The Nerds of Color, 21 September 2026. Visit LAIKA for behind the scenes insights for Wildwood and more.
Laika: the Magic Behind a Stop-Motion Dream Factory: Two Decades of Groundbreaking Animation From Coraline to Wildwood

items.title: Disney's latest Hexed announcement is causing even more controversy
paragraphs: With just six weeks to go until the release of Hexed, Disney's revealed a new detail that's reignited an old controversy – one of many to have followed the animated movie. Meanwhile, people aren't letting those same-face syndrome accusations go.

After the great Hexed vertical orientation conspiracy theory and the character design disappointment, the latest issue concerns an unexpected addition to the cast. It's reminding some people of where they think Disney took the movie's concept from.

Throughout the build up to the release of Hexed, some fans of The Owl House, Dana Terraces' Disney Channel animation that was cut short, have insisted that they think the cancelled show inspired the movie. Disney chief creative officer Jared Bush denied the idea at D23, but it's come up again now that Disney has named Sarah-Nicole Robles as part of the voice cast. The actor previously voiced Patience in Knights of Guinevere and Luz Noceda in The Owl House.
"They're not even trying to hide it any more," one person complains.

I'll point out that Sarah-Nicole is a fine actor and previously voiced Señora Ozma in Encanto. I don't think Disney is trying offend anyone here. But it shows the sense of grievance that remains among TOH fans.
@aakashgupta Totally true! Remove the hair and you can’t tell mom from daughter https://t.co/vQKeRSQApbOctober 15, 2026

Meanwhile, people continue to dissect the Hexed character designs and to diagnose an acute case of Disney same-face syndrome. Attention has turned to the question of why mother and daughter Alice and Billie Doe look the same age.

Disney has a 'rule' that makes it almost impossible for its animations to show a mother who looks a believable age, one person believes. It all goes back to a 1943 paper by Konrad Lorenz "about why babies look cute", apparently: large eyes, a high forehead, small nose and chin and round cheeks.

"Disney will even draw an old woman with real wrinkles when the role calls for it, like Gramma Tala in Moana. The mom in her forties is the one who falls through the cracks, and Disney Animation hasn't had to solve that much, because it almost never puts a mom at the center of the story," they suggest, writing on X.

The movie's directors, Josie Trinidad, who was head of story on Ralph Breaks the Internet and Zootopia, and Jason Hand, co-director of Moana 2 head of story on Encanto, have said that Billie is very different from Disney heroines like Moana or Mirabel, with a sharp and more dangerous personality.
The ensemble voice cast also includes Henry Winkler, Dan Stevens, Rachel Dratch and Ariana Madix.

items.title: India’s big river project – level 1
paragraphs: People in India are very angry today. The government wants to build a big dam. They want to connect two rivers.

The government says that the dam will bring water to dry places and help farmers. But water is now coming into villages, homes, and farms. Many people lose their houses. They do not have enough money to build new ones. People stand in the water to protest and ask for help. Nature experts are also worried because the water will hurt trees and tigers in a big park.
The government says that the project is important, but people want to stay on their land.
Difficult words: dam (a strong wall across a river), dry (without rain or water), important (when people need something very much).

items.title: India’s big river project – level 2
paragraphs: In India, many villagers are protesting against a big government plan to join two rivers.

The government wants to build a big dam to bring water to dry areas and help farmers grow food. But rising water from the construction is already flooding homes, farmland, and temples. Local people say the government is taking their land without giving them enough money or a new home. Some protesters say they will not leave their land. Nature experts are also worried because the project will flood a large forest and hurt tigers living in a famous reserve.
Government leaders say the project is needed to solve water problems, but many locals and experts want the government to stop and fix these serious problems first.

Difficult words: dam (a strong wall built across a river to stop or control the flow of water), flood (to cover a place with a large amount of water), reserve (a protected area of land kept for wild animals).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: India’s big river project – level 3
paragraphs: Villagers in central India are protesting against a massive government project to link two major rivers in order to help millions of local farmers.

The plan aims to build a large dam and move water to areas facing severe drought; however, construction work has already caused rising waters to flood nearby villages, homes, and a local temple. Angry residents say the government is not giving them enough money or a new place to rebuild their lives. Some protesters have even taken extreme actions, like lying on fake funeral fires to show their anger.

At the same time, environmental experts warn that the new dam will destroy large areas of forest and harm rare wildlife inside a famous tiger reserve. While government officials claim the project will solve long-term water shortages and bring power to the region, critics argue the scientific plans are flawed and urge leaders to protect both local communities and nature.
Difficult words: rare (not common or frequent; very unusual), shortage (a situation where there is not enough of something that people need), flawed (not perfect).

items.title: The Narnia: The Magician's Nephew trailer has a tiny Easter egg that's sparked big controversy
paragraphs: The trailer for Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew has made a big impact this week with its interpretation of CS Lewis's novel as a psychedelic cosmic fantasy transposed to the period when it was written.

There are a lot of big talking points, including the depiction of Aslan and the way it seems the movie may take the novel's creation myth as a means to explore the act of creation and the nature of creativity. But among Narnia fans, there's also a lot of debate around a small background detail that appears at around the 1.48 mark in the trailer below.
NARNIA: THE MAGICIAN’S NEPHEW | Official Trailer | Netflix - YouTube

As shown in the post on X below, there's scene towards the end of the trailer where Jadis appears to be using magic in London, something that wasn't possible in the novel. As a possible allusion to this deviation from the literature, she also appears to destroy a reference to one of CS Lewis's favourite hangouts.
@cbradedwards yes, insanely disrespectful to have Jadis using magic right in front of it, but ironically accurate that she us literally damaging it by doing soOctober 14, 2026

The pub in the background is named the Eagle & Child, the same as a pub in St Giles', Oxford, where Lewis and JRR Tolkien's literary discussion group The Inklings would meet. There are lots of pubs in England with the same name, and the scene is presumably London, not Oxford, but it seems unlikely to be coincidental given the attention to detail in other scenes, such as when removal van logo offers a premonition of Fledge.
The movie also moves the setting around 50 years forward in time, from 1900 to the 1950s when CS Lewis was writing the novel, increasing the possibility for meta references.

Some have suggested that the inclusion of the pub is a symbolic gesture, or a "confession", intended to show that movie will break with the novel. It's been compared to how Stanley Kubrick used a yellow VW Beetle in his film of The Shining and briefly showed a damaged red Beetle as if to clarify that the movie is a different story to that of Stephen King's novel.

"They deliberately chose to destroy Lewis and Tolkien's favourite pub," one person complains on X. "She’s destroying his story, so why wouldn’t she destroy the pub that the Inklings met in?" someone else asks.
Well, every act of creation is first of all an act of destruction, Picasso supposedly said.

items.title: 'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech
paragraphs: Fraser Fleming says his glasses help him navigate public transport and read street signs
ByHayley Jarvis and Steven GoddenBBC Scotland
Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.
A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.
For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information.
"I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says.
"If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace."
Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years.
They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public.

"People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online.
Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people.
"We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says.
"We're using them to lead an independent life."
Fraser, from Motherwell, told the BBC's Your Voice he would often take his glasses off if he thought there was a chance of a confrontation.
"I've got enough to worry about getting from A to B," he says.
"I'll just put the glasses away and have to rely on my other senses in order to navigate around, which is going to make life a lot more difficult for me."
Tracey Rogerson says the technology is a big part of her independence
Tracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns.
"I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says.
Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year.
It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities.

As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month.
This means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year.
He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked.
"Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip.
"I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group.
"You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses."
Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees.
The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices."
The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments.
Cosplay artist Teah Pearn says she was secretly filmed by someone wearing the glasses
Cosplay artist and performer Teah Pearn was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed.
She later discovered the footage was posted online.
Teah, who performs as Spill The Tea and has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated".

"He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist.
Teah says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities.
"For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says.
"They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them."
In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life.
"They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video.
"It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it."

items.title: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'
paragraphs: Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before.
"With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said.

She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start.
Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them".
She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered.
Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame.
"Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said.
"Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say."

Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to.
"Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw.
"Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important."
James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online.
"Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said.
He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms.
Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives.

Simmons-Read said the social media ban for under 16s, which is due to come into force in 2027, "doesn't go far enough", could be bypassed by criminals and could even discourage young people from speaking up about online grooming.
"We want tech platforms to invest more in detecting exploitation when it's happening on their platforms," he said.
A government spokesperson said it was preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images on their devices, which would make the UK the first country to do so.
"Alongside this, tech companies must be part of the solution and meet their legal and moral obligations. Where they fall short, the government will not hesitate to step in," the spokesperson said.
Kerry Smith, chief executive of the IWF, said: "We welcome the commitment to introducing nudity blocking technology on children's devices – but there really is no time to lose."
Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it is working to "fight and prevent grooming in a range of ways".
A Meta spokesperson said: "This includes restricting contact between adults and teens they're not connected to, and using technology to find and remove known child exploitation imagery.
"We also use behavioural signals to identify accounts showing possible signs of grooming or a sexual interest in children.
"Based on the strength of the signals, we either prevent them from finding and following teens or we remove their account completely."
Snapchat and TikTok have all been approached by the BBC for comment.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

items.title: Like dinosaur eggs in the sand: the pterosaur museum built to thrive in the Gobi desert
paragraphs: Viewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China, the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen.
Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment.

The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years.

Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds.

Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago.

Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm.

Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says.

Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years.

But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape.

The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu, the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “sponge cities”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas.

The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes.
The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water.
“Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says.
For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it.
Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says.
“It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.”

Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool.

The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds.
Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception.

“Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

items.title: Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"
paragraphs: Belgian gallery Objects with Narratives has curated a texture-heavy exhibition at PAD London called What Remains?, featuring pieces from Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge.
What Remains? marks the second show that Brussels platform Objects with Narratives has presented at design fair PAD London, which takes place annually in Mayfair's Berkley Square.
The emerging Brussels gallery's exhibition brings together a series of textured pieces united by amorphous shapes and patinated surfaces.
"Every piece was crafted in the present, yet many carry a sense of the past, as though found rather than fabricated," said Objects with Narratives.

Among the exhibitors is Belgian designer Ben Storms, who is known for his rough-hewn furniture that looks like jumbo pillows. Storms is presenting his most recent design, a cushion-like coffee table called Ex Hale, crafted from veiny red Mexican onyx decorated with mosaic veneer.
To create the piece, the designer used a hydroforming technique to blow up two pieces of metal sheet that were welded together and 3D-scanned to form a cushion shape.
After this, Storms used a CNC machine to mill the same shape from a block of stone.
"Ex Hale plays with our common notions of materiality," said the gallery. "The hard stone looks soft instead, an impression that is further enhanced by the delicate surface treatment."
Also on display is Critical Mass, a handmade Corten steel standing shelf by British designer Paul Cocksedge.

A trio of metal components were arranged to support three metal shelves, forming a piece that looks familiar to What Nelson Sees, a weathering steel installation by Cocksedge that was placed in Trafalgar Square for last year's London Design Festival.
"The Critical Mass series holds an energy, something on the edge of collapse or explosion," said Objects with Narratives.
Belgian designer Sofie Middernacht is showing a steel credenza, bench and duo of stools clad in gleaming crimson resin.
Middernacht works with discarded industrial materials to create her furniture, which is purposefully formed like archaeological artefacts.
Venezuelan artist Jojo Corväiá is presenting a trio of glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay, a material central to his practice.
A host of other materials feature in the show, from shaggy mohair and wool lamps by Belgian practice KRJST Studio to lighting by Danish designer Karl Monies formed from patchwork slabs of copper.

"What Remains? asks what gives an object the sense that it might outlive the moment of its making: the material, the craft, or simply the possibility that some objects belong to no single time at all," Objects with Narratives concluded.

Objects with Narratives was founded by Nik and Robbe Vandewyngaerde and Oskar Eryatmaz, who opened their first permanent brick-and-mortar gallery inside a historic 1920s fur atelier in Brussels in 2023.
The photography is courtesy of Objects with Narratives.
PAD London 2026 takes place from 14 to 19 October 2026 at Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EN, UK. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

items.title: Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
paragraphs: Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world’s quickest production car.
During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing
It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position.
A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings.

It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company".

The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour.
On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla.
Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles. Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver.

Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top.
The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls.
Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that "success is not guaranteed" before the test.
Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017, with deliveries planned for 2020.
Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck, unveiled in 2019.
Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle.
