items.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
paragraphs: Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.

“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.
Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.
Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

items.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
paragraphs: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.
The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.
Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".
Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.
It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".
Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent - but its depiction online is currently not illegal.
Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.
Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.
"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.
"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."
The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication.
According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online.
Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says.
Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November.
Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment.
Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences.
Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect.

"This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC.
But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material.

"While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added.

items.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
paragraphs: Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.

The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.

Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.

"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.

Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.

In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.

"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."

The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.

The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.

This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.

Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.

Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

items.title: Explainer: Taiwan’s Alaska LNG Bet
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Taiwan is looking to Alaska for more than natural gas. U.S. President Donald Trump announced this week that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 percent of the output from a proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska over a 20-year period. He also announced a $4.4 billion investment commitment from Taiwan.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs subsequently confirmed that the state-owned CPC Corporation had made significant progress in negotiations with the project developer, New York-based energy company Glenfarne. But key details, including ownership stakes and other contract terms, remain unsettled.
The announcement raises a key question: What does this deal mean for Taiwan’s energy security, U.S. energy exports, and cross-strait relations?

The Alaska LNG project is a proposed $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion energy development project. It would transport natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope through a pipeline about 1,300 kilometers long to a southern export terminal. The gas would then be cooled into liquid form and shipped to Asian markets.
The project could begin supplying Taiwan as early as 2032, if construction and financing proceed as planned.
Alaska has rich natural gas reserves. The U.S. Energy Information Administration says the state’s proved reserves rose nearly 7 percent in 2024, reaching about 103 trillion cubic feet.
Under the current plan, Taiwan’s CPC Corporation would purchase 6 million metric tons of LNG annually once production begins and invest up to $4.4 billion in the project.

Taiwan says the Pacific shipping route offers a geographic advantage. Buying gas from Alaska could diversify its suppliers and reduce dependence on existing import channels in the turbulent Middle East. To that end since the close of the Strait of Hormuz Taiwan has quickly pivoted to other suppliers. So far this year, LNG imports from Australia and the U.S. now account for nearly 60 percent of the Islands supply.

For an island that relies heavily on imported energy, supply diversification is more than a commercial decision. On Wednesday, Premier Cho Jung-tai said the government’s role is to ensure ‘the stability and resilience of the entire energy supply.”

For Washington, Taiwan’s participation could provide a major customer and fresh capital for a project that has struggled to advance. The deal also aligns with the Trump administration’s push to expand U.S. energy production and exports, potentially bringing investment and jobs to Alaska.
For Taipei, long-term supply contracts would provide greater predictability and another source of natural gas. Shorter Pacific shipping routes also would offer logistical advantages.

But the benefits are not guaranteed. A long-term contract could limit Taiwan’s flexibility to switch suppliers if market conditions change. And the final price, investment structure and purchasing obligations have yet to be fully established.

China’s Foreign Ministry criticized Taiwan’s participation, saying the island’s external affairs should be based on the “one-China principle.” Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning accused Taiwan’s current administration of promoting independence under the guise of economic cooperation.
Beijing claims the self-governed island as part of China. Taiwan rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims.

The dispute highlights how even an energy transaction can carry political consequences. Closer commercial ties between Washington and Taipei could draw scrutiny from Beijing, although the proposed gas deal is not itself a formal security agreement.

Whether the deal moves beyond a political announcement to actual construction will depend on three factors: whether Taiwan and the developer sign a formal agreement, whether the project secures financing, and whether construction proceeds as planned.
Taiwan sees an opportunity to diversify its energy supplies, while the United States gains a potential anchor customer for a long-delayed export project.

But a political announcement is not a commercial breakthrough. Until contracts are finalized, financing secured and construction moves forward, the deal remains a promising, though unproven, bet on energy security.

items.title: Gershkovich’s book marks end of chapter in his career covering Russia
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

Two years after his release from a Russian prison, Evan Gershkovich, a reporter for The Wall Street Journal, has published a memoir about his time in captivity. His book, This Cursed Beautiful Land, was released Sept. 29, and debuted on The New York Times’ hardcover top 10 nonfiction best-seller list at number seven.

In an interview with VOA, Gershkovich reflected on his 16 months in Russian custody, what helped him survive prison, what he learned about Russian society, and the challenges of rebuilding his life in prison.

Prior to his arrest on espionage charges in March of 2023, Gershkovich worked in Russia for five and a half years covering Moscow, Ukraine and the Former Soviet Union. Gershkovich says his knowledge of the Kremlin helped him understand what was happening to him. He recently told the Columbia Journalism Review, “I was taken specifically for a swap as a valuable hostage to be kept pristine.”

Gershkovich said his 2023 arrest shocked but did not surprise him. He said when he came to Russia, he had no illusions about how Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime operated. However, he said he did not expect Russian authorities to detain foreign journalists.

While Gershkovich says prison conditions were far from pleasant, he says he was treated much better than many other inmates, including Russian political prisoners or Ukrainians from Russia-occupied territories: “I wasn't tortured. I was fed adequately, and I could take hot showers,” said the American journalist. "The American ambassador was allowed to visit me, and the detention center's administrators would ask how I was doing."

Unable to change his situation, he thought to himself that he “could still talk to people and learn new things.” As the son of Soviet immigrants, he grew up speaking Russian, which allowed him to communicate with fellow inmates, guards and intelligence officers. “Not every journalist gets the opportunity to sit down and talk with FSB officers,” Gershkovich told VOA.

He said his sense of humor and having an extensive support network of family, friends, and lawyers helped a great deal as well. “The days, weeks, and months drag on endlessly, and you have to be able to laugh," he said. "And, of course, I was very fortunate to have Russian lawyers who supported me. They visited, joked with me, and helped take my mind off things.”

One thing prison did not change was the challenge of discovering what Russians actually believe about their situation: “It's very difficult to conduct public opinion polls in Russia, so you have to find other ways to understand what people really think,” explains Gershkovich. “It's very difficult to know what people actually believe. Some may support Putin but oppose the war. Others oppose both the war and Putin. And some simply don't want to think about politics at all.”

He found it interesting that this applied also to employees of the Federal Penitentiary Service: some FSB officers told Gershkovich that they generally supported what was happening, but acknowledged that, in the case of Ukraine, the Russian authorities might have gone too far.
After nearly a year and a half in custody, the journalist was released in August of 2024 as part of a prisoner exchange.
Gershkovich told VOA his time in Russian detention did not change his personality, but adjusting to life outside prison took roughly as long as the time he spent in captivity.

“In prison, you're deeply isolated and have very little contact with other people. Then, after your release, you suddenly find yourself in a vast, unfamiliar world," he said. "Your freedom of choice is also taken away from you, and afterward you have to relearn how to make decisions, act independently, and adapt to ordinary life."
While in prison, he said he learned to contain his emotions. But after his release, he said everything he had been holding in began to come out.

“I experienced panic attacks, felt angry, and couldn't sleep. I started working with a therapist who helped me cope with post-traumatic symptoms," Gershkovich said. “I think writing the book also became a way of dealing with the trauma. To get through a difficult experience, you have to think about it, talk about it, and try to make sense of it. The book allowed me to do exactly that.”
Gershkovich has a personal connection to Russia – his parents were born in the former Soviet Union, and he grew up speaking Russian at home.
In Russia, he said he developed personal attachments and friendships. His experience in prison did not erase that.
“What happened to me was about Putin's regime and the FSB, not the Russian language or culture,” he said.

While he expressed hope that someday opportunities for reform in Russia will emerge, Gershkovich told VOA his memoir This Cursed Beautiful Land represents the end of a chapter in his career covering Russia.

“I want to cover other subjects, too. After finishing the book this summer, I returned to work at The Wall Street Journal and reported on completely different topics. I'm interested in broadening the range of subjects I cover.”
A feature film adaptation of his book is also in development, with Oscar-winning director Edward Berger at the helm.

items.title: Paris City Hall unveils banner honoring Iranian Nobel Laureate Narges Mohammadi
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.
Paris City Hall unveiled a banner expressing solidarity with human rights activist and 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi.
The unveiling ceremony took place on Wednesday, October 14, in front of Paris City Hall, attended by officials, parliamentarians, human rights activists, and Mohammadi’s family and former colleagues.
Narges Mohammadi’s Instagram page posted a video showing Mona Armand — a lawyer and human rights activist — reading a message sent by Mohammadi from Tehran.

The message stated: "Today, I want to ask something very simple of the journalists, political leaders, civil society activists, and women of France: do not forget the people of Iran. We are going through an incredibly difficult time. I am deeply concerned about the future of the children."

Ali Rahmani, head of the Narges Foundation and Narges Mohammadi's son, said at the ceremony: "At this very moment as I speak to you, countless numbers of my compatriots — most of whom are very young — are on death row. Following the killings of January 8 and 9 [Dey 18 and 19], the Islamic Republic has continued its machinery of repression through the use of the death penalty.

“Not a day goes by without us seeing — with fear and anxiety while watching the news — the faces of young people who have been hanged or are awaiting execution; grieving, anxious mothers; and families who have lost their loved ones."

He added: "If my mother were here, she would say only one thing: ‘Be their voice. Be the voice of these mothers and their families. Expose and condemn the oppression inflicted upon them — especially we French, who since 1981 have said "no" to the death penalty and to a justice system that kills. Let us uphold our values and, above all, never — ever — become inured to the suffering of another nation far removed from us.’"

The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights previously reported that Komeil Mohammadi — a resident of Mashhad, Iran, and Narges Mohammadi's nephew — was arrested in the city by the regime's security forces on Thursday, October 1, and transferred to prison following an interrogation session.
Komeil Mohammadi is a laborer, and there have been no prior reports of political or social activism on his part.

While sanctioning Islamic Republic officials for their role in suppressing popular protests, President Donald Trump’s administration has emphasized that the United States is using economic tools to target the perpetrators of human rights violations against the Iranian people.

In many of its human rights reports on Iran, the U.S. State Department has cited the arrest and conviction of lawyers who defend political prisoners or support protesters as examples of the pressure exerted by the Islamic Republic on attorneys and human rights defenders.

items.title: UN approves US NGO’s medical aid to North Korea as Pyongyang Slams South Korean plan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

The U.N. Security Council committee overseeing sanctions on North Korea has approved an exemption allowing U.S. nonprofit organization IGNIS Community to bring medical and rehabilitation equipment into the country, according to a letter recently made public by the committee.

The letter, dated September 18, says the approval covers 125 items worth about $106,751 for a rehabilitation center at Rason Medical School Hospital in northeastern North Korea. The equipment is intended to support treatment and rehabilitation for children with developmental disabilities.
The approved items include physical therapy equipment, sensory therapy tools, walking aids and standardized tests used to assess child development. The equipment is listed as originating in China.
The exemption allows the items to be brought into North Korea within nine months of the approval. It does not confirm that the equipment has been shipped or delivered.

The committee has granted humanitarian exemptions on a case-by-case basis under U.N. sanctions procedures. IGNIS Community has previously received approval to send medical and rehabilitation equipment to North Korea.
The approval comes as North Korea has criticized a separate South Korean plan to provide medical equipment to a hospital near Pyongyang.

Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korea’s medical aid plan in a statement carried by state media on Thursday, calling it an insult to North Korea and saying Seoul had insulted the country and its people with a “list of dirty things.”
Kim did not comment on the separate exemption granted to IGNIS Community.

items.title: To train robots, AI companies are paying people in India to film themselves doing chores
paragraphs: Men and women across India are being paid to record themselves doing domestic jobs as developers train AI robots to do household chores.

items.title: Cable and camera: selfies in 1970s Handsworth
paragraphs: Nearly 50 years ago in inner-city Birmingham, photographers Derek Bishton, Brian Homer and John Reardon set up an impromptu studio in the street and invited their neighbours along. With no camera phones in 1979, long cable releases gave participants the power to decide how they wished to be seen and represented. The project’s original aim was to counter negative media images of Handsworth and its people. Now, in collaboration with Dewi Lewis Publishing, a Kickstarter fund has been set up to bring them together in book form Continue reading...

items.title: EU concerned about terrorist groups in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

The European Union says it is concerned about the presence and activities of terrorist groups with regional and potentially global reach, including the Islamic State Khorasan Province (IS-K) in Afghanistan.

EU Special Envoy Thomas Frellesen “underlined the importance that the de facto authorities [the Taliban] deliver on their commitment that Afghan territory will not be used to threaten the security of any other country,” the EU delegation in Afghanistan said in a statement Monday, as Frellesen concluded a two-day visit to the South Asian country.
The United Nations, in an August report, warned that the “ability of numerous terrorist groups to operate” in Afghanistan is an enduring threat to neighboring countries and the Central Asian region.
The statement said that the EU envoy to Afghanistan called on Afghanistan and Pakistan to restart talks to address their security concerns.
The Pakistani government and the Afghan Taliban continue to trade accusations amid recent border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Afghan Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said the Taliban continue to support TTP.
A new U.N. report released Thursday said the cross-border violence has killed 500 people and injured more than 1,200 in Afghanistan.

Twenty European Union nations, including France, Germany, Belgium, and Sweden, are in favor of establishing contacts with the Taliban to return Afghan nationals whose asylum cases have been rejected or who have been involved in crimes.
No country, except Russia, formally recognizes the Taliban, who seized power in 2021.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department, in an email on Thursday, told VOA the United States cautions nations against measures that could support terrorist groups, including the Taliban.
“In the United States, the Taliban remains a Specially Designated Global Terrorist group. That speaks for itself,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

items.title: London housing project wins top architecture award
paragraphs: Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there all the council houses have been sold off, they're in private hands.
"Which in a way can be a good thing - we're in a homeowning democracy - but the sad thing is they haven't been replaced.
"Every time I go back - without getting too emotional - I think 'where would we have lived?'
"So to me that's why this particular project was important. I think a lot of people from that sort of background live in terrible accommodaiton - temporary accommodation which isn't safe or secure.
"These houses are fantastic and they're part of a mixed scheme so it's got a fantastic feel to it.
"For me it was a very inspirational, emotional, part of the process."
Duggan, who was brought up in south-west London, said the scheme "challenged conventional suburban housing layouts centred on roads, private gardens and clearly defined front and back spaces".
Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks, connecting them and linking shared outdoor spaces.
She said she wanted it to be a public space people felt they could belong to.
"Housing needs to be progressive. People who live in the building have access to green space, allotments."
The site fronts onto Lion Green Road, with low-rise green belt housing set on higher ground to the south and traditional suburban streets to the north.

items.title: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
paragraphs: The Lion Green Road housing in south London, designed by local studios Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, has won this year's RIBA Stirling Prize for the UK's best new building.
Located in Coulsdon, the high-density development commissioned by Croydon Council provides 157 homes across five blocks, which are stitched together by a series of shared green spaces.
The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) named the project as winner of the prestigious prize at a ceremony in London this evening.

It is the fourth housing scheme to win the prize since its inception 30 years ago, following Accordia in Cambridge in 2008, Goldsmith Street in Norwich in 2019 and Appleby Blue Almshouse in London in 2025.

The jury hailed Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for "addressing the pressing need for national housing" and providing environmentally considerate homes with ample access to light, nature and community.
"More than a housing development, the scheme has created a welcoming and inclusive place where people can connect with one another, and with nature," read the citation.

Lion Green Road comprises five blocks with a mix of private and socially rented homes. They are staggered across its steeply sloped site – a topographically challenging plot previously used as a car park.
The blocks have faceted, star-shaped plans, which are rotated to offer unique views across the landscape and ensure each home is dual-aspect, maximising natural light.

A trio of complementary brick types clad the buildings, helping to visually unify them while giving each its own unique aesthetic. Shared outdoor spaces that weave through the blocks enhance this unification, giving residents opportunities to meet and engage with each other.
RIBA president Chris Williamson said the scheme demonstrates how high-density housing "can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create".
"Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity," he reflected.
"The architects have created a new kind of garden neighbourhood that balances privacy and generous views with a strong connection to nature – it's a living landscape," Williamson continued.
"This is thoughtful, resourceful architecture that proves that even the most challenging of sites can be transformed into truly distinctive places for people to call home."
The RIBA Stirling Prize has been awarded annually to the UK's best new building since 1996. Lion Green Road was chosen from a six-strong shortlist, revealed in July.
It was announced as this year's winner at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate this evening, where RIBA also revealed the recipients of its four Special Awards.
This included the RIBA Neave Brown Award for Housing, which was won by Satish Jassal Architects for Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters.

Collaborators Samuel Chisholm Studio and Takero Shimazaki took home the RIBA Reinvention Award for Oru Sutton, a co-working space in an old department store, while Tonkin Liu Architects won the RIBA Client of the Year Award in recognition of the York Minster Centre of Excellence.

Finally, the RIBA Conservation Award was given to Architectural Thread for The Buttermarket, an arts-focused community hub in Cornwall, which also won the RIBA Stephen Lawrence Prize for emerging architectural talent.
Previous winners of the Stirling Prize include London's Elizabeth Line in 2024, The New Library at Magdalene College in 2022 and a seaside pier in Hastings in 2017.

Last year's award, which was won by the "hopeful and imaginative" Appleby Blue Almshouse social housing, sparked concerns about London bias, with four of the six shortlisted buildings located in the capital city.
Earlier this year, the shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize was a topic of conversation in our Dezeen Weekly podcast, with our journalists pondering if architecture has become too boring.
The photography is by Lorenzo Zandri unless stated otherwise.

items.title: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building
paragraphs: If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.

Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, when Goldsmith Street in Norwich scooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner, Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.

“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes,” says RIBA president, Chris Williamson, “Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create. Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity.”

Burnham’s first allocation of £10bn, announced in August, is planned to kickstart 70,000 affordable homes across the country. Yet few people in Britain welcome the prospect of new housing in their backyards, even if it’s prize-winning. The planning application for Lion Green Road, submitted in 2017, received 18 letters of support and 257 objections, mostly about the loss of parking. Now built, almost a decade later, the project demonstrates how more homes than you might imagine can be constructed on the most unpromising of sites in a sympathetic way, without sacrificing greenery, views and public access – and keeping plenty of parking, too.

“We really pushed against the suburban model of terraces dominated by cars, with little front and back gardens,” says Duggan. The original brief asked for 80 homes, arranged as she describes, but Duggan proved she could fit 157 flats, distributed between five pavilion-like towers, retaining the mature trees and bluebell woodland on the site. The result feels like it has grown out of its woodland setting, with a public route that winds its way through the site, up to a historic railway embankment at the rear, and not a perimeter fence in sight.

“Brick by Brick was an amazing client,” says Duggan, who also had a small mews project in Crystal Palace on the drawing board for the council’s housebuilder, before the plug was pulled. “It was a refreshing change from how private developers think about affordable housing. Here, they weren’t talking about the land as a commodity, but as a genuinely public asset.”

The council cared about the interior spaces, too. Thanks to the “pinwheel” plan of the blocks, with flats radiating outwards from a central lift core, each home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views. The flats all enjoy an inset loggia balcony, with a bulge at the base of the balustrades to accommodate plant pots, while cuts in the form (to preserve historic views) create some with larger roof terraces. In the interests of efficiency, the five towers all have the same star-shaped plan, but each is subtly rotated to reduce direct overlooking between neighbouring homes, enabling the buildings to stand close together without sacrificing privacy. Half of the flats are private rental, in two towers, while half are affordable, in three blocks retained by the council, rented at local housing allowance rates. Unlike the Norwich project, this is not true social housing.

The RIBA judges describe the project as a “new kind of garden neighbourhood”. The space between the blocks feels consciously planned, rather than a leftover afterthought, designed with landscape architecture practice Planit-IE to include a sensory garden, allotment plots and play areas. Walking around the development’s zig-zagging slopes and stepped pathways gives the feeling of exploring a bucolic hill town. Little bug hotels in the same faceted star-shaped form as the towers are a delightful touch; even the insects get a dignified dwelling.

Duggan says the project “expands the idea of the threshold”, and the arrival feels more welcoming than most. The entrance of each block is framed by a paved terrace, with seating and planting, while all have generous lobbies, no matter the tenure. It’s a far cry from the “poor door” apartheid of so much developer-built housing, where private owners get the hotel concierge treatment, while affordable tenants enter around the back by the bins. It all oozes quality on a budget, down to the choice of three dusty colours of brick, some projecting to create a textured, tweedy finish. The quality belies the tight construction budget of £2,500/sq metre – making it the cheapest project on the shortlist by far. Other Stirling Prize contenders this year included two exquisitely built projects for well-heeled Cambridge colleges, a large private house in Essex, an arts centre in Hertford, and an £825m office block in Paddington.

If there is a cloud hanging over Croydon’s triumph, it is the fate of Brick by Brick. It was established in 2015, as a wholly council-owned company, because the conventional development model was failing to deliver enough affordable homes. The idea was that Croydon would use its own land, often small leftover sites, and borrow against its own resources, to build a mix of private and affordable housing, while turning a profit for the public purse. But the sites often proved to be trickier than expected, adding additional costs, while the financial forecasts were overly optimistic, with Brexit and Covid introducing huge delays. Housing experts attribute its collapse to poor financial structuring, governance and risk management, rather than a failure in development expertise or quality of delivery.

Nonetheless, Brick by Brick built 751 homes, over half of which are affordable, of a design quality higher than most standard developer fare. With renewed housing cash from central government, might there be a chance for some of the halted schemes to be resurrected, and more of the imagination and innovation of Lion Green Road spread across the borough and beyond?

items.title: Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
paragraphs: Campus architects at Florida Southern College have updated the only planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as part of a decades-long restoration project at the school, which was masterplanned by Wright.

The restoration included interior and exterior updates of the building, known simply as the Planetarium. The structure, which sits at one end of the Polk County Science Building, has been largely closed since 2004, when the projection system stopped working.

The renovation was guided by Jeff Baker, resident campus architect and a principal at MCWB Architects. Baker has worked on Wright projects at Florida Southern College (FSC) for twenty years and said the Planetarium has long been a goal.

"Since the outset of these overall restoration efforts, the college was always looking for an opportunity to restore the Planetarium, knowing full well its potential to excite and inspire audiences of all ages as they get a glimpse into the heavens and the great genius of Frank Lloyd Wright," Baker told Dezeen.

Work on the exterior began in 2021. The team replaced the roof, flashings, failed stucco on upper portions of the facade and replaced over 280 hand-cast "textile" tiles that line the building's perimeter.
The team then moved inside starting in 2023, where "decades of interventions since Wright's death had dramatically altered the room", according to Baker.
The team updated the Planetarium's technology and audio, repainting the walls from a deep blue, and paring down or removing insertions such as a computer closet built in the 1980s.
It also included working with local craftsmen to restore the original Wright-designed seating made of plywood and colored vinyl upholstery, and repositioning it to its rightful orientation.

"The removal of the old computer closet retrieved the space as it was designed," said Baker. "This removal allowed us to restore and reinstate all the seating in its original circular form, which we learned is a very rare survival in planetariums throughout the country."
Other updates included reinstating the original paint and plaster, and restoring the floor in a "Cherokee Red" finish.
It is one of thirteen Wright buildings built between 1938 and 1958, which the university has been updating since 2007.

Previous restoration work included updating the Waterdome, Wright's largest built fountain, the Esplanades, monolithic covered walkways that traverse the campus and the towering Annie Pfieffer Chapel.

Baker said, like working on other buildings on campus, Wright's "elemental" architecture proved to be the most challenging aspect of the project, as there are "no 'poche' spaces to hide modern building systems".
"Frank Lloyd Wright spent his life conceiving architecture as a synthesis of art and structure," he said.
"At Florida Southern College, this is manifested in buildings that are elemental – the concrete floors are the ceilings for the rooms below, the concrete ceiling is also the roof above."
"We believe we were able to devise methods to insert these systems in sensitive ways that meet the needs of the college yet allowed us to retrieve Wright's vision for the space."
The team completed the ongoing work through grants from institutions such as the J Paul Getty Foundation, which supported the preparation of the original Campus Heritage Plan in 2007.
The college has used the plan as a guide to update Wright's buildings.

It is the only college Wright master-planned. FSC president Ludd Spivey commissioned the architect in 1938 and, deemed a National Historic Landmark in 2012, it is the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture in the world.
The Planetarium is now open to the campus and public for tours and screenings.
Dezeen recently rounded up six other Frank Lloyd Wright preservation projects across the US, including recent updates to the famed Falling Water house in Pennsylvania.
The photography is courtesy of Florida Southern College.

items.title: Suspected fly tippers shamed with online photos
paragraphs: The council said it had received thousands of comments on the social media posts from residents who had also "had enough" of fly tipping
ByVictoria CookBBC London and Chris SleggBBC London
A west London council that says it has "had enough" of fly tipping has begun sharing CCTV images on social media, showing people allegedly being caught in the act of dumping rubbish in public places.
Hillingdon Council described the crime as a "blight" on the borough, and as a local authority, it had "allowed the problem to get bigger".
Cabinet member for community environment and enforcement, Adam Bennett, said the action was a "really good first step" adding: "We really need to up our game on all forms of of enforcement."
He said since its CCTV images were shared earlier this week they had over 850,000 views, received 2,500 comments including information on who the perpetrators might be.
Hillingdon Council's enforcement teams have identified a hotspot outside the car park for St Anselm's Church in Hayes
Bennett said the reaction to the posts showed fly tipping was "a really important issue to residents".
Hillingdon Council says it issues a £1,000 fixed penalty fine to culprits, and last month it seized and crushed a vehicle that was linked to fly tipping.

"We've had enough as have residents, of the very small minority of individuals who choose to blight our neighbourhoods and communities by thinking it's acceptable to just dump their waste here on the pavement, on a verge, or on a lay-by."
He said by sharing images of suspects' faces the council was "taking action to try and bring the perpetrators to account".
Bennett added: "If you see your face on social media or perhaps on one of our screens in our libraries, our leisure centres, you're going to think twice about wanting to fly tip again."
Bennett explained that "a certain evidential threshold" had to be reached before identifying individuals online, but said as a council they did not want to "shy away" from the problem.

"If you're going to do it in Hillingdon, we're going to call you out for it, and we're going to take every opportunity we can to penalise you for what is unlawful environmental crime that blights the lives of our communities and all of the hard-working taxpayers in this country."
The council said images like this would be shared on their social media platforms as well as on screens in libraries and leisure centres, to identify individuals
Liberal Democrat London Assembly committee member Gareth Roberts said he was "interested" to see if Hillingdon's tactics of "naming and shaming" individuals worked to prevent fly tipping.

"We need to use everything at our disposal to make sure that we clamp down on these people who think that they can simply trash London because they're too lazy to take things to the appropriate recycling or dumping sites," he said.
This week, City Hall's Environment Committee looked at how London boroughs are responding to the problem of fly tipping, as well as the overall coordination of the response to it.
Roberts said fly tipping is a "major problem" for London and explained there were nearly half a million incidents, across the capital, last year alone.
"Unfortunately clearing up this mess costs councils money and it costs Londoners money," he said.

"What we need is governments to recognise that there is a particular problem in London. We have more fly tipping than anywhere else and it would be great if they could find a way to give councils the money and the resources and the powers to tackle this scourge which is blighting parts of London."

items.title: With $150 off, this 27in 4K monitor just became a great buy for creative work at home
paragraphs: I'd normally suggest waiting until Black Friday to invest in a monitor, but B&H Photo just rolled back the price on a 4K display that has decent colour coverage for creative work and a hub full of connectivity options.

The Dell UltraSharp 27in 4K reduced from $799.99 to $649.99 at B&H Photo was a little on the expensive side at its original price, but a $150 discount brings it into sweet-spot territory given how many boxes it ticks. items.title: Marvel fans to meet Welsh villain - complete with Cardiff accent
paragraphs: Marvel fans around the world are set to meet a Welsh villain - complete with a Cardiff accent.
Lauren Morais, from the Welsh capital, will play Lisa Molinari in the new superhero series VisionQuest - a spin-off from the miniseries WandaVision.
The Disney+ show, exploring whether AI and humanity can co-exist, also stars Paul Bettany, returning as Vision, and James Spader as Ultron.
Morais said getting the role was a "pinch me" moment and that she was "very proud" to introduce her accent to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU).
Speaking to Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales, Morais said she initially auditioned with an Essex accent for the part.
In the fourth round of auditions, she also did a northern accent and American.
But during a reading, not knowing if the Marvel team wanted a Welsh accent, Morais decided just to "go for it".
"I said, 'can she be from Cardiff?' and they were like, 'of course'. So she's from Cardiff now," she said.
Morais recalled being like "a rabbit in the headlights" surrounded by all the stars of the show, but was also worrying about who was going to cover her shift at a cinema in London.
During the audition process she was given time off for the VisionQuest auditions, even though she could not tell her manager what the auditions were for.
She said: "I went to my final Pinewood audition and then went back to the cinema to the west end to finish my shift.
"It's such a dichotomy of worlds and that's what it is as an actor, you're always grafting and then it happens and you're like, what is life."
The character of Lisa Molinari has undergone a transformation from the original Marvel comic book character - known as Coat of Arms - who gains extra arms and weapons from a mystical coat.
In VisionQuest, she is instead given a high-tech backpack equipped with robotic arms.
Morais said co-ordinating the choreography for the fight scenes was "funny".

"I'd be with the fight director who was like 'you just need to imagine that a huge arm is coming out of your right side and just absolutely go for it and imagine where it's hitting.' So I used a lot of imagination on that job," she said.
But Bettany, whose character Vision is an android attempting to piece together his wiped memories and fragile humanity, had some sage advice.
"He said 'you're going to feel very silly while you're doing these scenes, but if you commit to it, it's going to look really sick'. And I can confirm, he was right," she said.

items.title: The new GTA VI trailer looks too good to be real, but graphics aren't even its biggest achievement
paragraphs: With barely a month to go until the big release date, the real hype now begins. Rockstar Games has released a new GTA VI trailer that should win over anyone who may still be wondering what the fuss is all about or how the game could justify its price tag.

The environmental detail, lighting, character animation is of a quality that in many games would impress even as a pre-rendered cinematic, but Rockstar says the trailer was captured entirely in-game on a PlayStation 5. Yet, stunning graphics are only part of what makes the new trailer so powerful. Photorealism alone isn't enough for a game this big; the real magic is in the art direction.
Grand Theft Auto VI Launch Trailer - YouTube

More than just the end of the video game look, the new GTA VI trailer blurs the line between game design and cinematography. The saturated Florida-inspired colour palette, neon-soaked nightlife, sun-bleached suburbs and social-media-inspired imagery all work to build a world that's as cohesive and convincingly realised as a well-directed movie.

Rockstar has clearly thought about how it builds the story through environment design: the colour scripting in turquoise, pink, orange and gold, the scenes backlit by sunsets, the contrast between glamour and decay. The lighting is expressive rather than realistic, with humid atmospheric haze, neon spill lighting and strong silhouettes.

Meanwhile, Jason and Lucia's relationship is finally taking centre stage, pushing the Bonnie-and-Clyde narrative harder and giving the game a more character-driven identity. They look more natural and expressive than in earlier marketing: small gestures, posture changes and eye movements convey convincing relationship dynamics. References to Jason's military background and Lucia's time in jail build deeper motivation and a backstory with the power to draw in newcomers as much as lifelong GTA fans.

It's a story as much as a game. The impact is made complete by the introduction of Flower in a Hurricane, an original track from the French music producer Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard. Included on Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, this adds another rich cinematic element, and a blend of electro house and retro vibes that seems the perfect soundtrack for Leonida and Vice City, the game's fictionalised versions of Florida and Miami.

items.title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’
paragraphs: Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.

Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.

Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.
Attorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.

According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.
Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”

Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.

Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.

Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.

items.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
paragraphs: After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.

Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.

The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.

“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”
The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.

“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.

The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.

Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.

Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.

Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.

The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.

“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.

“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.

Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.
To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.

Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.
The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.

Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

items.title: Cinema 4D finally gets one of the most-requested features in new 2027 release
paragraphs: The software developer Maxon has rolled out its 2027.0 releases of Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Redshift, Red Giant and Autograph, bringing new creative capabilities and workflow improvements across a package that includes some of our picks as the best 3D modelling software and the best animation software.
Highlights include the introduction of new ways to populate and simulate complex 3D worlds in C4D, more complete production workflows in ZBrush and faster rendering feedback in Redshift.

Following the recent introduction of support for third-party chatbots in Cinema 4D, 2027.0 introduces a new Scatter System, delivering one of the most-requested capabilities. Artists can now procedurally populate environments with vegetation, rocks, debris, crowds and other assets while retaining precise artistic control.

Environment scattering has long been an area where Cinema 4D lagged behind dedicated ecosystem-building tools and some competing DCC applications. It makes creating forests, landscapes and large-scale scenes dramatically easier.

The new Scatter Generator and Scatter Tag support distribution, filtering, clustering and transform controls, while integration with Cinema 4D’s MoGraph toolset lets artists use familiar Fields and Effectors to shape, animate and influence scattered objects. The updates give artists a quicker and more approachable path to building dense environments without having to turn to complex workarounds or separate third-party scattering tools.
What's New in Cinema 4D 2027 - Scatter Generator - YouTube

The other feature generating buzz is Liquid FX, which adds automatic foam, spray and bubble generation to Cinema 4D's simulation system. The secondary effects respond to the underlying liquid behavior, adding the visual detail that makes pours, splashes, waterfalls and other fluid effects feel more convincing without requiring artists to construct separate complex simulations.
Cinema 4D for iPad remains in beta, with a full release expected by the end of the year.
