items.title: Two 1960s London housing estates saved from demolition after decade-long battle
paragraphs: Two architecturally celebrated council estates in south London that have been under threat of demolition for more than a decade have been saved.

Residents of Cressingham Gardens and the Central Hill estate have campaigned tirelessly for their homes to be saved, saying the low-density 1960s developments are significant in design and popular with those living there.
Lambeth council argued that the estates were in poor repair and that razing them would create badly needed social and affordable homes.
The plans were pursued when Lambeth was controlled by Labour but the Greens won the most seats at elections in May and now run the council as a minority administration.
They oppose the demolition plans, which are expected to be reversed at a meeting of the cabinet next week.
The fate of the estates attracted wider attention, in part because of their design but also because of the many years of limbo faced by tenants and leaseholders as the council pursued demolition.

A 2022 review of Homes Lambeth, the now defunct body which managed housing for the council, questioned the redevelopment plans, saying the net number of social rent homes to be created was very small.

Sir Bob Kerslake, the former head of the civil service who led the review, said “feedback was uniformly negative”, with residents of estates earmarked for development citing inconsistent policy, delays and poor communication. He added: “As a consequence, levels of trust in the council are exceptionally low.”
Both threatened estates were designed by a team of Lambeth architects led by Ted Hollamby, who championed a move away from tower blocks toward lower-rise housing.
Cressingham Gardens, which adjoins Brockwell Park, was built to encourage neighbourliness, with front doors facing each other and green spaces for play.
The Central Hill project was led by Rosemary Stjernstedt when women were rare in social housing design. It was built on a sloping site near Crystal Palace, with homes maximising natural light.

Martin Abrams, the Green leader of Lambeth, said: “This is a decisive moment for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. It recognises the relentless work of my colleagues in securing the future for these communities without demolition. We can now focus on investing in residents’ homes and bringing empty properties back into use.”

Pete Elliott, the cabinet member for housing, said: “For over 12 years, we have fought for a better future for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. These proposals end years of uncertainty and put the focus where it belongs: repairing homes, supporting communities and filling empty properties.”

items.title: From a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms back
paragraphs: The phrase “two things can be true” is a frequent refrain in popular psychology and it’s also a frequent response, I find, to witnessing the farther reaches of live art. Hmm, is this performance confusingly self-indulgent or utterly profound? Sometimes it can be both. In fact, it’s not just two things that can be true, it’s as many things as there are people in the audience, since this is all about the live subjective experience, in the moment; presence and connection.

Launched in 1998, Fierce is Britain’s longest-running live art festival. For one week it takes over Birmingham’s conventional theatres alongside unconventional spaces, especially in ex-industrial Digbeth, which is fast becoming a creative hub. Also on the bill this year: late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool, and a six-hour performance jam at a grand gothic hall that was apparently the inspiration for Cluedo.

There’s a focus on the sensuous and sensory; it’s all about the physical body. But the first piece I experience is actually in virtual reality: Traversing the Mist, by Taiwanese artist Tung-Yen Chou. The setting is a gay sauna, and the VR tech is impressive. You walk through the grey concrete corridors, locker room, showers, cubicles, pushing aside curtains that you know aren’t really there. You can open doors, pick things up, press buttons in the lift. You’re an observer of the uncanny scene, which is peopled by identical blank-faced men; a sense of searching pervades, but there’s zero joy or pleasure to be found.

The experience is a combination of immersive and detached. It’s engaging, and yet eerily lonely – and also unnerving when the floor falls away, messing with your own proprioception. You feel, but what you feel is exactly the lack of connection. (Chou is also showing a short, sit-down VR piece called In the Mist, which was a precursor to the longer work, but is basically a sad porno.)

What you’re missing in VR is the smells, the heat, the sweat. But don’t worry, there’s plenty of that elsewhere. Wojciech Grudziński’s sweaty, hairy, all-too-human fleshy body is front and centre in his solo Threesome, his bum in the air as he does upside down pliés in a shoulder stand and other yogic moves wearing bottomless frilly knickers. In voiceover he tells us of three Polish ballet dancers who were shamed for their homosexuality, and Threesome is his attempt to reclaim their true identities, and make peace with his own “ghastly” body. Is a series of bum-bearing contortions followed by a ravey, repetitive jig the best way to do that? Well, it’s Grudziński’s way. And it’s strangely compelling, building to a sort of catharsis, with lights and music and defiant mood.

Artist Melissandre Varin is known as n:u, and calls themself an “atmosphere-maker”, which is interesting branding and perhaps modifies the expectations of the audience. Fierce is a thoroughly international festival, but n:u was previously based in Birmingham, although the work is rooted in Congolese, Guadeloupean, and Beninese heritage. I caught part of a rehearsal for the piece FREE(HOLD), an opaque ritual, in which performers drag ropes around their ankles and keen to the sky. Endurance, suffering, slavery and colonialism all rushed to mind.

This is a festival full of intriguing, conversation-starting stuff, but American choreographer Faye Driscoll blows everyone else out of the water with her acclaimed, award-winning piece Weathering, which gets its UK premiere here. Driscoll’s work is a few levels up in terms of concept, commitment, execution and scale. It’s essentially 10 performers on a rotating platform, a tableau vivant, or maybe less a living tableau than one that’s slowly distorting and decaying and caving under the gravity of life’s pressures, or just the passage of time.

items.title: Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?
paragraphs: Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.
The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.
But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.

"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.
But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.
In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.
And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.

As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.
But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too.
Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

items.title: This 75,000-year-old wound suggests Neanderthal life was more violent than we thought
paragraphs: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.

A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.

Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.

The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

items.title: How Unreal Engine 5's Chaos physics was modified for this indie game about tearing down your hometown with a sledgehammer
paragraphs: Valencia-based indie game developer Deconstructeam has been around for almost 15 years and is known for its narrative games presented with 2D pixel art. But according to its founder and creative director, Jordi de Paco, the studio has always wanted to make "real" games, albeit jokingly, which brings us to its first commercial 3D game, Virtue and a Sledgehammer.

That desire to expand from 2D to 3D isn't uncommon, as with the developers of Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, but instead of expanding the team, Deconstructeam partnered with Selkie Harbour, a two-person studio with 3D expertise. But before they even started making their sledgehammer-based narrative game, they also had time to experiment together, which has already been part of the studio's process between projects.

"Oftentimes if you get too experimental the result is that you fail, so we tried to accelerate that process by making many small things to eventually find out what's next," De Paco explains. "We took that same approach with 3D games, just making small games and releasing them for free on itch.io, so we could just fail freely. The most important part of developing a successful creative endeavour is developing a context that allows you to fail. So we created that space so we could fail several times and find what's interesting for ourselves to do in 3D."

From those projects, including the short interactive essay Many Nights a Whisper, which is free to download on Steam, the two studios arrived at Virtue and a Sledgehammer, which has the player character returning to their hometown where "you are so angry, the only way through is just smashing everything" with a sledgehammer.

Although Unreal 5 has Chaos physics that allows for destructible physics, creating the destructible gameplay in Virtue and a Sledgehammer, which allows you to take your sledgehammer to any building or even the android inhabitants, required heavily modifying how its physics work.

"The logical system is totally different because the model is using a Voronoi noise on top of a mesh," Selkie Harbour's Guillermo Ferrando explains. "You have a static mesh, and you can subdivide it. When you start, you see a building that hasn't been broken; you see the static mesh is a proxy, but the moment you break it, it detects what's the closest Voronoi chunk that you've hit, generates a sphere around it, and then it breaks around that space in that moment. Instead of drawing a single mesh, you're drawing as many chunks as that mesh is subdivided into."

That kind of complexity can affect shadows and dynamic lighting, throttling the GPU, though fortunately there was an easy way to handle it. "The moment you break something, if you are playing in low or medium graphics, we kill the shadows," says Ferrando. "It's not noticeable when you play it unless you look at it, but otherwise the Steam Deck wouldn't be able to run it."

Even as a 3D game, Deconstructeam's 2D roots are still present in other ways. Take the dramatic framing of its cutscenes, which De Paco admits was directly influenced by indie narrative game 1000xResist's cutscenes, but even more so by comic books.

"To me, it's like an illustration, and I need to have in my mind where the text is going to come up and where the characters are," he explains. "It would have been way easier just to have subtitles, but to lay out the exact point, like graphic design for a magazine, for every shot was really worth it because it really draws you into where we want you to be looking at with the text."

Meanwhile, the lo-fi 3D aesthetic gives off a PS2 vibe, the console that first gave us Red Faction and is also famous for its destructible-environment gameplay. However, De Paco says it neither specifically emulates lower-poly PS2 graphics nor is it a performance choice in Unreal Engine 5.

"It's a result so that our audience from previous titles who were expecting a pixel art style that has been Deconstructeam's signature style until now can still connect with this 3D game," he explains. "We actually work with pixel art concept art, and we develop mockups for how this would look if it was one of our 2D games. Then we think about how we can port this into a 3D space."

Ferrando adds: "It's also faster to develop the pixel art models as we can get away with just displaying the shadows because the fidelity is not super high. So it makes the whole development easier, even though that's not the main reason we chose this aesthetic."

Despite the low-poly textures, the environments still had distinct details, from the architecture to small appliances, that made it clear this hometown was set in a mountain forest area on Spain's east coast rather than, say, the Pacific Northwest.

"We try to be really Spanish and convey our culture," De Paco concludes. "In cinema or other works, we are used to seeing other cultures, but for some reason with video games, we worry about making things more palatable to bigger audiences. So we need to try to actively change and be able to have different settings and cultures in our games."
Virtue and a Sledgehammer is releasing on PC on 24 October, and a free demo is available to download on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: £15m for zero-emission testing at Belfast Harbour
paragraphs: Testing technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption
Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems.
It comes after a £15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.
The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology.
Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption.
Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use
Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use.
"What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport.

"But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'.
"Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean?
"It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added.
Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said it will be "developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the Harbour"
This is the second project announced from the £30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor.
Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user.
"We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added.
It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland.
Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else."
"We already have real buy in from Foyle Port and other regions within Northern Ireland," he added.

items.title: Apple consolidates smart-home capabilities in HomeView dashboard
paragraphs: Technology company Apple has released a screen that consolidates the functions of its app products and its home-management software into one device.
HomeView is a seven-inch display meant to function as a centralised location for home controls, signalling a step forward in Apple's home integration and smart home services.
The screens come in two versions. One sits on its own, standing on a base with an integrated speaker, while the other is wall-mounted.

HomeView works similarly to other Apple touchscreen products, with a home screen, apps, widgets and a built-in front-facing camera. It has many of the same functions, including FaceTime video calling.
The product creates a physical dashboard for the Apple Home app, which was released in 2022 to control integrated functions such as smart locks, appliances, cameras and thermostats.
HomeView uses face recognition for up to six people per device in a household with personalised settings for each user, instead of the app sitting on personalised devices.
The product also includes an intercom system that can connect multiple devices within one household.

The tabletop version of the device has a distinct form, with a case and a thick base made from recycled aluminium. Its rounded base and movable screen evoke the design of the 2002 iMac G4 desktop computer.
Apple emphasised the device's potential as decor, calling it "the perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table."
It comes in four colour options: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey.
The company also noted the integration of its next-generation AI, called Siri AI.
"HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon," said Apple.
"Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness."
The release also included a lineup of updated home products such as cameras, locks and thermostats.
HomeView comes after a slate of recent releases from Apple, including the brand's first foldable smartphone.

items.title: GTA 6 - all you need to know about Rockstar's blockbuster game
paragraphs: To put it simply, the GTA franchise is one of the biggest and most profitable entertainment properties in history.
GTA 5 has sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time - which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for Rockstar.

The game's sandbox gameplay, where players can explore vast open worlds with considerable freedom - sometimes controversially - has seen it be continuously lauded as the ultimate expression for what the interactive medium can do.

Freelance video games journalist Vic Hood said each entry in the series "continued to push technical and gameplay boundaries", with GTA Online helping to "pioneer the live service model as we know it".
She added that the games were also "extremely culturally relevant" too.

"Rockstar has always had its finger on the pulse of music, entertainment, societal, political, celebrity, and online culture trends, and they've never shied away from satirising these things in GTA games," she said.

British gaming entrepreneur Sir Ian Livingstone told the BBC's Today programme that the series, originally developed in Scotland, was "bigger than any film or song" and an "incredible achievement in interactive software".
Speculation as to how a sixth game can top even the gigantic heights of its predecessor has meant that any latest news, no matter how small, has been met with a flurry of hype and excitement.
Both of GTA 6's previous gameplay trailers currently have a total of roughly 447 million views combined.

items.title: Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent
paragraphs: Naked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.

I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994.

And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.

Frieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid.

Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders.

Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest.

So do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist.

Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?

Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists, as the Guardian recently reported, are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.

Frieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes.

But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money.

This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification.

The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. The lavish view of the model’s bum as she lies on silks and the fact that she’s wearing high heels make it comically clear this is finely painted soft porn. The African art, made for religious purposes, is reduced to decor in front of this commodified body. John Berger, the radical critic who saw nude paintings and other forms of commodified art as playthings of western capitalism, might have said: told you so.

items.title: Sheep are disappearing from our hills - and our dinner plates
paragraphs: For four generations, Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm, perched on the hillside of Malhamdale amid the dramatic landscape of the Yorkshire Dales. And for most of that time, sheep were the mainstay of the business.

But, Neil says, over the past 20 years there has been "a complete turnaround" and he has shifted away from sheep farming to stay afloat. In that time the 1,500-acre farm has gone from a peak of over 800 lambing sheep to just 45 this spring.

"I dread to think where the farm would have been financially had we not started to make those changes," he tells me. "I either continued along the sheep-farming route because of sentimentality or made bold decisions."

While most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land, the changes here have been mirrored across not just the Dales but the entire British farming industry. The shepherd's life has never been an easy one, but for many it's getting tougher and more difficult than ever to make a profit.
Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm for four generations

The average British farmer is 60 years old, according to the National Farmers' Union (NFU), and prices for everything from fuel to fodder have risen hugely for them in recent years. Meanwhile, many farmers are facing significantly reduced income from subsidies and there are worries that recent trade deals will mean increased competition from overseas.
The UK's recent trade deals with New Zealand and Australia, struck since Brexit, eliminate tariffs and give producers in both countries large quotas on the amount of lamb they can export into the UK.
There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK - the lowest figure in living memory according to Phil Stocker, chief executive of the National Sheep Association.

Overall the national flock is also falling, down to 30.4 million sheep in 2025 - numbers last seen in the mid-20th Century, when the UK population was smaller and thus the potential market for lamb and mutton reared here was much lower.

And over the last 50 years there has been a significant fall in lamb and mutton consumption according to Becky Smith, a senior analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), which represents farmers.
In 1980 the average UK household purchased 128g of sheep meat (lamb and mutton) per person, per week. In 2024 that same measure was down to 23g per person, per week.
Sheep farming has shaped the image many of us have when we picture somewhere like the Dales with drystone walls to keep livestock enclosed and green, rolling hills kept short by seasonal grazing.

But any desire to protect the heritage of one of the UK's oldest agricultural industries is rubbing up against not just a diminishing appetite for sheep meat but also the question of whether some of our uplands might be better used to promote nature recovery and biodiversity.

All this raises the question of whether we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK - and, in turn, what that might mean for consumers. Will my children still be eating our lamb for their Sunday roast or in their baltis and bhunas in 25 years time?
And, what will happen to some of our most revered and beloved landscapes like the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, Scottish Highlands and Welsh mountains, and the people who live and work there?
At Craven Cattle Mart on the outskirts of Skipton, North Yorkshire, the auction ring is buzzing as farmers from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors come to buy and sell livestock.
To an outsider, business might look brisk - but general manager Jeremy Eaton says it's nowhere near as busy as when he started in the industry 47 years ago.
"We'd have some sales at this market where we'd regularly be selling 19,000 store lambs," he says. "Now we're fortunate if we get to 8,000 or 9,000."
At Craven Cattle Marts, farmers come from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors to buy and sell livestock

People who work sheep know that it's some of the hardest farming there is. A former shepherd once told me that sheep are only ever trying to do one of three things: "Escape, or die, or escape and then immediately die."

Globally, lamb consumption is expected to grow by 15% between now and 2032, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Food and Agriculture Organization.

But changing tastes in the UK mean mutton, made from mature sheep, is no longer eaten in the same volume it was by previous generations and lamb has seemingly gone from a weekly staple to a meat more often eaten on special occasions, with "white meat" like chicken being increasingly chosen over lamb and beef.
The drop in the national flock has actually led to robust growth in the price paid for lamb according to Becky Smith from the AHDB, with the sheep price hitting record highs in 2024.

But despite the higher price for their sheep, upland farmers with tight margins feel the pinch more than many when diesel and oil costs go up. And on top of that, the cost of feeding sheep has also rocketed - the average cost of a bale of hay is £155 a tonne this spring compared to £75 a tonne this time last year.
There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK, according to the National Sheep Association

Farmers and groups such as Compassion in World Farming have also raised concerns that new trade deals could undermine UK agriculture because farms here must meet high welfare standards that may not be not required in several partner countries.
Extremely tight margins mean growing numbers of younger people can't see a future in farming.

This is immediately apparent as you wander around Craven Cattle Marts. "You can see here today, most of the generation of farmers are over 60," says Hayley Baines, a 39-year-old sheep farmer from Gisburn in the Ribble Valley. "There [aren't] many young ones because there's better options."
And some welcome the decline in sheep farming.

"Fewer sheep means less suffering […] a sheep's life in the wool and mutton industries belies our reputation as a nation of animal lovers," says Mimi Bekhechi, senior vice president at the UK's People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta).
The UK's Climate Change Committee has also previously advised the government to encourage people to cut the amount of meat and dairy they consume, to combat climate change.

Matthew Cole of the NFU says a further issue has been the move - especially post-Brexit - away from farmers receiving paid subsidies from the EU either for the volume of livestock they have or amount of land they farm.
In their place, successive UK governments have introduced new schemes with a stronger focus on farming for nature - meaning many farmers are facing significantly reduced subsidy income.

For example the Westminster government's Sustainable Farming Incentive scheme, which was updated last month, includes further incentives for farmers in England to graze moorland with cattle and ponies instead of sheep as it "contributes positively to biodiversity". Cattle, for example, do not graze as low to the ground as sheep, allowing smaller plants to flower.
UK governments have introduced new schemes with a stronger focus on farming for nature
Neil Heseltine of Hill Top Farm now has 300 cattle who graze outside all year round, a shift that he says has made the farm more profitable and dramatically reduced the hours he has to put into it.
But while these new subsidy schemes are welcomed in principle by many farmers, some find the funding available falls far short of the levels provided under earlier support systems.

"Going forward, do I see a future? I'm not sure where we're going with it," says James Foster, who has been farming beef and sheep on the Bolton Abbey Estate for 30 years. "I do believe the government don't want us, but people have to eat and we just have to adapt with that."
Defra says that an average of £2.3bn a year is being invested through its farming schemes in England and insists it is protecting farmers in trade deals and also making supply chains fairer.

Today, Scottish sheep and upland farmers face many of the same challenges of tighter margins, rising costs and falling appetite for lamb and mutton and the Holyrood government have likewise tried to move towards a subsidy regime which gives greater weight to the environmental benefits farmers can provide. One example is the "Sheep and Trees" initiative which aims to help farmers and land managers plant more woodlands without cutting the size of their flock.

There have been complaints from farmers that some of the schemes introduced in Scotland have not been easy enough to access, leading the Agriculture Minister Jim Farlie to commit to reviewing certain projects. At the start of this year NFU Scotland and other farming organisations also raised concerns that the amount of government money budgeted to support agriculture was not enough either to support farmers to profitably make food or to help them meet climate and nature goals.

In Northern Ireland, the sheep population has fallen for several years with the most recent stats from 2024 showing 1.9 million sheep across the region. The Ulster Farmers Union has criticised the exclusion of sheep farmers from the devolved administration's future agriculture policy and called on Northern Ireland's Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs to engage with the industry.

Sheep were first domesticated approximately 10,500 years ago in the Middle East, and were eventually brought to British shores by Neolithic farmers some time around 4000BC. Sheep became such an important part of the landscape that by medieval times the phrase, "half the wealth of England rides on the back of the sheep" became familiar.
In Scotland, sheep have also played a pivotal role in the rural economy for generations and Scotland's sheep population there has been more stable in recent years at around 6.5 million.

The history of Scottish sheep farming is also indelibly tied up with the controversial Highland Clearances when, in the late-18th and 19th century, traditional crofting families, were moved off the land when landowners realised they could make more money from farming sheep than leasing their land.

In 2004, sheep were removed from the limestone landscapes of Ingleborough, the second-highest mountain in the Yorkshire Dales and replaced with roaming native cattle breeds, who are less intensive grazers as part of the Wild Ingleborough project.
"Going forward, do I see a future? I'm not sure where we're going with it," says James Foster (right)

Two new scientific studies published in the academic journal Ecological Solutions and Evidence, show the huge impact that change has had for nature across the 1500-hectare landscape, with plant diversity increased by over 40% and a five-fold increase in the number of butterflies in the absence of sheep.

Robyn Wrigley, from the University of Leeds School of Earth and Environment, co-authored both studies and says the research provides long-term evidence of how different grazing impacts biodiversity and can help inform discussions about restoration.
Neil Heseltine of Hill Top Farm now has 300 cattle who graze outside all year round

These changes, however, are not ones that all farmers welcome. Some I spoke to look at the landscape and see only lost livestock pasture and question how their way of life and livelihoods fit into such a future.
But David Stanners, Uplands North Group Chair at the NFU, says it's possible for the rewilding lobby and the farmers to find common ground.

"To understand better what Natural England wants from the uplands, what wildlife trusts want, they need to understand what we (the farmers) want," he says. "There needs to be compromise and respect on all sides."

But there is a ray of sunshine for the industry, according to Phil Stocker from the National Sheep Association. He believes the domestic market for sheep meat is going to keep driving forward, in large part thanks to demand from the increasing number of Muslim people in the UK.
AHDB statistics suggest that 80% of halal consumers eat lamb on a weekly basis and 64% eat mutton weekly. By contrast, only 6% of the general UK population eats lamb each week.

According to the AHDB, while Muslims make up around 6.5% of the UK population they account for 30% of lamb sales annually. Lamb is often Muslim consumers' meat of choice for family occasions and festivals like Ramadan and Eid, while mutton is a popular ingredient in curries and stews.

Because of this, Stocker says he doesn't envisage the total demise of the industry. But right now, he adds, "we're surviving by people's interest and by market demand almost in spite of the work that the policy makers and others are doing on agricultural and land management policy".
Most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land

A worst-case scenario for farmers and consumers would see UK lamb become even more expensive and less common on our shelves in favour of ever more sheep meat imported from major suppliers like New Zealand and Australia.

The AHDB project sheep are likely to decrease in number across many farms but take a walk in the Lake District or Welsh mountains in another 25 years and you will likely still see sheep dotting the hillsides.

Farmers and conservationists alike told me they need to see clear plans for what policymakers want from the uplands for the next generation. Their hope is that, as we move into the second quarter of the 21st Century, traditional sheep farmers and rewilders alike find their place in the nation's cherished uplands.
Top picture credit: Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Correction 15 October: This article was amended to make clear that the Sustainable Farming Incentive and the £2.3bn a year Defra investment apply only to England, not England and Wales as we reported. When it was first published the article mentioned the SFI but did not make clear where it was available. It was updated shortly afterwards to say it applied to England and Wales but this has now been corrected to state it only applies to England.

items.title: Young people and concussion – level 1
paragraphs: Hannah Parmenter hits her head hard when she is playing soccer at age 11. She is 21 years old now. She still has problems today.

Many young people hit their heads when they play sports. Rest is the best thing for people with head injuries. That is what doctors think in the past. But now, doctors say that going back to school soon might be better. Children who miss less school have fewer problems later. This means that going back to school helps the brain feel better.

Doctors say that parents should help kids be with their friends, not worry about school, sleep well, and exercise a little. Doctors can help kids with head injuries. Parents should not just wait for them to feel better.
Difficult words: hit (to bring the head in contact with an object), injury (when someone gets hurt).

items.title: Young people and concussion – level 2
paragraphs: Hannah Parmenter, who is now 21, got a serious concussion when she was 11 while playing soccer. She still has problems from the concussion today.

1.7 million to 3 million young people get concussions every year from playing sports. Doctors used to think that rest was the best treatment for concussions in children. But these days, researchers think that returning to school soon after a concussion might be better. Children who missed less school had fewer problems after two weeks. This means that returning to school and daily life may help the brain recover.

Doctors recommend that parents with children who get concussions should help them socialize, not miss too much school, sleep well, and do light exercise. The research shows that doctors can help kids with concussions, and they should not just wait for them to get better.
Difficult words: concussion (brain injury), treatment (medical care), recover (to be healthy again).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people and concussion – level 3
paragraphs: According to data, 1.7 million to 3 million young people suffer concussions each year while playing sports.

Previously, the treatment for concussions in young people was rest. However, researchers at Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C. suggest that rest may no longer be the best treatment for young people with concussions. Pediatric neuropsychologist Dr. Chris Vaughan said that there was a time when a diagnosis involved a couple of fingers and if the patient could stand, they could return to play.

Researchers found that children who missed less school after a concussion had fewer lingering symptoms, indicating that returning to school and daily life may be therapeutic for the brain. The study suggests that parents with children who suffer concussions should push socialization, reduce school-related stress, maintain a normal sleep/wake schedule, and encourage light-to-moderate physical activity. The findings reinforce the idea that there are things that can be done to help treat concussions in children and that it is not a wait-and-see type of injury.
Difficult words: lingering (lasting for a long time), socialization (the activity with others), reinforce (to strengthen or support).

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2: 10 things the hands-on previews have told us
paragraphs: I fully expected we’d still be arguing about Link’s face by now, because when The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake first debuted, the new art style split opinion right down the middle, and plenty of fans wondered whether Nintendo had binned the look of one of the most loved adventures ever made. Those fears eased the more we saw, and when Nintendo finally revealed what its Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake looks like on Switch 2, it began to convert even the harshest critics.

Now, the first hands-on previews are out, and the conversation has moved on. Journalists got an hour or two wandering Kokiri Forest, the Great Deku Tree, Castle Town and the Forest Temple, and the general feeling is that this is a lot more than a fresh coat of paint on the 1998 classic, with new controls, richer environments, extra dialogue, voiced cutscenes and fixes for some of the creakier bits of the original, even if not everybody is sold on every change.

Pretty much every preview agrees. The new Hyrule keeps the shapes and colours of the N64 original but rebuilds all of it with far more detail, and Nintendo Life’s Gavin Lane loved the little environmental touches, from the grain in the wood and foliage to the stitching on Link’s tunic, while GamesRadar+ reckons the softer, warmer art direction works a lot better in motion than it did in that first reveal.

The lighting gets praise, and the Forest Temple gets pools of sunlight, deep shadow, drifting mist, and wooden corridors you could stare at for ages, so places feel different rather than just sharper. Some people have spotted shimmering in close-up footage of hair and foliage, which is worth keeping an eye on, but plenty of doubters seem to have come round.

Nintendo could have upscaled the 3DS version and called it a day, and clearly didn’t. The environments have been rebuilt, the camera updated, and familiar areas given new touches, with Castle Town now feeling connected rather than like the string of fixed-camera spaces we remember.

The broad layout is still what you’d expect, so you’ll know exactly where you found the Kokiri Sword and where the Deku Tree and Forest Temple sit, and VGC’s Chris Scullion came away feeling the appeal of the original had survived while the clunkiness that lingered in the 3DS version had been smoothed off. Nobody’s turning this into Breath of the Wild, which is the point.

It sounds minor, but in the original, Link hopped automatically off certain ledges, which was clever for its time and a pain when you were lining up something fiddly. Now there’s a dedicated button, and you decide when to leap, but Nintendo Life says it takes some getting used to, especially mid-fight, when years of muscle memory will have you reaching for the old way. Don’t expect Link to start scaling every wall in sight, mind you, because exploration is still the structured, Ocarina kind.

Z-targeting is still there, so locking on and waiting for an opening is still how fights work, which should put anyone who feared Nintendo would swap the paced encounters for something more frantic at ease. The jump button changes jump attacks: you now jump and then swing instead of doing it in one go, and veterans will fumble that for a while. The bigger gain is the move to 60fps, and VGC points out the original ran at 20, so dodging and reacting to enemies feels far more responsive than it ever did on N64.

Anyone who remembers pausing the game repeatedly to swap boots in the Water Temple will understand why this matters. You can now switch equipment quickly without sitting through the old pause-menu animation, so the bow, Hookshot, and potions are far less of a faff, and the on-screen map makes it easier to track where you are and which rooms you’ve done.

You also get different HUD options, including a minimal one and one that turns the HUD off completely, which suits both the modern-conveniences crowd and the cinematic-purist crowd. The Water Temple will still test your patience, but at least the boots are less of a chore.

You’d expect the dungeons to get the biggest changes, but it’s the town that seems to have had the most thoughtful overhaul. In the original, the market and its backstreets felt like separate spaces, with fixed camera angles hiding what the hardware couldn’t do; now the centre, shops, and alleys all connect, and you can rotate the camera freely.

It’s livelier too, with more detailed surroundings and extra dialogue, and characters will chat to Link as he walks past instead of waiting for him to start every conversation. GamesRadar+ also spotted new backstreets and a fleshed-out layout, plus the famously bearded man in the market, who can now point Link to another character by using his beard as a sort of tracking device, daft and brilliant in equal measure.

This is the one that’ll keep getting argued about until the full game lands. Cutscenes feature voice acting, including Navi and the Great Deku Tree; Ganondorf gets his own lines, and Link stays silent.

Some people love hearing the characters speak because it brings the game closer to modern Zelda, while others find the performances a bit cartoonish compared with the atmosphere they remember, and early Reddit threads are split between both camps, with a few comparing the English voices to an anime dub. It isn’t a fully voiced RPG, mind you; ordinary conversations still rely on text, and the voices are reserved for selected scenes.

The overhaul isn’t just about prettier scenery, and the Forest Temple is the best example so far, with dark wooden corridors, heavy shadow, stained-glass windows, and shafts of sunlight that make it feel more unsettling than the stark original. GamesRadar+ was especially taken with the lighting, and The Verge’s preview said much the same about how the visuals make the temple scarier.

Ocarina was never a horror game, but its dungeons were always a bit eerie, and the music and ghostly encounters here are some of the most memorable in the series, so leaning into that makes sense. All that detail can backfire, too, because Kotaku pointed to a preview account of a player missing an important key chest simply because the room was too busy to look at.

For longtime fans, the most reassuring thing is that the dungeon layouts, puzzle solutions and progression all seem faithful to the original. Don’t go in expecting Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, because Ocarina’s dungeons focus on keys, locked doors, backtracking, and figuring out where a newly found item fits on the bigger map.

The game tweaks enemies and encounters, and the new movement options will change how you approach a few situations, but nothing suggests a radical redesign. Nobody can say yet whether that slower, more deliberate structure will land with players raised on modern Zelda, and a couple of hours isn't enough to judge every dungeon.

The mood has shifted a lot since the reveal. On Reddit, some people who were unsure about the art style say the new footage has won them over, while others are excited to play with modern controls and a few extra details. The voice acting is divisive; some aren’t convinced by the new dialogue, veterans will have to adjust to the jump button, and Navi’s extra commentary has people wondering whether the remake sometimes explains things the visuals already make obvious.

These are previews, not reviews, so we still don’t know how the changes hold up over the whole adventure, how it runs in handheld mode, or what else Nintendo is keeping back. Either way, Nintendo clearly took this seriously and revisited how Ocarina of Time feels to play instead of just updating the graphics, which could make it a lot more than a nostalgia trip for anyone who played it in 1998.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on 5 November, 2026.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Physical Edition)

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
paragraphs: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the competition watchdog, forcing it to investigate the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the investigation so the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) could address public interest considerations including:
The need for free expression of opinion in news media
The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of viewers.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.

A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."

An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.

"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.

She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

items.title: People have a lot of big feelings about Aslan's character design
paragraphs: For many, the Chronicles of Narnia bring back fond childhood memories, whether it's the original children's book series or the iconic 2005 movie. With Greta Gerwig's new adaptation on the horizon, there are already some strong feelings about the film's stylistic choices – especially when it comes to Aslan.

As a key figure in the franchise, Aslan's character design is not something you want to mess up. Taking a more abstract approach to the lion's look, Narnia purists are already kicking up a fuss, proving that, to some, character design can make or break a movie.
NARNIA: THE MAGICIAN’S NEPHEW | Official Trailer | Netflix - YouTube

Our glimpse of Aslan in the new trailer is fairly brief, but by no means forgettable. Prowling out of the darkness, the lion emerges as a cluster of stars whose mighty roar births the universe, but the more spiritually abstract take on the character has divided audiences.

"Looks like an LG TV commercial," one critic wrote. "Tell me this doesn’t look like AI I dare you," another added. "Why are people calling this magic? It looks like every cheap sci-fi flick. The average fan just eats up any blurry colors and calls it genius," one X user critiqued.

Many critics have brought up the book's supposed representation of Aslan as Jesus, stating that Gerwig's explosive universe-building is a take on the Big Bang, and thus a snub to creationism. Others have said the scene isn't book-accurate, as Aslan sings Narnia into existence, contrasting with his ferocious roar in the trailer.

I find myself torn on Aslan's representation, and until I see the full film, I'm anxious to pass judgement. To me, Gerwig's adaptation captures the magic and whimsy of the original book series, even if it isn't strictly accurate. Having a less literal depiction of Aslan feels more enriching than the 2005 film, giving him a transcendental quality that's open to interpretation. At its core, the Narnia franchise is for children, and the director's modernised take is an immersive experience set to ignite the imaginations of a new generation of fans.
For more design inspiration, take a look at the Narnia posters or check out the response to the Narnia logo.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: I asked Nvidia RTX Spark's AI agent to run Blender for me – here's what happened
paragraphs: Agentic computing is here, as Microsoft and Nvidia recently announced. Nvidia’s RTX Spark technology is at the centre of this new way of thinking about your PC, and the company is aiming it squarely at creatives.

The idea is that local AI agents running on your machine can act as “teammates” rather than “tools”. RTX Spark lets you use them as productivity assistants, which could be a real help for anyone who struggles to get their admin done. But the bigger news is that the built-in agents (Hermes, Perplexity and OpenClaw) are designed to interact directly with a whole host of apps, including creative ones. You can read more in my RTX Spark explainer, which goes into the benefits of local AI as opposed to running it on the cloud and exactly what the technology can do.

The premise is that an agent saves you time on busy work, freeing you up to do more creating. Nvidia also hopes it will help specialist creatives become more multidisciplinary, a skill increasingly in demand. That raises a bigger question about whether this is a good thing. The more technology democratises skills, the more creatives are expected to do, and the implications for the creative industries are enormous. But for the individual creative who can use Blender but not DaVinci Resolve (for example), there is clear benefit, and it could help small teams punch above their weight.

I’m not a professional creative by any means: Photoshop is about the limit of my skills. But I wanted to see how these agents work with creative apps, so I picked Blender, which I don’t know how to use and which gave me the highest possible barrier to entry. A creative pro will explore multiple apps in more depth soon, but for now I tried some tasks in Blender to see how easy it was to dive in as a complete beginner, whether the agent could do the work of a teammate, how quickly it worked, and what the experience was like.

Setup was straightforward, with instructions for installing the Hermes agent. Hermes then guided me through which software versions I needed, how to download them and how to grant the relevant permissions.

As a beginner, I started by asking the agent what it could actually do in Blender. It came back with an extensive list of abilities, from editing and scripting to rendering stills and setting up cameras and lights. It also said it could do “scene surgery”, such as moving an object from one scene to another, and batch file operations.

I ran a few tasks through Hermes, and it handled the simple ones really well. I started by asking it to open a stock file of a barbershop scene and make the lighting much warmer. It did this with a script instructing Blender, then offered to confirm visually that the scene looked warmer. I said yes, and it checked and confirmed. I then asked it to put the before and after images side by side and export, which it did easily.

Hermes struggled with more complex, multi-step edits on this first time round. I asked it to change the hair colour of a stock model with curly hair and add clown make-up to its face. It changed the hair and eye colour quickly and easily.

The clown make-up was harder. Hermes spent a long time trying to render the additions before bringing back an approximation of the design. From then on it worked one step at a time, asking for approval almost every time, even for small iterations like bringing the mouth more in line with, well, the mouth. I stopped after about half an hour, and this is where we got to (above). If I had the skills and inclination, I could refine the model by hand, so it could work as a starting point for a more in-depth project. Alternately if I had more experience in Blender, I could probably have been clearer with my instructions, which may or may not have helped.

I then started a project from scratch and asked the agent to build a mouse with a long tail and big ears (see above). The result was a little rough looking (that mouth!), but it was built quickly and simply. The first render didn’t show the long tail because of the camera position, so Hermes asked if I wanted to change the camera angle so it could build a visible tail, which was helpful. I confirmed and it made the image quickly.

Next I asked it to remove a model from one file and put it in the barbershop chair in my barbershop scene. After about 25 minutes of prep work, it estimated the job would take 5-10 minutes, and promised me it could do it after I repeatedly checked it was sure. By my deadline it had been working for about an hour and a half and still hadn’t finished.

So the agent is slow when you first ask it to complete a new task. But the technology works by learning the skills you train it in, so when you return to a task it should know what to do, including logging any mistakes and feedback. If you understand the software well, you can probably speed this up with better prompts. With time invested, it’s easy to see how this could become more useful, whether for beginners or for repetitive tasks you’d rather avoid.

The agent talks to itself constantly while working through more complex tasks. It’s unclear whether that is a genuine thought process or a simulation designed to make you feel in control. It is reassuring to see what it’s doing, but frustrating to watch it tie itself in knots over something that could be searched online in a couple of seconds. At times I wanted it to just say “I can’t do that” rather than go around in circles – but maybe it would have got there in the end if I'd had left it for long enough. That may be part of its learning process, and as it logs its steps into skill files the behaviour may lessen over time, but I can’t say for sure.

As a beginner, I appreciated how Hermes offered a gateway into a creative app I had never used before. It lowered the barrier to entry in a practical way, which could help creatives who are branching out or new hobbyists. Human direction will still be needed to steer, choose and refine the final outputs, but for many people this could be a significant productivity boost. That said, it was slow and needed a lot of hand-holding on complex tasks, and the usual AI concern remains that the technology could replace human teammates. We’re a long way from anywhere near that skill that at the moment – currently it has potential as a useful assistant, which is exactly how Nvidia is pitching it.

It’s impressive how the agent communicates with Blender through Python scripts and keeps the user informed throughout. Creative software apps are reportedly being rewritten for Spark, which suggests the creative tech companies are behind it. If the agent keeps improving with training, it could become more useful for the tasks creatives would rather not spend time on, and for speeding up workflows. It's one to keep an eye on.
Stand by for our full testing overview from a creative professional across multiple apps, coming soon.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.

items.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark: All creatives need to know
paragraphs: “iPhone made people think differently about smartphone, RTX Spark is going to make people think differently about the PC”: Nvidia.

Nvidia Spark is here to usher 'a new paradigm of personal computing' that puts agentic AI front and centre on a Windows PC. The RTX Spark technology puts a Blackwell RTX GPU and an Arm CPU on one chip, sharing up to 128GB of memory, in Windows laptop built for local AI agents. This could change the workflow of creatives in a host of different ways – including opening up how you interact with creative software and accelerating a spectrum of creative workflows.

I went to the launch day last week, and saw a room full of demos showcasing the tech's potential for creative workflows and gaming – including video editing, CAD, community game modding, productivity overhauls and more. It's clear Nvidia and its partners are committed to the future of agentic computing: but what does this mean for creatives?

NVIDIA announced RTX Spark on 31 May at GTC Taipei, calling it a superchip for Windows PCs built around personal AI agents. It joins a Blackwell RTX GPU, with 6,144 CUDA cores and fifth-generation Tensor Cores, to a 20-core Arm-based Grace CPU over NVIDIA's NVLink-C2C link. MediaTek collaborated on the CPU design.

The CPU and GPU share up to 128GB of unified memory, and NVIDIA quotes up to 1 petaflop of AI compute. Laptops from ASUS, Acer, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Gigabyte, Microsoft Surface and MSI are all up for release, in 14 to 16-inch designs as thin as 14mm.

It runs Windows 11 on Arm. Apps with a native Arm version run directly, and everything else goes through Microsoft's Prism emulation layer. NVIDIA also says the laptops deliver equivalent performance on battery and plugged in – which is one of the biggest improvements compared to its older laptops.

A normal laptop GPU has its own small pool of video memory. On RTX Spark the GPU shares the CPU’s pool of up to 128GB, so big scenes and models aren’t capped. NVIDIA says that means rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes, editing 12K 4:2:2 video and running 120-billion-parameter language models locally. The GPU’s share is adjustable in the NVIDIA App, and NVIDIA’s largest local model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, needs a 128GB machine with at least 78GB given to the GPU.

Important parts for creators are privacy and cost. Local models mean footage and client assets don't have to leave the machine, and there are no per-generation cloud fees. The data example I saw at the launch is that the 61m tokens it would take to complete a heavy creative workflow will cost $20 in electricity, as opposed to the $1200 token cost it would take in API fees.

As this is hybrid intelligence, and the local AI can't yet do everything, there's the NeMo Switchyard Verifier, which kicks in when the task is sent to the local LLM. This decides if the task can stay local, or needs to be sent up to the cloud.

One of the most impressive parts of the launch is how many apps Nvidia has worked with to ensure optimisation with the Spark technology. More than 100 Windows software providers, including Adobe, Blackmagic Design, Blender, CapCut, ComfyUI and OTOY, are backing the platform. With Adobe actually rewriting its Premiere Pro and Photoshop apps from the ground up to suit Spark, it's clear many software companies see the potential here.

I saw a CAD workflow move from proposal to fully rendered 3D design in 26 minutes using AI. This is a process that usually takes weeks. For solo creatives, this kind of tech is potentially a good thing – it will allow you to create whole studio's worth of work individually. But as usual with AI advancements, the impact on team structure and the need for jobs will be immense. When we're talking about some creative workflows, the old Adobe-style argument is that that just means creatives can do more – but in this instance, how many buildings really need to be built?
Anyway, let's look at the impacts on other creative apps:

Nvidia frames the new PC tech as moving from "tool to teammate". Essentially, you can use a trio of AI agents as a team of assistants, who will prepare assets and set up workflows. Two open-source agents, Hermes Agent and OpenClaw, are getting native Windows apps that can carry out tasks in Windows applications, work across apps, generate images and video, and search local files. Adobe says it will extend Premiere and Photoshop so people can create, edit and design with Windows agents.

That means that the most powerful advancement is that these AI agents will interface with these creative apps for you. Yes, you read that right. You don't even have to go into the app to utilise its tools and features – you can describe to the agent what you want it to do, and it will open the app, individual file, and apply the edits or create the work natively within the application.

This is exciting and alarming, depending on how you look at it. In a world in which creatives are increasingly expected to be multi-disciplinary, this functionality will allow you to use apps you don't have specialist knowledge of. Alarming because, well, obviously it's another shortcut on human skill. However, in line with much of the creative AI narrative, the sell is that the human remains the director, the refiner, the ultimate creative – the technology is there to speed it up, make it simpler, enable more creativity and eliminate busy work. Where you sit on this probably fluctates, and it isn't a simple conversation.

The agents can also work as admin/productivity assistants. They can connect to your files, email account, calendar and more and stay on top of your daily workflow. This is probably appealing for the majority of creatives, as this is the true busy work we'd all like to eliminate.
