items.title: BBC News channel launches on YouTube for viewers in UK and US
paragraphs: The BBC News channel has been made available to stream live on YouTube for viewers in the UK and USA.
The trial, which began on Thursday, external, has been described by BBC bosses as "a significant step" in expanding access to "trusted, impartial journalism in more places people use every day".
The move is an expansion of what the BBC has already done in other countries, with the news channel also available to YouTube viewers in Australia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Poland.
Broadening access to the service forms part of the BBC's wider strategy to reach digitally-native new and younger audiences.
The channel offers rolling coverage of international and domestic news, as well as breaking news and the latest developments in the worlds of politics, business, technology, culture and sport.
The BBC's YouTube strategy is widely seen a response to the increasing fragmentation of audiences.
The guarantees that viewers sit down and turn on their favourite channel - whatever is on it - are long gone.

Now, their TV sets take them into a world of infinite choice and the BBC (along with the UK's other public service broadcasters) knows it needs to go to where audiences are - as well as trying to entice them to its own platforms.
Thursday's development is part of the specific drive by the BBC to take its trusted news to audiences who aren't tuning in to the news channel directly or via the iPlayer.

BBC News's director of AI, innovation and growth, Anjali Kapoor, said in a statement that audiences "increasingly expect news to be available wherever they are, on the platforms they use throughout their day.
"Launching the BBC News channel on YouTube in the UK and US is an important step in bringing our trusted journalism to even more people."

She added: "It will make it easier for audiences to access live coverage of the stories shaping our world, while helping us reach new audiences in the places and at the times that work best for them."
The move is all part of the fight to combat the disinformation taking hold across social media and beyond.
But it also won't hurt in the continuing negotiations over the BBC's charter and its future funding after 2027.

This is another signal to the government that the BBC takes its mission seriously; that it is the place for trusted, impartial news and that it understands it must make that news available as widely as possible.
However, viewers in the UK, watching the channel live on YouTube, may not realise they still need a TV licence to do that.

But with no guardrails around who's watching, no ability - for now anyway - for the BBC to insist you prove you've paid the fee before you can access its YouTube channels (or its own streaming channels), it's going to be hard to enforce.
First launched on UK TV in 1997 under the name BBC News 24, the service became the BBC News Channel in 2008.
In 2023, it merged with BBC World News into one channel called BBC News, which is also available via the broadcaster's iPlayer, website and app.
Last year, broadcast regulator Ofcom revealed in its annual report that YouTube had become the UK's second most-watched media service, behind only the BBC.

One in five young viewers were going to the video sharing platform first when they turn on their smart TVs, the country's media watchdog found, while older people were also watching more of its content.
Earlier this year, the BBC announced a landmark deal with YouTube, which will see the corporation make content that is tailor-made for the video streaming service.
The new programmes will feature adverts when viewed from outside the UK, generating extra funds for the corporation at a time when its future funding model is being debated.

items.title: Pope.L review – savage satire from Y-fronts-wearing trickster famed for gruelling ‘crawl’ across New York
paragraphs: Seven squares are pinned to the wall, each one painted in the high style of American minimalism: pure, austere variations on a theme. At the centre of each is printed the phrase “negro idea” followed by an apparently random number (51, 37, 666). What is Pope.L, the late, great trickster of contemporary American art, getting at?

Perhaps it is a critique of how minimalism, with its ethos of art-for-art’s sake, excluded politics from art? Or a comment on how racial categories are as constructed (and as subject to fashion) as the theories underpinning contemporary art? Or is it a riff on how the edifice of western modernism is built on stolen ideas? Then again, maybe the deployment of an outmoded racial category is simply designed to discomfort the liberal pieties of those people likely to visit this art gallery just off Piccadilly.

All that is certain is that Pope.L cannot be pinned down. Best known for his gruelling “crawl” across New York, this influential artist and writer didn’t use art to make himself understood. Instead, he used its tools to dismantle the liberal presumption that other people and communities can easily be understood, categorised and explained away. He was less interested in being “seen” than in making his audience look again at themselves and the world, and paved the way for a new generation of artists for whom identity – in the sense of conforming to external expectations – is not only a creative trap but a form of control.

This is most apparent in Pope.L’s deep suspicion of the commercialisation of Black culture, and the stereotypes that serve to commodify and defuse it. His satire is savage and furious, closer in spirit and ambition to the provocations of Dada than to any more straightforward satire of the art world. Take the photograph Foraging (Mr Mau Mau), in which he appears in white Y-fronts and white bunny ears, with a note pinned to his chest referencing the Kenyan anti-colonial uprising (and Britain’s notoriously brutal repression). More Y-fronts are framed on the walls, smeared in brown and white fluid and handwritten insignia (“I have something important to share with you – Cliff G”). The numbered series is entitled Real Kitsch.

The way that words and images settle into fixed categories (cliche and kitsch, respectively) is a recurring theme. In Identity What We Lose to Real For, completed a year before the artist’s death in 2023, block wooden letters like those used to teach children the alphabet fall off their frame, further confusing a short text that reads like a dense concrete poem. The surface is spattered with paint, recalling painterly expressionism and a toddler’s paint-flinging (neighbouring series of scrawled Xs and Os likewise summon conceptual painting and a half-understood game of noughts and crosses). Art here is dismantling conventional ways of thinking and naming.

Short films documenting a selection of Pope.L’s performances are screened in a back room. Dressed in a figure-hugging Superman costume and with a skateboard strapped to his back, the artist crawls on his belly from the Statue of Liberty to the Bronx. As he is barracked by strangers, you wonder why so many are offended by the performance yet unmoved by the numerous homeless people in New York.

In a performance-lecture he situates his work on the “sidewalk of national consciousness”, and the world crowds into every work in this show: a white painting might look like a romantic abstraction but is in fact, as the text along its edge tells us, a picture of Martin Luther King’s Dick as Seen from Pluto. Fifteen years after Pope.L made this gag, incidentally, research was undertaken on Kazimir Malevich’s 1915 Black Square. It was discovered that the monochrome painting, long hailed as an icon of art’s transcendent possibilities, had a hidden title: Negroes Battling in a Cave.

Here is more evidence for Pope.L’s argument that art can never entirely be insulated from the nature of the world that produces it, no matter how pure a painting might appear to the eye. This point is most clearly illustrated by his long-running and highly complex engagement with the work of Robert Ryman (a survey of whose monochrome white paintings is now on show at the Barbican in London).

Pope.L memorably described himself as “the son” of Ryman and therefore duty-bound to “walk in his footsteps to the front door of the family mansion and burn it to the ground”. While it is a shame that this show does not include more of his direct responses to the painter, the two exhibitions can constructively be seen in counterpoint.

items.title: Resident Evil 2, 3 and 4 are great on Switch 2, but Capcom has missed a trick
paragraphs: Content warning: this article discusses graphic violence, disturbing imagery, and mature themes in an 18+ game.

Capcom's remakes of Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3 and Resident Evil 4 are big, cinematic games, full of moody lighting, detailed environments and things I'd rather not encounter in a dark corridor. Read our Resident Evil 4 Remake review on PS5 to see why this game is considered a modern classic.

Getting all three running on Nintendo Switch 2 is an impressive technical achievement, and the RE Engine does a fine job of bringing their grim worlds to a portable screen, something the publisher has excelled at in 2026 following successful versions of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata and Dragon’s Dogma 2.

After spending time with the collection, though, I can't help but think Capcom has focused on getting the games running and given less thought to how they should play on Nintendo's handheld. Now, we all know, and if you didn’t, Resident Evil 2 Remake is exceptional, Resident Evil 3 Remake is good but takes some liberties, and finally Resident Evil 4 Remake is a fantastic update of many fans' favourite game of all time (I have my own peccadillos with its controls and repetition, but that’s me). So the question isn’t whether they're good games, but whether they're good on Nintendo Switch 2.

My biggest gripe is the inconsistent approach to motion controls. Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3 lack gyro aiming on Switch 2, even though motion controls fit this kind of game naturally. I like being able to make small aiming adjustments with the controller while using the analogue stick to turn and move. When ammunition is scarce and a zombie is closing in, that extra precision can make a real difference.

Resident Evil 4 does offer gyro aiming, but the implementation is restrictive. While you’re holding the right stick, motion aiming is locked to horizontal movement only, so you can’t use the gyro for fine vertical adjustments. It’s a curious compromise, especially when the other two games don’t offer gyro aiming at all. That’s a shame, because gyro helps most with vertical precision when lining up headshots.

I'd also have liked to see support for the Switch 2's mouse mode, as too few games do, and these three, RE4 in particular, would have been a fun adaptation. It would have given us another way to aim and helped distinguish these versions from straightforward ports of games we've been playing for years on PlayStation and Xbox. In fairness, Capcom producer Masato Kumazawa has stated they tried to get mouse control working, but it "confused the gameplay and became too complicated". As repirted on on time coins Instead, Capcom has left some useful hardware features on the table, unless it plans to add extra touches in post-release updates, which is always on the cards for a publisher like Capcom that loves supporting fans.

The frustration is that the games themselves make such a strong case for playing on Switch 2, especially after RE Requiem proved so successful at bringing survival horror to handhelds. Resident Evil 2 is the highlight for me (and always has been of the three), with the Raccoon City Police Department retaining its oppressive atmosphere and carefully staged lighting. The game targets 60fps, and the overall presentation makes a convincing transition to Nintendo's console.

Resident Evil 3 fares well, too. Its streets, fire effects and neon-lit environments retain much of their visual character, and the faster pace suits portable sessions. My reservations are more about the game itself than the conversion. The remake's shorter, more streamlined approach still leaves me wanting more after the excellent Resident Evil 2.

Resident Evil 4 puts more pressure on the hardware with its busier combat and detailed environments that make compromises easier to spot, particularly when playing in Switch 2’s handheld mode; for example, some textures look softer, and pop-in and performance dips can take the edge off the presentation in demanding sections, such as the infamous village encounter.

These aren't problems that make these three classic Resident Evil games unplayable. Far from it; in fact, it's worth celebrating that such substantial games can run on a handheld at all, and there's real pleasure in dipping into a survival horror campaign away from the television. But visuals are only part of the job, and controls matter just as much, which is where Capcom's approach feels a little uneven.

If you haven't experienced these three remakes yet, the Switch 2 is a compelling entry point. You get three major Resident Evil adventures in a portable format, plus bonus content to round out the package, and it’s a nice narrative run-up to the events of Requiem for completionists. Being able to explore the police station, escape Nemesis, or work through the Spanish countryside wherever you are is a genuine draw.

I'm less convinced that existing owners need to rush out and buy them again. If you already have the games on PC or PlayStation, the main reason to double-dip is portability and the option to have a complete collection on one new system. There's no substantial new content here to change the experience, and the control options don't do enough to make these versions feel purpose-built for Nintendo's console.

That Nintendo-designed intent feels like a missed opportunity, especially since RE4 made the Wii famous (alongside Resident Evil 2 on N64, Resident Evil 0, and other entries that made Nintendo a destination). Gyro aiming could have been a useful addition to two games that currently lack it, while a more flexible implementation in Resident Evil 4 would have made the feature worth using. These are small changes in the grand scheme of a port, but they're the kind of details that can make a familiar game feel right at home on a new platform.

Capcom deserves credit for bringing three demanding remakes to Switch 2 without losing what makes them work. The atmosphere remains intact, the games look good on a portable screen, and Resident Evil 2 in particular is a fine showcase for the hardware.

But I want more than a game that simply runs on a new console. I want the developer to think about what that console can add to the experience, too. Here, the lack of gyro aiming in Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3, coupled with the feature's limitations in Resident Evil 4, makes the collection feel like a missed opportunity.

If you're new to these games, I'd happily point you to them, not least because each comes as the Deluxe/Complete/Gold edition, loaded with extras, new modes, and more. If you've already played them elsewhere, I'd weigh up how much you value handheld gaming before buying again. These are excellent remakes, but Capcom could have made their Switch 2 versions feel considerably more at home.

Resident Evil 2 stands out in Capcom's Switch 2 trilogy, bringing the terrifying corridors of the Raccoon City Police Department to handheld with impressive visual detail and a 60fps target. Its lighting, atmosphere and tense exploration remain as effective as ever, making this an excellent way to experience one of the series' best remakes.

Resident Evil 3 makes a convincing transition to Switch 2, retaining the neon-lit streets, spectacular effects and frantic encounters that give its shorter campaign plenty of energy. Performance is generally impressive, making it easy to dip into Jill Valentine's escape from Raccoon City on the move. The port can't fix the remake's biggest weakness: its streamlined story feels slight next to Resident Evil 2.

Resident Evil 4 remains a superb action-horror adventure on Switch 2, with Leon Kennedy's trip through rural Spain delivering tense encounters and wonderfully chaotic combat. The hardware handles this demanding remake impressively, though softer image quality, texture pop-in, and occasional performance dips reveal the compromises. Gyro aiming is included, but its restrictive implementation feels undercooked.

items.title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
paragraphs: Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.
A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.
Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.
Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.
Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.
"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.
He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.
The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.
More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

items.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
paragraphs: An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in ChatGPT owner OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, logging its worst performance since July.

The sell-off comes after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher than expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid, said.

Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”

The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said earlier this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.

The latest jitters hit China, where Shanghai’s CSI 300 slipped as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.

European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.
In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

items.title: No amount of renaming can fix AI's growing reputation problem.
paragraphs: It's the oldest branding trick in the book. If your product has a reputation problem, just change the name. Simple!

In 2000, the California Prune Board persuaded the authorities to allow prunes to be called "dried plums". More recently, Patagonian toothfish have become known as Chilean Sea Bass. (Be honest, which would you order in a restaurant?)
Similarly, political strategists in the early 2000s such as Frank Luntz advised conservatives to use the term "climate change" instead of "global warming" because it sounded less alarming.

So I wasn't entirely surprised when a few days ago, Elon Musk took issue with a term people have started using to describe AI music. "Calling it slopcore is a misnomer," he said. "Frankly, it's awesomecore."

It sounds like a joke, but the owner of X was deadly serious. And it echoes recent attempts by President Trump to rebrand "artificial intelligence" as "super intelligence". He even declared on Truth Social that anyone who still says "artificial intelligence" should be considered "THE ENEMY!"

As a journalist, words are my bread and butter, and I've spent 30 years keeping track of this stuff. In the same way people remember what they were doing on 9/11, I remember when Philip Morris became Altria, when Windscale became Sellafield, and when Royal Mail briefly became Consignia (before everyone laughed and it changed back).
All these stories point to the same clear lesson. It's rare to rebrand something that's going well. A new name is usually a sign that the old one has become toxic.

That, then, is the deeper truth here. The people pushing AI hardest are starting to wake up to the fact that the public isn't buying it. And I'm not talking about conspiracy nuts, the kind of people who spend their whole life lurking on Reddit. I mean the actual general public, all of us, in our billions.

I've yet to meet anyone who likes AI music, even though many of us have been tricked into listening to it. Nor do data centres seem to have many fans, regardless of people's political leanings. In the US, a national Gallup survey found 70% of Americans were opposed to them being built in their communities. And according to Data Center Watch, some 45 data centre projects worth $68 billion were blocked or delayed by local pushback between April and June.

For those of us who work in a creative profession, there's something reassuring in all this. The AI-boosting elite know they're losing the argument. If they were winning, they wouldn't need new words.

That's not to say I'm an AI luddite. But to my mind, there's a big difference between a tool that helps you work and a flood of autogenerated content that's drowning out real creative voices. Thankfully, ordinary people are increasingly able to tell the difference, they're calling out slop, and it's making the elites realise they can't just do what they like.

A good brand is what people say about you when you're not in the room. Right now, what they're saying is "slop". Elon can call it awesomecore all he likes. But ultimately, he just sounds like an unpopular schoolkid trying to give themselves a cool nickname: very desperate indeed.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
paragraphs: Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

items.title: This artist's epic pencil art has made him a rising star in indie comics
paragraphs: Fábio Simão dos Santos is a rising talent in the US indie comic industry who has been making a living as an artist since 2019. Currently working as a freelance comic book penciler, he says he has always loved comics and graphic arts.

items.title: The $20,000 MrBeast logo auction isn't as ridiculous as it seems
paragraphs: The world's biggest YouTuber is in the news again, and this time it's not for a controversial business or branding venture. An original pencil sketch from the brainstorming session that led to the design of the MrBeast logo has come up for auction, and its estimated value is raising eyebrows.

Heritage Auctions' guide price for the 4x4 inch sketch on a sheet of stained and creased paper is $20,000. On social media, people are suggesting that's a bit ridiculous for what the auction house says was a 10-minute job. But is it really?

Cool piece of pop culture history in our Fall Auction, the sketch used to create Mr Beast’s logo The YouTube sensation met our consignor’s design firm to create it and this is the sketch he approved which has become one of the world’s most recognizable https://t.co/BiDqv2GE52 https://t.co/ppth2mbE4sOctober 9, 2026

MrBeast, AKA Jimmy Donaldson, started his channel on YouTube in 2012. His increasingly elaborate productions featuring challenges, game shows and enormous giveaways have earned him over 521 million subscribers and helped to reshape expectations around what independent digital content creation can be. He's since created a global media brand, launched branded snacks and even expanded into youth-focused financial services.

A recognisable part of his brand identity since 2018 is the blue cat logo with the magenta lightning bolt trailing from its eye. One aspect that makes the price estimate for that original sketch surprising is the anonymity of the design's authorship.

A logo isn't like art, where the artist's name is a large part of what defines its value, but iconic designs do often have known creators. We know that Carolyn Davidson designed the Nike swoosh, for example, or that Milton Glaser created the I love NY logo, the original drawing of which is in the MOMA.
In the case of the MrBeast logo, Heritage Auctions mentions only an "artist" and a "design team".

"According to its provenance, MrBeast initially used a generic image found online before being advised to develop an emblem that would be uniquely his own," the auction house's description says. "Working directly with the design team, he described what he envisioned. A brainstorming session ensured with MrBeast and the design team.

"The soon-to-be YouTube sensation indicated he wanted a big cat vibe and the artist's first attempt produced this drawing during an approximately ten-minute session. MrBeast approved the design, establishing the visual identity that would accompany his extraordinary rise to online prominence."
MrBeast, who is reportedly not involved the auction, told Wired earlier this year that he "put very little thought" into the logo design.
“When I was a little kid I just kind of designed a tiger, and here we are,” he said. “My name, my logo, probably should have had more thought behind it, I’ll admit it.”

Does that make $20,000 a ridiculous price? The fact that the sketch took 10 minutes is neither here nor there. A drawing isn't inherently worth more the longer it took to make. The auction house will be gauging that its value comes from the design's contribution to the MrBeast phenomenon and, for better or worse, its connection to a significant part of modern pop culture history.

A sketch of a logo isn't a logo. It doesn't confer rights over the intellectual property or its use, which is where the real value is. But some of the comments about the auction indirectly revive the eternal debate about how much a logo is worth.

Some graphic designers do quote for work based on time. But time alone is a problematic way to price logo design work when you consider the potential value that the mark can create for a brand (see our guide to pricing creative work).

Nike's worth over $50bn (down from a peak of $264bn in late 2021). What would it be worth without the Swoosh? Carolyn Davidson was famously paid $35 for the original design, charging a rate of $2 per hour in 1971. She was later gifted shares after Nike went public, perhaps recognising that she had been severely underpaid in terms of the value her design created.

Some designers charge according to who they're working for and where the logo will appear, not how long the process takes. The branding of a local coffee shop doesn't need the same process and the same amount of assets as a multinational bank (or the world's biggest YouTuber?). The Pepsi logo redesign of 2008 reportedly cost $1 million, but the brand did get a ridiculously psuedo-scientific manual to help justify that cost.
The MrBeast logo sketch is part of Heritage Auctions’ October 23 – 25 Fall Sports Catalog Auction.

items.title: 2026 Chemistry Nobel Prize – level 1
paragraphs: Two scientists win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. They solve a secret about molecules.

Molecules are very small parts of life. Many molecules have two forms, like a left hand and a right hand. Nature only uses one form to make living things grow. This discovery helps doctors and scientists make safer medicine. Sometimes, one form of a drug can help a sick person, but the other form can be dangerous or bad.
Now, scientists know how to make only the good and safe form of a drug. This discovery saves many lives and helps people stay healthy every day.
Difficult words: secret (something what most people do not know about), discovery (finding or learning about something new for the first time), dangerous (not safe).

items.title: Figma finally answers the question of what design feels like – using dance
paragraphs: A lot of AI tech advertising aims to show you what a product does or how it works. Sometimes that's necessary, but it can also go wrong like in the dystopian ChatGPT Astra advert or, more recently, the terribly stressful Apple HomeView advert.

The UI design platform Figma took a different approach with its recent launch video for its AI agent. It aimed for emotion by capturing nothing less than the the feeling of not just a product but the process of design itself. And it used an unexpected medium.

The Figma Agent is a system-aware AI assistant that works in the platform's files, layers and frames. It can be sued to rapidly explore layout directions, build user flows, generate new screens from text prompts, and remix existing designs.

To announce the transition out of beta, the digital product and marketing agency IVERSON eschewed the traditional feature walkthrough to focus on the experience of the software. To do that, it sought to capture the whole design process, from the tyranny of the blank page to research, the first ideas, iteration, feedback and the moment the work starts to flow.

The film was written and directed by Iverson's founder David Dinetz. He settled on dance as the ideal way to capture the invisible internal processes involved in design. He worked with choreographer Tony Testa, whose career has included work with the likes of Janet Jackson, Britney Spears and Jennifer Lopez, to build a language that would reveal that experience through physical movement.
The resulting film was made almost entirely in camera with live performance, moving sets and practical effects set to a Fred Again track.

The piece follows IVERSON’s Webby-winning Figma Slides film (below) but takes the collaboration into a more physical world. The shape of the choreography captures the emotion of design, while the pace seeks to capture the speed and fluidity of the software

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain
paragraphs: Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades.

For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.

For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.

“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.
“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.

Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.

National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.
“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.

Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.

However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped.

For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.

Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.
Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.

On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.

Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe.
“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”

On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.
The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.

Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.

There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.
Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.

For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.

Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.

Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.

“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”

He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.

“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.
“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”

As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.

There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.
On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.
As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.
Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.
“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”

Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”

Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.
“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.
“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”

items.title: Little tern colony has worst breeding season
paragraphs: A little tern colony has experienced its toughest breeding season since establishing themselves at a site.
Since 2019 the seabirds have travelled about 3,000 miles (4,828km) from West Africa to Seaton Carew, near Hartlepool.
But this year the colony's 83 nesting pairs produced just 17 fledglings, compared to 67 in 2025.
Tees Valley Wildlife Trust said flooding and damage to the colony's perimeter fence contributed to difficult conditions for the birds.
The protective fencing around the nesting ground was washed away in high tides earlier this year.
Lead warden Derek Wood said a late arrival of their inshore food supply as well as predation also contributed to the birds' tough season.
In June, it was reported numbers were down 50%, which the team attributed to dogs being inside the exclusion zone.

items.title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region
paragraphs: As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.

Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.

“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”

Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.

For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.

The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.

Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.

On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.

“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan ​on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed ​thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.
Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of which occur in peatland areas, can burn for weeks underground, and are difficult to extinguish.

“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

items.title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.

It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have fallen in recent days over concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.
Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.
Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. Trading on South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq was temporarily halted after falling by more than 8%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by over 5%.

items.title: Dog that hunts invasive 'sea vomit' honoured as animal of the year
paragraphs: "When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Dr Sim.
"No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."

Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Dr Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed".
"She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.
Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.
It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.
It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.
Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients.
"These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.
Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.

items.title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
paragraphs: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.

Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.

"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?

India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.

Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.

Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.

A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.

Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.

Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.

While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.

The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.

Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.
"What happened after that no one knows," he added.
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.

But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.

China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.

"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value.

"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.

The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow.

"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.

Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay.
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain.
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

items.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
paragraphs: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.

items.title: Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuit
paragraphs: Eight US states sued OpenAI Wednesday, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse.
Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four others allege the company’s products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves.

“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Brenna Bird, the attorney general for Iowa, said in a statement. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide – all while pretending to be their fake friend.”

All eight states accuse OpenAI of violating consumer protection laws and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users. They are additionally seeking monetary damages, and asking the court to halt OpenAI from developing artificial intelligence models that can improve upon themselves until the company shows those models are in line with human values.
This is the first time several US states have banded together in a coordinated legal action against an AI company.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company had “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri continued. “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company.”

The lawsuits allege that OpenAI has been misleading the public into believing that ChatGPT is a safe tool and that the company puts safety first. The states say that in reality, the chatbot has been designed to be “overly agreeable and feign human compassion”. The attorneys point to examples of ChatGPT being dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and coaching people to commit suicide or harm others.

This comes after a groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”.

Dozens of cases have also been filed against OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged role in mass shootings. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University. The company has also been sued by the families of 37 victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in Canada, who allege ChatGPT induced the shooter to carry out the attack.

The eight states that filed suit on Wednesday say there is a growing body of research that allegedly shows ChatGPT can harm critical-thinking skills, encourage paranoia and delusions, offer dangerous medical advice and promote unhealthy behavior.

The lawsuits also note that the recent examples of OpenAI’s models going rogue, with its AI agents hacking into other companies and government entities, show that the technology is prone to deceiving human users.

Pusateri said OpenAI had strengthened its safeguards in regards to those episodes and would “continue sharing information about the extensive steps we’ve taken in response to incidents of misalignment”.
The eight states are suing OpenAI independently in their state courts and include Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana.
