items.title: Journalist Michael Nacke Rejects Criminal Cases Against Him as Unlawful
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.
Journalist and popular YouTube host Michael Macke, a dual U.S. and Russian citizen, has rejected recent criminal proceedings against him by Russia in absentia as unlawful, in an interview with VOA.
Nacke, also known as Michael Naki, is the host of “Popular Politics" and “MackNack” YouTube. Despite living outside of Russia, he is on a Russian government "wanted list."

On Tuesday, Moscow’s Basmanny District Court handed Nacke a second – in absentia conviction. He was found guilty of publicly calling for “actions against the security of the Russian Federation, committed via the internet.” The court sentenced him to five years in prison.
The criminal case stemmed from a video published on the journalist’s YouTube channel on May 7, 2024. Prosecutors alleged that the video contained calls for actions against Russian state security.
Commenting on the new sentence in an interview with VOA Russian, Nacke said he did not consider the criminal proceedings against him legitimate.

“As for the legal side of things – all these criminal cases and everything else – I don’t take them particularly seriously. I don’t really understand why other people do. I consider them unlawful. I believe these trials, based on fabricated charges that have no legitimate basis, contradict the Russian constitution, the law that has direct applicability,” he said.
However, Nacke said that court rulings were not his primary concern. He was more worried about the activities of Russian security services.

“It was clear that there would be prison sentences and so on. Basically, the only thing that worries me is the activity of the Russian security services. It’s not just about court rulings; it’s about the fact that they kill people and hunt them down," he said. “And I’m most likely on some list of people they want to target. That concerns me much more."

During in absentia court proceedings he was represented by a court-appointed lawyer. However, Nacke said, this lawyer had not gotten in contact with him, even though she declared his innocence during the hearing.

“I read in the news that she – and I greatly appreciate it – said I was guilty of nothing and pointed out that she had no contact with me. That’s obviously disappointing; she could have reached out. You managed to find a way to contact me, after all. I think she could have found a way, too, if she had tried,” he said.
The defense lawyer had asked the court to acquit him. Russian authorities have placed Nacke on a wanted list and ordered his arrest in absentia.
Nacke said the proceedings would not change his work.
“In the end, I have neither plans nor intention to adjust my work in any way to accommodate their fabricated sentences,” he said.
Nacke left Russia in the summer of 2021. In September 2022, Russia’s Justice Ministry added him to its register of “foreign agents.”

In August 2023, Nacke and Ruslan Leviev, founder of the Conflict Intelligence Team, were sentenced in absentia to 11 years in prison in a case involving the dissemination of what Russian authorities described as “false information” about the Russian military.

Nacke previously worked as a presenter and commentator for the Echo of Moscow radio station. Since leaving Russia, he has focused on developing his own YouTube channel, where he publishes coverage and analysis of Russian politics and the war in Ukraine.

items.title: Cultural initiatives bringing Ukraine to American audiences
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
More than 35 years since Ukrainian independence, Americans’ perceptions of Ukraine have evolved — and that change has accelerated in recent years.

In the 1990s, Ukraine was often viewed through a Russian lens. But after nearly five years of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukrainian culture is increasingly being recognized in the United States on its own terms — as a vibrant and competitive cultural force.
Americans are studying Ukrainian, reading Ukrainian authors in translation, attending Ukrainian concerts and enrolling their children in programs created by Ukrainians.
What is driving this growing interest? Voice of America looks at five Ukrainian initiatives attracting growing American audiences.
Bringing Ukrainian books to American readers

New York-based nonprofit HUCUS Foundation, in partnership with the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute, has launched the Ukrainian Literature and Scholarship Program to support the translation and publication of Ukrainian literature in English.
The program began with a $250,000 budget and its first publication, Felix Austria, a historical Gothic novel by prominent Ukrainian writer Sofia Andrukhovych, translated by Vitaly Chernetsky.
HUCUS founder and director Oleksii Prokopenko says the program aims to introduce Ukrainian culture to American academics and decisionmakers.
Craft is an English-language website and print magazine featuring Ukrainian writers, musicians, photographers and other artists.
Co-founder and editor Kateryna Kazimirova says the project quickly attracted readers in the United States and Britain, followed by Germany and other European countries.
The platform focuses on interviews with Ukrainian artists. One of its projects brought prominent writers Andriy Kurkov and Serhiy Zhadan together to interview each other.
Kazimirova says American readers are discovering a culture they believe has been overlooked for too long.
The Washington-based Ukrainian music group Gerdan was founded by Grammy-winning musician Andriy Pidkivka and his wife, musician and DC Music Academy co-founder Solomiya Gorokhivska.
The group has performed for diplomats and politicians at institutions including the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Gorokhivska, Gerdan’s vocalist and violinist, says the annual Ukrainian Independence Day celebration is one of the most visible showcases of Ukrainian culture in the United States.

She recalls Republican U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham approaching the group after performances to say, “Good job.” Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin once went a step further and joined Gerdan for an impromptu jam session.
“Raskin, by the way, plays the piano very well, and his father was a concert pianist,” Gorokhivska said to VOA.
Gerdan collaborates with American musicians, including guitarist Ian Knutson of the U.S. Army Band, bassist Greg Watkins and accordionist Kalin Kirilov, a Towson University professor.
Since February 2026, the Ukrainian National Women’s League of America has hosted an online book club where readers discuss English-language books by Ukrainian authors or about Ukraine.
The club invites English-speaking experts who do not necessarily have Ukrainian roots.
“This gives us a foreign perspective on Ukrainian authors and their works from someone who did not grow up in a Ukrainian context,” said the club's cofounder, Anna Petelina.

She points to a discussion of Cassandra by renowned Ukrainian writer Lesya Ukrainka. Written more than a century ago, the play explores issues that remain relevant today, including propaganda, society’s refusal to confront obvious realities, patriarchy and the subjugation of women.
At least 10 schools in the San Francisco Bay Area have adopted an alphabet-learning method developed by Ukrainian educator Yulia Kalyuzhna.
Kalyuzhna created her “Finger ABC” method in Kherson to teach her own children English. After Russian forces occupied her city in 2022, her family moved to the United States.

Working as a teaching assistant, Kalyuzhna began using the method with American children. It combines letters with movement: children use their fingers or bodies to form letters, come up with words beginning with those letters, and repeat the exercises through games.
“Children expand their vocabulary, visualization and imagination. They cannot sit still, so movement helps them stay focused,” Kalyuzhna told VOA.
She now works with several U.S. educational organizations. She is also developing a Spanish version of her method.

items.title: US races to build rare earth supply chain as China tightens controls
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The United States is stepping up efforts to build an independent rare earth supply chain, as tensions with China over the issue of critical minerals threatens to complicate the two countries’ trade relationship.
The summit between the two countries’ leaders in late September extended a trade truce by only two months, while rare earths remained a key unresolved issue in negotiations.
Washington has responded with efforts to expand domestic production of critical minerals, support processing and magnet facilities, promote recycling and strengthen partnerships with other countries.

Rare earths are 17 metallic elements used in products ranging from smartphones and electric vehicles to fighter jets and nuclear submarines. They are especially important for permanent magnets used in motors and other high-tech equipment.

Until the 1990s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and exporter of rare earths. But rising environmental concerns and production costs gradually pushed the industry overseas, creating an opening for China to build a dominant position. China went on to develop a supply chain spanning mining, refining and magnet manufacturing — at one point accounting for more than 90% of the global market.

Analysts generally estimate that building a supply chain largely independent of China could take five to 10 years. Peter Navarro, the White House senior adviser for trade and manufacturing, has offered a much shorter timeline.
Speaking on Bannon’s War Room on September 25, Navarro said the U.S. could become self-sufficient in rare earth magnets — and even have enough capacity to export them — within six to 18 months.

Chia-Wei Jui, director of the Research Center for Science & Engineering at the Taiwan-based China Technical Consultants Inc. Foundation, questioned that timeline. But he told VOA that Washington is moving in several directions to reduce its dependence on China.
Jui pointed to Japan, which he said reduced its dependence on Chinese rare earths from 92% in 2010 to below 60% today.
The process will be difficult and time-consuming, Jui said, but the United States is “absolutely moving in the right direction.”

The U.S. strategy includes building strategic reserves of critical minerals. In February, Washington launched an initiative modeled on the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, aiming to maintain a 60-day emergency supply of minerals such as gallium and cobalt.
The U.S. government is also investing heavily in domestic mining and magnet production.

A September 27 Wall Street Journal report, citing White House officials, said 180 projects had been initiated. Data from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that U.S. government non-equity investment in rare earth and magnet projects reached $7.6 billion between 2025 and June. That’s more than four times the total invested from 2020 through 2024.

Washington has also taken a direct stake in the industry. In July 2025, the Department of War spent $400 million to acquire 15% of MP Materials, a leading U.S. rare earth company. The government agreed to purchase the entire output of the company’s second magnet plant for 10 years and established a price floor.

Jui said the United States is also looking to “urban mining” to recover rare earths from electronic waste. Washington is supporting recycling programs and pushing legislation that would require manufacturers to collect and recycle used products, while offering tax incentives for companies that use recycled rare earths. The goal is to have recycled materials meet 20% of U.S. demand by 2030, he said.

U.S. companies are already making moves in that direction. Apple signed a $500 million agreement last year with MP Materials to produce rare earth magnets for the company using recycled materials, giving the emerging recycling market a major corporate push.
On the world stage, Washington launched the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement, or FORGE, involving 55 countries, and assumed its chairmanship in July.

Yuki Kobayashi, a senior research fellow of the Japan-based National Security and US-Japan Program at Sasakawa Peace Foundation, told VOA that cooperation among the United States, Japan and Europe could be critical.

Western and Japanese companies originally helped introduce rare earth refining and magnet-making technology to China, he noted. He added that although some of these companies now hold small market shares, they still possess the technology for refining rare earths and manufacturing high-performance magnets.
“Consolidating these technologies — with the U.S. and Japan at the core — is key to breaking China’s monopoly,” Kobayashi said.

items.title: Pakistan, Afghan Taliban trade blame for cross-border violence as tensions rise
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban continue to trade accusations amid recent border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan.
Speaking at a think tank in Islamabad on Monday, Pakistan Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar warned the Taliban in Afghanistan not to support the militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan.

The Taliban’s spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid, in a post on X, rejected Pakistan’s accusations, saying that Pakistan is “blaming Afghanistan for its own failures,” and that Pakistani officials were using ‘propaganda' instead of finding solutions.
Pakistan rejected the Taliban’s statement, however, insisting that any negotiations would require the Taliban to act against Pakistani militants operating from Afghanistan.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
In response, Pakistan launched multiple airstrikes inside Afghanistan, which the Taliban said struck civilians.
The Taliban and the U.N. said airstrikes in the eastern province of Kunar and the southern province of Helmand on October 1 killed at least 10 people and injured 10 others.
The United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in September that it had documented more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border attacks in Afghanistan.
The Taliban retaliated by launching attacks on Pakistani border posts, escalating clashes between the two sides.
The U.N. said that the Pakistani Taliban’s attacks inside Pakistan have increased.
Pakistan has said that more than 3,000 people have been killed in 2,800 militant attacks since January.
Amid rising violence, Pakistan also is facing political tensions.
On Sunday, Pakistan imposed emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending the provincial government led by the party of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan.

Authorities detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, the top elected official in the province and several cabinet members. The federal government accused the provincial administration of colluding with militants of TTP.

Ghaus Janbaz, a former Afghan diplomat, told VOA that suspending the KP provincial government would not ease the crisis but would further escalate it, as there already is tension between the province and the federal government.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told VOA Afghan in an email that “it is aware of the reports.”
“We expect that local authorities will act in accordance with Pakistani law as they seek to maintain order,” the State Department.
Amnesty International condemned the declaration of emergency in KP.
Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s deputy director for South Asia, said the action “raised concerns about the proportionality of these emergency measures.”

“Pakistani authorities must avoid using military personnel for ordinary policing tasks and ensure that military forces remain accountable and comply with international human rights law and standards,” Amnesty International said in a statement released Monday.

items.title: OpenAI accuses employee who left for Apple of leaking plans for unreleased device
paragraphs: An ⁠OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal ⁠account and later ⁠made a presentation ​about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.

In the filing ⁠in US federal court in San Jose, California, OpenAI alleged that the presentation happened months ago and that Apple is now making ⁠AI products of its own, citing the release of Apple’s HomeView product this week.

“OpenAI ​is very concerned that its trade ‌secret and confidential information is ‌now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s ‌confidential and innovative work,” OpenAI said in its filing.

The two companies were due to face off in court on Wednesday in an ongoing trade secrets lawsuit, but the new allegation delayed the showdown. OpenAI said it may file a countersuit based on the new claim.

Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI’s allegations.

The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of a trade secret dispute ‌filed by Apple earlier this year against OpenAI. The iPhone maker alleged its own employees left and took confidential information to OpenAI’s hardware ​division. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
Earlier this week, US district court judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple’s request for early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit.

Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees’ devices and ⁠sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the ​two defendants in ​the case – Chang Liu, a former ​senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice-president of product ‌design for iPhone and ​Apple Watch.
The case ​is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.

items.title: Popular Iranian band cancels national tour, citing Islamist ban on its female musician performing on stage
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.
Popular Iranian fusion music band Pallett says it has cancelled a national tour because authorities in the Islamic republic barred its female musician from performing on stage.

In a Tuesday statement posted on Instagram, Pallett said it recently decided to go back on tour across Iran after a hiatus of many years but scrapped the plan after “we were told in some cities that the female musician is not allowed to go on stage.”

The statement did not specify the cities involved or the Iranian regime entity that blocked its female performer, flutist Shaghayegh Sadeghian, from appearing on stage with the rest of the 7-member group.

“For years, our hearts have hoped to see and hear the art of our (fellow) vocalists, and now after all these years of efforts and protests by male and female musicians, we are witnessing a return to the point where female musicians are not even allowed to perform. We, the Pallett band, are 7 people ... and we appear on stage when all 7 people can perform the same way,” the band wrote.

Iranian state media reported the band’s statement about canceling its national tour due to Sadeghian being banned from performing in several regions. But there was no immediate public comment from Iran’s Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, the governmental body responsible for issuing and revoking concert permits.

Women in Iran face official restrictions on performing music and often are denied permission to perform on stage and penalized for doing so. While Iran’s Islamist Penal Code does not explicitly ban women from singing, bans are enforced under the pretext of preventing "public indecency."

One recent case involves female singer Parastoo Ahmadi, who sang without a headscarf alongside several male musicians at a historic fortress or caravanserai near the holy city of Qom in December 2024. The performance was livestreamed on YouTube and went viral, but led to her and her fellow artists being briefly detained by police and later prosecuted.
A criminal court in Qom sentenced Ahmadi to 74 lashes, a two-year ban on artistic activities, and a two-year travel ban in June. The province's appellate court subsequently upheld the verdict.
The charges in the Ahmadi case included the production and dissemination of content contrary to public decency online.

In another case, singer Alireza Ghorbani’s March 2024 concert in the central city of Isfahan was cancelled hours before it was scheduled to begin. Isfahan’s Headquarters for Enjoining Good and Forbidding Evil had insisted the concert proceed without female musicians, despite a permit being issued by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance.
In December 2015, the Tehran Symphony Orchestra withdrew from performing at the closing ceremony of an international sporting event after officials demanded the exclusion of female musicians.

Pallett also previously experienced a concert cancellation due to Islamist restrictions. In September 2016, Pallett said authorities abruptly canceled a scheduled concert at the historic Bisotun site in the western province of Kermanshah Province, citing a need to use the site instead for a memorial service for Islamists killed while fighting for Iran-backed armed groups in Syria.

items.title: Iraqi Kurdish leaders raise prospect of peace talks between Iran and Kurdish opposition
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Senior leaders in Iraq's Kurdistan Region have publicly discussed efforts to facilitate peace talks between Iran and Iranian Kurdish armed opposition groups based in the autonomous region.
Bafel Talabani, the head of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), said on Monday that a process similar to peace efforts between Turkey and Kurdish militants had begun with Iran.

"We are at the beginning of a similar process with our Iranian brothers and sisters," Talabani said at an event in Erbil, adding that the issue had been discussed extensively with Tehran, which had responded positively.
"Iran has offered to help us create a general peace process in the region," he said. "I think this dialogue will be very, very important."
The PUK, which holds Iraq's presidency, maintains close relations with Tehran.

Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani, however, offered a more cautious assessment, saying discussions had not yet reached the level of the peace process in Turkey, where the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) has announced a decision to disarm last year.
"A process similar to Turkey's peace process in Iran may not have begun yet, but it is being considered," Barzani told the Middle East Research Institute (MERI) in Erbil on Monday.
Barzani said Kurdish leaders had repeatedly raised the issue with Iranian officials and stressed that Tehran and its Kurdish opposition should seek a peaceful settlement.
The comments mark a rare public acknowledgment of diplomatic efforts involving Iran and Kurdish opposition groups that have been exiled to the Iraqi Kurdistan for decades.
Security concerns and opposition response

Iraqi Kurdish leaders have long viewed tensions between Tehran and the Iranian Kurdish opposition as a threat to their region’s security and an obstacle to improving relations with Iran. They argue Iran often uses the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition in their region as a pretext for missile and drone attacks.
Barzani criticized the Iranian Kurdish groups on Monday, accusing them of acting irresponsibly since the launch of the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran on Feb. 28.
"The Kurdish opposition of Eastern Kurdistan [Iran], with deep regret, acted very irresponsibly," he said.

Iranian Kurdish opposition groups say they favor a peaceful settlement with Tehran but remain deeply distrustful of the Islamic Republic, citing decades of conflict and the assassinations of Kurdish leaders during previous diplomatic efforts.

Khalid Azizi, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), told Rudaw on Monday that his party was open to negotiations but questioned Tehran's intentions and who could represent Iran following the reported deaths of senior officials in recent U.S. and Israeli strikes.
Iraq and Iran officials are scheduled to meet on Oct. 19 to discuss the opposition groups' presence in Iraqi Kurdistan, Iraqi National Security Advisor Qasim al-Aboudi told Rudaw on Tuesday.
Under a 2023 security agreement, Baghdad agreed to relocate Iranian Kurdish armed groups away from the border and prevent cross-border attacks while allowing them to remain in Iraq as refugees.

Tehran has repeatedly targeted the groups, accusing them of threatening its security, allegations they deny. Opposition representatives told VOA that more than 420 Iranian attacks since Feb. 28 had killed 23 people, figures that could not be independently verified.

Iran's Kurdish population is estimated at around 9 million, or roughly 10% of the country's population, although some estimates are as high as 15 million. Iran does not publish official ethnic population figures.
UNHCR estimates that 10,000 to 30,000 Iranian Kurdish refugees and asylum seekers live in Iraq, mostly in the Kurdistan Region.
Despite the public statements by Iraqi Kurdish leaders, some Iranian Kurdish political figures remain skeptical that negotiations would produce meaningful results.

Jalil Azadikhah, an Iranian Kurdish political analyst and activist based in Washington, told VOA that efforts to initiate a peace process had been underway for a long time but were only now being discussed publicly.
He argued that Tehran's objective was not to resolve the Kurdish issue but to weaken and ultimately dismantle the Kurdish opposition movement.
"At this point, I think any form of negotiation between the Kurdish parties and Iran is inappropriate, because there is no right opportunity for it now," Azadikhah said.

items.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
paragraphs: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.

Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."
Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.
Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.

Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.

The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.
Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.
Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.
Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

items.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
paragraphs: The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

items.title: DOJ charges 14 in North Korean IT worker scheme
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

A federal grand jury in Ohio has indicted two Americans, 10 Chinese nationals and two defendants whose identities remain under seal for helping North Korean IT workers obtain remote jobs at U.S. companies using stolen or fabricated identities, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

The two Americans, residents of Pennsylvania and Texas, were arrested. The other defendants, many of them from Dandong, a Chinese city on the border with North Korea, remain at large. They face charges of wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit identity theft, and aggravated identity theft.

The Justice Department said more than 70 U.S. companies were affected and that about $3 million in revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by North Korea. The victim companies were not named.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.

At the center of the schemes are so-called laptop farms, where work laptops issued by victim companies are kept at the homes of U.S.-based facilitators. North Korean workers connect to the devices remotely from abroad, appearing to work from inside the United States.

From September 21 to 25, under “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” the FBI searched more than 40 homes in Texas known or suspected to be laptop farms and seized about 187 laptops and KVM devices, which allow a computer to be controlled remotely. The Justice Department did not say whether anyone was arrested or charged in that operation. The 14 charges come from a separate Ohio case.

“Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas.

The 58-page Ohio indictment offers a detailed look at the scheme. According to the indictment, overseas co-conspirators directed a U.S.-based facilitator in Ohio to hire an actor to sit for an in-person job interview and to pay for advertisements recruiting actors with a stolen credit card. One fake employee submitted a form purportedly signed by a “psychologist” to avoid using a video camera.

In a public service announcement issued the same day, the FBI said North Korean IT workers pay Americans who are facing financial hardship to sit for video job interviews and to complete urinalysis tests and fingerprint submissions on their behalf. In some cases, after being fired, the North Korean workers made death threats against former managers and their families to demand money, the FBI said.

The FBI estimates that the North Korean government receives about 85% to 90% of the revenue these workers generate and said the largest operator of such workers is likely the Workers’ Party of Korea’s Munitions Industry Department.
The Justice Department said the actions are the latest in a series of efforts to disrupt North Korea’s illicit revenue generation and its U.S.-based enablers.

items.title: Taliban Suspends BBC Broadcasts Across Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The Taliban has suspended British Broadcasting Corporations’ (BBC) FM radio broadcasts across Afghanistan, the broadcaster confirmed in a statement on October 13.
"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the statement said.

Khubib Ghufran, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's Information and Culture ministry, said the BBC’s broadcast had been suspended for the "time being due to repeated violations," but did not provide details about the alleged violations.

The BBC had been the only major international broadcaster operating on FM radio in Afghanistan since the Taliban banned Voice of America (VOA) and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) from domestic broadcasting in 2022.

Despite those restrictions, VOA has continued providing daily news to Afghan audiences through alternative distribution methods. The broadcaster transmits radio programs through medium-wave transmitters located outside Afghanistan and delivers television content to Afghan audiences via satellite.

The suspension of the BBC’s FM broadcasts in Afghanistan comes at a time when radio remains “the primary source of information among Afghans, with 80.4% of the population being regular listeners and 72.1% owning a radio,” according to a United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) report.

The latest move adds to growing concerns over media freedom in Afghanistan. Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban have imposed wide-ranging restrictions on journalists and media organizations, leading to the closure of dozens of outlets and significantly reducing access to independent reporting.

“They have largely destroyed Afghanistan’s media landscape, creating such a climate of fear that Afghan journalists cannot genuinely investigate or report,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“The Taliban have detained and tortured journalists, severely limited what the media can report, and worked directly in newsrooms to suppress any critical content,” Abbasi added.

In the five years, the Taliban “have methodically turned Afghanistan into a prison for information” media freedom watchdog, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said in a report. “Journalism is increasingly throttled as criticism of the regime is forbidden, women face sweeping restrictions, political debate has been silenced, and broadcasting images of living beings is banned.”

The BBC said its radio programming remains available through satellite services as well as shortwave and medium-wave frequencies, allowing audiences in Afghanistan to continue accessing its broadcasts.

items.title: Behnaz Farahi creates Ocean of Dreams video installation for MIT Future Fest

items.title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
paragraphs: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK.
"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.
Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.
Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.
Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.
Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.
Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.
Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."
Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."
The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.
The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza.
In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK.
"The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."

In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested.
On Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence.
"After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."
Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced".
Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action".
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action.
About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month.

items.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
paragraphs: A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

items.title: Was this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness?
paragraphs: Age: Arthur Guinness began brewing porter in the 1770s. Guinness draught was first poured in 1959.
Appearance: Espresso martini in a pint glass.
But it’s beer. It’s stout, yeah. Irish stout.
Sort of an old man’s drink, isn’t it? Not these days. Fans of Guinness include Kim Kardashian, Olivia Rodrigo, even the Princess of Wales.

That’s just a bunch of celebrities pretending to like Guinness either because they’re visiting Ireland or it’s Saint Patrick’s Day. Or both. Some of them have actually tasted it: Mark Zuckerberg, for example.

I wouldn’t have guessed Zuckerberg drinks Guinness. He has drunk it – and apparently for the first time – on a recent instalment of the Irish billionaire John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast, which is set in a pub.
What makes you think it was his first time? The look on his face.
Did he look as if he was enjoying it? He looked as if he might be allergic to it.
What do you mean? At the start of the podcast, while discussing his new Muse AI app, the Meta founder picks up the full pint in front of him and takes a sip.
Like a regular person, you mean. Close enough, up to that point. But his subsequent reaction went viral.
What did he do? He looked surprised, for a start. Then as if he was having trouble swallowing. He pursed his lips, squirmed in his seat and seemed to be looking around for the nearest exit.

Oh my. After that he clutched at his shirt collar a bit. He even tried smiling briefly before realising he’d selected the wrong human facial expression from the dropdown menu. Eventually he managed to power down and reset himself.
Did he at least finish the pint? He kept at it, but by the 1 hour 20 minute mark he’d only managed about half.
Then what happened? There was an apparent break in filming, and when they resumed he had another full pint in front of him.

His worst nightmare! Still, I suppose Guinness can manage without Zuckerberg’s endorsement. You would have thought so – it sells 1.88bn pints a year globally, with sales continuing to rise, while the overall beer market declines. And Guinness 0.0 is the No 1 non-alcoholic beer in the UK.
So what made Zuckerberg think he ought to pretend to like it? Well, he did buy a castle in Ireland last month for €20m (£17m), so maybe he’s planning on popping down to his local more often?
Do say: “Guinness is an acquired taste, and I’m in the process of acquiring it in the same way I’ve acquired many startups and competitors. Was this answer helpful?”
Don’t say: “Then, when my new AI model kills everyone, I’ll drink what I like.”

items.title: ‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the world
paragraphs: When the call came early one morning, Tehran resident Elham Issari knew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint! It’s overpriced and I know it’s overpriced but, if you want it, you have to buy it right now because there’s this other guy in this other city who wants it and you have to tell me within the next five minutes.”

The tube of white paint would have cost Issari 5m tomans (about $36), she recalls. “I was like, I don’t think so, because that’s overpriced, and the next thing you know is it’s 4am and I’m on YouTube watching how to make lead white in your backyard without getting lead poisoning.”

It is a revealing slice of life in Iran these days. Since the US and Israel launched joint airstrikes and combat operations on 28 February, and turned the screws on Iran’s economy, thousands of visual artists have been plunged into economic and professional limbo.

The sudden onset of war shuttered commercial galleries in central Tehran, cancelled scheduled solo exhibitions, severed shipping channels and destroyed the fragile domestic market that allows creators to pay rent and sustain studio practices.

But it was out of this systemic breakdown that Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran was born. The initiative connects contemporary artists living and working inside Iran with international audiences, collectors and institutions through a dedicated platform at iranartistrelief.org.

The project owes its existence to Dario Duran, a Canadian-Iranian curator and founder of Duran Art Projects. Born in Shiraz, but raised in Canada, Duran holds degrees in photography, art history and curatorial studies. Six years ago, driven by nostalgia and a desire to connect with his heritage, he moved to Iran, where he fell in love with the dynamism of the domestic art scene.

When war broke out, Duran found himself caught directly in its crosshairs. “I was displaced,” the 38-year-old explains from Shiraz in Iran. “My mom and dad were visiting from Canada and we had to flee Shiraz because Shiraz was being hit pretty hard every day. It was becoming unbearable. We went by ground to the north of the country, where it was relatively quiet.”

In the north, Duran encountered dozens of other displaced cultural workers who had fled bombed urban centers such as Tehran and Isfahan. He linked up there with Mariam Rasti, co-founder of Duran Art Projects, who had also fled the capital.

“We were in constant communication with the artists,” Duran recalls. “One thing we saw over and over again was that, like never before, the artists were losing hope. Cancelled exhibitions, galleries closing, not being able to find materials, artists being displaced – every single person was going through the exact same uncertainty of what happens tomorrow.”

Iran’s contemporary art world operates inside a structural bubble, isolated from international banking networks. Typically, an artist works for one or two years to prepare a body of work, relying on a single gallery showcase to generate enough sales to survive for the next two years. When conflict brought that domestic cycle to a dead halt, creators faced immediate ruin.

Duran says: “We realised that at this moment, exhibition making, curation, archiving – these things do not matter. What matters, more than anything else, is simply sales. These artists were not able to pay their rent.

“One artist put up his paintbrushes and paint tubes for sale on Divar [a classifieds site] just to carry on. Another artist told me: ‘I’m going to go work in a coffee shop for the time being because I have no idea if this art thing is going to work out for me’.”

Determined to make a difference, Duran bought a couple of gigabytes of internet access so he could get on WhatsApp. From his laptop in the north, he drafted an open letter to international collectors, museum directors and gallerists across the diaspora, laying bare the plight of creators inside Iran.

The response was immediate and overwhelming. Gallerists and curators in London, New York, Paris, Dubai, Toronto and Mumbai wrote back, eager to assist. What had originally been planned as a modest PDF catalogue featuring a dozen imperilled acquaintances rapidly transformed into a nationwide initiative.

Over five months of feverish development, Duran, Rasti and a coalition of domestic galleries built Continuum. The digital platform brings together more than 500 original artworks by over 200 contemporary artists living and working inside Iran.

Eleven commercial galleries across Iran agreed to voluntarily waive 100% of their sales commissions. Duran Art Projects charges no platform fees. As a result, 100% of every completed artwork sale goes directly to the artist. To make acquisitions realistic for global buyers during an economic downturn, prices were capped across three accessible tiers: up to $500; $500–$2,500; $2,500–$5,000.

While the online front end of Continuum offers a catalogue of striking abstract canvases, delicate line drawings and minimalist photography, the back-end operation is a masterclass in guerrilla logistics. Delivering physical artworks out of a country under heavy military bombardment and stringent international sanctions requires ingenuity bordering on subversion.
“The logistics of it – we thought about this ad nauseam,” Duran says with a weary laugh. “Currently, this matter is changing on an hourly basis. The sanctions obviously have been very disruptive.”

Initially, Continuum relied on two domestic courier services capable of flying artwork packages from Tehran to shipment hubs in Dubai and Istanbul, where international carriers could take over. But as geopolitical tensions soared, regional airspace closed and commercial flight paths dissolved.

Duran explains: “The flight connections through the UAE were cancelled so the couriers told us that UAE is off the table. But the second UAE comes off the table, they figure out another way. There is a man who had a courier company that was forced to shut down. In order to keep his business going, he is now using the ground borders, moving overland from Iran into Armenia. He goes by the land border, carries the artworks into Armenia and ships them out from there with full insurance.”

To manage expectations, Continuum informs international buyers that delivery may take three to six months. Yet collectors worldwide, ranging from private patrons in North America to major European institutions, have shown extraordinary patience.

For Duran, the real tragedy of the current crisis lies in the indiscriminate cruelty of international economic sanctions, which target ordinary citizens while doing nothing to alter political outcomes. “These sanctions are not putting much pressure on the government,” he observes. “It’s mostly punishing everybody that’s trying to live a life here. Everyone’s complaining but we’re trying to find solutions.”

Among the artists trying to make a way out of no way is Mehrdad Jafari, 43, who grew up in the northern province of Mazandaran, where his relatives worked as sculptors and painters. Speaking from Tehran through a Farsi interpreter, he says: “Growing up, I always had the dream that one day I would be in Tehran and have an art studio in this city, to create work and fully realise my potential.
“My entire life has been dedicated, and continues to be dedicated, to my work. In fact, my existence is connected to my work. I have no other way of being. I must continue until I die.”

As the father of a three-year-old child, Jafari’s experience of the war is filtered through the anxieties of parenthood. His artwork, which centres on the complex emotional tapestry of human relationships and community interactions, has had to adapt to severe material deprivations.

“Because of the effect of sanctions, we’ve had to be a lot more imaginative in order to decide what materials we use,” Jafari explains. “Materials are quite difficult to find right now. But what I’ve had to do, and what others are doing, is replace this lack of materials with imagination. We use alternative materials to carry on.”

Jafari views this enforced improvisation as a double-edged sword. “In one way we use our imaginations more, creating a more creative space and ways of thinking. But on the other hand, of course, we would love to be part of the global system and have access to the things everybody else has access to. That’s just not available to us right now.”

For Jafari, Continuum’s launch during a time of active military conflict carries symbolic resonance. “It’s an extraordinary moment. It’s a bridge for us to connect with an international audience. For me personally, it brings a sense of calm – that we are not forgotten. Because of Continuum, I am more invigorated than ever to work. It gives us hope that life can carry on.”

From the outset, Duran and Rasti insisted that the initiative would not function as an exhibition about war, nor would it force artists to turn their pain into visual entertainment for foreign viewers.

Duran argues: “Iranian contemporary art doesn’t look like any one thing. Iran is not a style, and the Iranian identity is not a medium. An artist living in Shiraz shouldn’t have to make work that visually announces ‘Iran’ before an international audience is willing to take it seriously. We wanted the work to be encountered first as art, not as evidence about a country.”
While some participating artists choose to directly address conflict, Continuum refused to make political commentary or suffering a requirement for inclusion.

“There is a difference between giving artists visibility during a crisis and asking artists to make the crisis visible,” Duran adds. “I definitely didn’t want crisis to become the reason their work deserves attention. Context should deepen our understanding of an artwork; it shouldn’t imprison the artwork.”

The breadth of work included on the platform bears out this philosophy. Across 500 pieces, viewers encounter delicate geometric abstraction, haunting figurative portraiture, avant-garde photography, experimental printmaking and sculpture.

The financial relief generated by Continuum is already providing vital support to Iran’s artistic ecosystem. In a country where currency devaluation has eroded savings, a single $500 artwork sale can provide significant income towards studio rent or much-needed pigments.

Issari, 38, reflects: “It creates a chain. If an artist is not so worried about their income, maybe they can continue teaching. If they can continue to teach, kids can continue to learn. The whole chain does not stop and we don’t fall into this pit of absolute hopelessness.”

Issari could not bring herself to work during the first weeks of heavy bombardment in Tehran. “I was here for the whole show. Hearing explosions five times, six times per day, every day – having to gather the cats and run to your safe place and count to 10. Then, as soon as it’s over, pick up the phone, check if your father is alive, if your mother’s alive, if your loved ones are OK. On repeat. It does a number on you.”

The trauma was physical as much as psychological. “I didn’t touch a brush,” she recalls. “Actually, I did once, and my hands were shaking so badly that I literally just put it down. I was like, ‘I am not going to do this right now.’ And that’s OK, because I’m just not there.”

While Issari, who studied art in London, is hopeful her paintings on Continuum will find homes in international collections, the initiative’s primary gift is emotional validation. “Even if you don’t sell, it’s that feeling of being seen,” she says with quiet determination. “For me, it’s tremendous. It’s easy to feel like you’re a pariah and you’re invisible. Just the fact that you’re being seen means a lot.”

She adds: “I always have faith in the fact that art will survive, regardless of everything and anything. Artists are the best. If problem-solving were an Olympic sport, we would win a gold medal every time. We will find a way.”

items.title: A dominatrix and her tightly bound client: Giada Ripa’s best photograph
paragraphs: Ten years ago, my dad called to say he had found these amazing images hidden under piles of maps and stuff in an attic in our family home in Piemonte, northern Italy. He had come across a leather-bound album of 53 black and white photographs: portraits of Japanese “native types”, reflecting the 19th-century colonial way of representing people, cultures and views of Japan.

It turned out we had a treasure in our hands: it was an album of photographs by Felice Beato, the first foreign photographer to arrive in Japan in 1863 at the end of the Edo period and on the eve of the Meiji era.

When Beato arrived, Japan was still largely closed to foreigners. He started accompanying British diplomatic and military delegations and later set up a portrait studio where he photographed geishas, fishers, samurai, teachers, government officials – creating a kind of visual encyclopedia of people, professions and ways of life. These were the first images of Japan that the western world saw.

I have always worked with historical archives. Finding this album was amazing, but I couldn’t understand why it had ended up in our house. I needed to know and decided to look for clues. A year later, I found a 19th-century manuscript written by one of our ancestors, Mathilde Ruinart, an intellectual and a painter. She had married the first Italian ambassador to Japan, who was sent there in 1867 partly to help secure Japanese silkworms, as a disease was devastating the European silk industry. She had accompanied her husband – the journey took four months – and they stayed for four years. The manuscript was her diary, as well as letters, detailing her time there.

I was so fascinated that I read it all in one night. While Beato is well known, no one had heard of this remarkable woman, who knew she was witnessing a major transition in Japan and wanted to leave a trace of her years there. She rode her horse through parts of the country forbidden to foreigners with a gun in her dress and reportedly once shot a group of bandits dead.

I found as many of Mathilde’s descendants as I could and uncovered more of her archive, including her netsuke collection, brought back from her time in Japan. I photographed her objects and belongings – I dedicated an entire year to her. She was the same age as Beato and in Japan at the same time, so it was obvious to me that they must have met there, and that she must have selected and bought the photographs from him, which is how they came to be in my house.

From that came The Yokohama Project, a dialogue between the three of us – Beato, Ruinart and me – across 150 years. Three ways of seeing Japan, past and present, trying to understand and build a bridge. In the first chapter of the project I followed their footsteps, going to places they went, shooting on large-format film, echoing the slow process of observation. For the second chapter, I photographed about 40 Japanese professions, some still linked to those photographed by Beato, such as the geisha and the shamisen player, but also going beyond them to contemporary Japan. I invited people to a studio in Tokyo to present themselves in the ways they wanted to be seen. I photographed Lolita girls, and a fishmonger who was like a movie star. In Tokyo fishmongers are superstars – he came with €1,000-worth of red snapper in a basket and told me we had 10 minutes or the fish would go bad, which is a problem shooting on large-format as it’s a very slow process.

Karen, who appears in this portrait, describes herself as a BDSM dominatrix and a rope artist. She practises shibari with cross-dressing, tying and binding – a broader term than bondage. It is a visual and technical practice of tying the body with rope that can be erotic or not. It originates from the way samurai would bind their prisoners. Karen also practises kinbaku, a specific term for tight binding. She uses it in an intimate way with her clients, who are mostly men with high social and professional pressures.

Her practice allows them to step outside their day to day identities and express a side they can’t show elsewhere. She is a therapeutic person for them, and they talk to her – it’s not just a physical relationship but a cathartic experience. It allows her clients to transcend daily life. The man in this image is actually an assistant who worked on the project with me and agreed to be part of the picture. The two of them talked, and she decided how to tie him. He had never experienced it before – and he admitted afterwards that he enjoyed it.
The Yokohama Project by Giada Ripa is published by Gost Books

Born: London, 1974High point: My first museum solo exhibition, Displacement, at the Moscow Museum of Modern Art in 2011Top tip: Follow what genuinely makes you curious. Research can give you the starting point, but it’s through looking, questioning and having a personal encounter with the subject that the work begins to come alive

items.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).
The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.
She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”
Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”
The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

items.title: Hands-on with the Ocarina of Time remake, the most ornate Zelda game ever made
paragraphs: The titular Princess Zelda, reworked for the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Nintendo hide caption
Mario had his moment. Now it's Zelda's turn.

After The Super Mario Movie and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie made billions, Zelda is heading to the big screen next April. So to keep the franchise front and center, Nintendo is lavishly remaking its 1998 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game debuts Nov. 5th, two weeks before the meteoric arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI — the only major release to dare compete with it that month.

As other companies dodge the Grand Theft Auto juggernaut by avoiding the November release window, Nintendo's wholesome throwback is poised to stand out against the glitzy violence of Grand Theft Auto. While many will play both games, the early holiday season offers a contrast: a family-friendly fantasy or a modern-day crime epic.
Protagonist Link appears before the Great Deku Tree with fairy companion Navi. Nintendo hide caption

They're both gorgeous to look at. GTA's Netflix preview showed off the obsessive photorealism developer Rockstar Games is known for. The Ocarina of Time remake, alternatively, maintains the original game's cartoony aesthetic but layers it with intricate detail.

Your tunic isn't just flat green; it's a hand-stitched jumble of embroidered fabrics and leathers. And fairies aren't just simple balls of light; they're furry creatures with mosaic wings. Yet, as someone who grew up with the original game and lost count of how many times I beat it, I found that the remake's baroque environments could confuse as well as dazzle.
The busy central plaza of Hyrule Castle Town. Nintendo hide caption

Nintendo gave me 90 minutes to play through a cross-section of the game at a New York City preview. I blazed through Kokiri Forest, drinking in its dappled light and rippling waters. Then I dashed through Hyrule Field. Though it's tiny by today's gaming standards, it still felt as vast as I remembered thanks to clever atmospheric lightning. Castle Town bustled more than ever, teeming with banners, flowers and colorful citizenry. Even as I raced to explore as much as possible from the main plot, I couldn't help but stop to admire the scenery and shops of the city.

I was then thrown ahead to the Forest Temple — my favorite dungeon in the entire series. I was making good time and expected to reach its final boss before my session elapsed. Alas, I somehow skipped a chest containing the key I needed to progress. A Nintendo representative pointed me in the right direction, acknowledging that the rich details could overwhelm the eye and make it hard to know exactly where to go next.
The Forest Temple's most notorious corridor. Nintendo hide caption

I dwell on the game's aesthetic transformation because its mechanical changes are comparatively restrained. After all, why fix what's not broken? The original Ocarina of Time pioneered 3D video games and established action mechanics that still reign over the industry. Modest updates hit the game when it was repackaged for the GameCube and 3DS. For the Switch 2, Nintendo is applying a user interface reminiscent of 2017's The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and a quest log in the pause menu called "Threads of Time." It's also adding movement features I almost forgot were missing: a jump and a sprint.
I was so accustomed to the automatic jump that I failed to time this leap properly when I came to it in my own playthrough. Nintendo hide caption

In the original Ocarina of Time, you'd automatically jump when you ran off a ledge or gap. While you can choose to keep the old control scheme, the game now allows you to hop on command. It's not too useful in combat, but I did manage to jump to the roof of a forest hut otherwise only accessible through a winding footpath. Don't expect Breath of the Wild openness. The game still seems to be a linear adventure, just one that now allows the occasional vertical shortcut. Also, you can hold a button to sprint, a boon to those who constantly rolled around because it was faster than jogging.

While I've protested Nintendo remakes before, I'll readily admit that Ocarina of Time is not just a safe bet but a smart one. With Zelda so close to its movie debut, the game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players. Its sky-high production values also fit a new priority for the company, which has lavished attention on animation as well as gameplay since 2023's Super Mario Bros. Wonder.
The Ocarina of Time remake is the prettiest Zelda game I've ever played. But I'll need more than a 90-minute preview to see if its beauty is more than skin deep.
