items.title: Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremism
paragraphs: In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake-up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.

The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.

FBI officers fear the scenario is set to repeat itself: “Threat actors will likely increase their use of GenAI tools for attack planning,” said the memo, which was distributed by the bureau’s Los Angeles division in May 2026. “Current built-in GenAI safeguards are insufficient to prevent illicit use as malicious actors successfully employ ‘jailbreaking’ techniques to access dangerous information.”

AI executives and staff at leading AI companies have focused their public remarks on potential doomsday scenarios, a long-term, hypothetical harm of the technology they are developing. Law enforcement officers, by contrast, have been grappling with what they fear are the present-day threats that AI enables, including violent crimes.

A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists. Law enforcement has been trying to keep pace with the ways bad actors may be using AI for harm, concerned that the rapidly evolving technology may supercharge new and existing types of crimes.

At the same time, as public sentiment over AI and its impacts on society and the environment has soured, agencies have sought to protect AI infrastructure. The documents show police and intelligence officers are closely monitoring online opposition to datacenters among various groups with what they describe as extremist ideologies.

The Guardian exclusively reviewed more than 80 documents and memos that were distributed among a nationwide network of federal, state and local law enforcement offices – including the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the FBI and the New York City police department (NYPD) – between 2021 and 2026. They were obtained by the government transparency non-profit Property of the People and shared with the Guardian.
How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members
How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)
How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection
How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools
Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters
The FBI did not respond to detailed questions on its monitoring of anti-AI sentiment and use of AI, but pointed to a general fact sheet on the agency’s use of the technology.

The NYPD stated that its threat analysis report on artificial intelligence was related to the “AI 2027” project – an influential forecast from several AI researchers that speculated about the technology’s rapid growth and the threats it could present. In one of the project’s possible futures, it predicted bioweapon-armed drones wiping out humanity.

“This NYPD Intelligence Analysis Report contained a summary and assessment of AI 2027,” the NYPD said. “It was distributed to appropriate NYPD members and partners for their awareness, as part of the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau’s mission of analyzing developments and trends that have implications for public safety and national security.”

The DHS said it “prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and remains committed to mitigating all forms of ideologically-motivated violence”, and regularly shares intelligence with state and local law enforcement related to threats from violent extremists.

“DHS threat assessments draw on available intelligence, law-enforcement information, and other reporting to inform partners of evolving threats,” the DHS said in a statement. “DHS assesses that malicious actors may seek to use artificial intelligence to enhance existing harmful activities, including cyber-enabled activity, fraud schemes, and the production or dissemination of violent extremist propaganda”.

Law enforcement agencies’ concerns over AI and extremism fall into two broad categories, the documents show. One focuses on the burgeoning threat of extremists using new tools such as generative AI to plot attacks or promote their ideology. The other involves extremists targeting the modern technology that underpins society and has a long history within far-right movements.

Before mainstream, widespread opposition to datacenters swept the US, there was a strain of violent extremism that targeted tech facilities and other critical infrastructure, hoping such terrorism could lead to the collapse of society and instigate a race war.

Law enforcement officers expressed concern over the threat these militias posed to datacenters’ security before the 2022 launch of ChatGPT. Several bulletins, such as an October 2021 joint threat analysis from DHS, National Counterterrorism Center and FBI, highlighted a plot by Seth Pendley, a January 6 rioter and far-right militia member, to blow up an Amazon Web Services facility.

“Pendley believed a successful attack on the Amazon facility would disrupt 70 percent of Internet service, expose perceived abuses of power, and lead to revolution,” the bulletin said. Pendley pleaded guilty to a charge of malicious attempt to destroy a building with an explosive and was sentenced in 2021 to 10 years in prison for plotting the attack.

Although law enforcement agencies have long tracked extremist militia threats to infrastructure like Pendley’s, the documents show that in the years since the generative AI boom began, agencies more frequently expressed concern over anti-tech and anti-datacenter sentiment. Multiple fusion centers – law enforcement hubs for collecting information and coordinating between agencies – around the US warned of growing threats from domestic violent extremists – pointing to posts across social media platforms, messaging apps and forums like 4chan in which commenters vowed to destroy datacenters.

“I bring a sort of ‘tannerite and gasoline’ vibe to ai data centers,” an account associated with a white supremacist posted on Facebook last year, according to a 2025 Philadelphia police department intelligence bulletin. Combining gasoline with Tannerite, a brand of well-known explosive compound, produces a large and fiery detonation.
On some far-right forums, users discussed killing CEOs of AI companies and local officials who support datacenters, agents warned, as well as arson and bombing attacks against data facilities.

Law enforcement agencies also monitored real-world anti-datacenter incidents or protests, including a demonstration in Michigan in March where the documents said that three people allegedly associated with a white supremacist group held a banner opposing what they called a “Jewish data center” being built in the state.

As opposition to artificial intelligence and datacenters have become more widespread, however, questions have arisen over how law enforcement agencies’ tracking anti-datacenter and anti-tech ideology may bleed over into surveillance of non-violent protest movements. Distrust of the AI industry and mobilization against datacenters has now become so prevalent that it is a mainstream issue of the midterm elections, far from an extremist position.

The documents show agencies casting a wide net as they track opposition to the tech industry, including broadly monitoring public social media and opposition such as proposed legislation against datacenters. In a Nevada Threat Analysis Center report from April 2026, law enforcement officials cited a local city council hearing on a datacenter moratorium as part of a trend of increased negative sentiment towards the facilities.

“The Reno City Council heard a strong public opposition to data center development in the area. The concerns focused on water consumption, rising utility costs, pollution, and long-term climate impacts,” the document said.
Some experts and activists have expressed concern that as mobilization against datacenters grows, peaceful anti-AI organizations could face surveillance from authorities.

“There’s nothing extreme about not wanting to lose your livelihood to AI, your drinking water to AI datacenters, your privacy to ubiquitous AI surveillance or your life to runaway rogue AI,” said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People. “What’s extreme is law enforcement treating these legitimate objections as threats to be neutralized.”

In the months after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in 2022, law enforcement agencies across the US began to pay attention to the way the novel technology was being used. Even in its infancy, the tool could produce images that were indistinguishable from “authentic images”, according to one May 2023 law enforcement document. Police in Minnesota and in California worried that function could exacerbate problems with child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and “terrorist propaganda materials”.

At the time, many of these risks were largely theoretical in the eyes of law enforcement, the documents show. In one memo distributed by two California intelligence centers, officials warned that officers should remain vigilant because they predicted AI may one day make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, that it may be used to produce and disseminate deepfakes and that it may increase the volume of propaganda.

But as generative AI expanded in both its capabilities and reach, so too did law enforcement concerns about the types of crimes it could enable. By April 2024, the DHS’s intelligence department sent out a memo suggesting, without citations or evidence, that foreign terrorist organizations and domestic violent extremists who were “presumably US based persons” had “successfully bypassed generative Al guardrails” in order to generate bomb-making instructions and “general tactics for conducting attacks against the United States”.

Warnings about the ways violent extremists exploit AI grew in their intensity in 2025. Individuals and malicious groups across the US were weaponizing AI tools “to spread hate speech, recruit new members, and radicalize online supports more efficiently”, according to a memo from the Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center. In one example the memo cited, users of rightwing social media platform Gab created an Adolf Hitler chatbot that was programmed to say that the Holocaust was exaggerated, climate change was a scam and the 2020 election was rigged. Other examples had less evidence. The intelligence center wrote that a 17-year-old student who opened fire in Antioch, Tennessee, in January 2025 was “likely influenced by the vast amounts of extremist content readily available through the AI-enhanced web”. The source the center cited in this example included no mentions of AI.

A few months later, in April 2025, the Joint Regional Intelligence Center (JRIC), a Los Angeles-based DHS fusion center and the largest such facility in the country, published a five-part series issuing a stern warning: the misuse of generative AI for nefarious purposes was on the rise. Among the concerns was the surge in AI-created CSAM. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), a child protection non-profit, received more than 7,000 child exploitation reports involving GenAI between 2023 and 2025, the memo said.

By 2026, the documents showed that law enforcement agencies were paying more attention to how AI could make their jobs harder. In April, New York state’s intelligence center warned that AI-generated images were being used to prank people, including officers. In March, a man was arrested in Florida for showing an officer an AI-generated video of his patrol car being broken into. That same month, a man in New York was arrested for using AI to create false evidence that his car was damaged by police.

“This activity involving a patrol car represents a form of law enforcement harassment,” the memo said. “While often intended as humorous and not intentionally seeking to create dangerous situations, the prank can elicit an armed law enforcement response.”

AI’s proliferation could also make it harder for police to be tipped off to planned violent attacks, officers’ memos warned. In an FBI public safety awareness report, the agency cautioned that the private nature of AI models made it easier for bad actors to evade any “tripwires” or anything that would trigger an alert – like posting in an open forum with bystanders who might report them to the authorities. In the memo, the FBI encouraged agencies to develop relationships with AI companies to streamline “reporting avenues”.

Law enforcement agencies have grown wary of the ways AI could be used against them – even if they also use those very same tools for their police and investigative work. As the Guardian previously reported, police have warned that Meta’s AI-enabled smart glasses could be used to surreptitiously record their activities. In an August 2025 NYPD memo, police warned that law enforcement agencies needed to keep pace with AI advancements so they were prepared to respond “to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, other Al-enabled crime, and advanced malign influence campaigns”. But they also worried about the public questioning police use of AI including for social media monitoring.

“Law enforcement organizations may also face the challenge of calming public fears over the extent of the use of Al in policing, including rumors surrounding surveillance, the loss of privacy, and even the future integration of humanoid robots into the police force,” the memo said.

In January, an officer from a Maine intelligence center warned that a new AI-enabled software in Amazon Ring and other video doorbells could be used to monitor and alert residents of police activity. Several companies have implemented a feature that sends alerts about activity that the doorbell cameras detect, describing what’s happening outside using AI. Police and law enforcement have a long history of obtaining and accessing Amazon Ring footage as part of their investigations.

“This notification feature can compromise officer safety, as it could provide advanced warning of an officer’s presence, tactics, formations, equipment, and could expose officers to increased risks,” the memo said.

items.title: Isle of Wight fossil identified as new dinosaur species
paragraphs: Invictibellatrix amberina is thought to have lived in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years ago
A new species of dinosaur - a long-clawed predator the size of a large tiger - has been identified from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight more than 100 years ago.
The dinosaur, named Invictibellatrix amberina, is described in a new paper in the journal Royal Society Open Science and belongs to a group of agile, two-legged carnivores called megaraptorans.
Megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs including Tyrannosaurus rex but had slender heads and attacked prey with their large arms and giant curved claws instead of their jaws.
Dr Cassius Morrison of University College London (UCL) said it was a "real mystery" why the fossil - a chunk of the back of a skull - had been overlooked in the Natural History Museum.

The fossil was originally found at the foot of a cliff on the south-west coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur palaeontologist Reginald Walter Tooley and was acquired by the Natural History Museum in 1924.
Invictibellatrix, meaning "unconquered female warrior", is one of the smallest and earliest of the group to be found, living in the Early Cretaceous period about 120 million years ago.
The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossil
Researchers believe Invictibellatrix would have been three to four metres long and just over a metre and a half in height - about as tall as a human.
It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long.
It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals – occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.
Megaraptors are regarded as the most mysterious of the large, meat-eating dinosaurs, as few megaraptor fossils have been found.
Until now no megaraptorans had been found in Europe.
Lead author Dr Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years.
"Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."
The researchers undertook a CT scan of the fossil, creating a 3D model of this part of the skull.
They compared the fossil with skulls and brain cases from tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors and other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs.
Cliffs on the Isle of Wight are hotspots for fossil discoveries

The research team also used mathematical modelling to investigate how the spread of megaraptors around the world might have changed over time, based on fossils discovered so far, dinosaurs' evolutionary trees, geography and climate.
It was one of more than 1,000 specimens discovered by Tooley that were acquired by the Natural History Museum after his death.
Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species.
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made."

The study did not explain why megaraptors likely died out in the north, but this may have been a result of shifts in climate or environment, or the presence of competing predators such as other tyrannosaurs.

items.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
paragraphs: "Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.
"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.
"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.
He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".
"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.
A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.
In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.
That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.
Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.
"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.
Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.
"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.
But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.
"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.
Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.
She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.
"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.
The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.
When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".
In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.
The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.
Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.
"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.
She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).
"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.
She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.
Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.
Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".
Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.
Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.
"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.
He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."
But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.
"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

items.title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
paragraphs: Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?
Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?
We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.
But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?
Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.
He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.
"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."
Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.
He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates.
"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".
According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.
EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.
EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.
Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.
"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."
Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.
It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.
But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.
"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.
While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.
"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"
According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.
And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.
EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future.

She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.
"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

items.title: Obama receives honorary degree from Queen's University Belfast
paragraphs: Obama gave an acceptance speech in which he discussed the peace process, the fragility of democracy and the role of young people in shaping Northern Ireland's future
Former US President Barack Obama has been awarded an honorary degree from Queen's University Belfast (QUB).
Receiving his doctorate, the 44th US president praised Northern Ireland's progress and challenged the next generation to continue building a peaceful and inclusive future.
The Good Friday Agreement peace agreement "is still a shining example of what can happen when people put aside old wounds and choose peace," he told university staff and students.
During his visit to Northern Ireland, Obama was due to address an audience of paying fans in Belfast's O2 Arena on Tuesday night.
Obama spoke and shook hands with students during his time in Belfast

Accepting the honorary doctorate during a special ceremony at QUB, Obama made a speech that touched on a number of subjects including the peace process and the role young people can play in shaping Northern Ireland's future.
Obama said that, while peace had transformed opportunities across Northern Ireland, its benefits must continue to be shared by all.
Comparing Northern Ireland now to the place he encountered on a visit back in 2013, he said young people today faced significant challenges but also had reasons to remain hopeful.
"But," he added, "as we have seen in many countries, including in my home country the United States, peace and democracy are not inevitable.
"They have to be chosen, again and again."
During the ceremony, Obama heard from Emma McAllister, a first-year Law with Politics student from north Belfast.
McAllister first engaged with Queen's through a cross-community programme that helped young people from the Ardoyne and Shankill areas to access leadership and educational opportunities.
After listening to McAllister, Obama said: "That's what peace makes possible. And it's what Queen's and the supporters in this room are helping to make real."
In his closing remarks, Obama set out a challenge for students.
"And that is to keep showing the way," he said.
Queen's President and Vice-Chancellor Professor Sir Ian Greer congratulated Obama.
"We are privileged to welcome President Obama to Queen's.
"His commitment to peace, dialogue and public service has left a lasting impact around the world, and particularly here in Northern Ireland."
According to the university, honorary degrees are awarded to those who have achieved distinction or given significant service in one or more of a number of broad constituencies.
This includes business and commerce, the arts, education, medicine, and more.
In 2025, former Manchester United footballer Gary Neville received a QUB honorary degree for his contribution to sport, business, education and philanthropy.
Other notable recipients include boxer Carl Frampton, poet Seamus Heaney, former Irish President Mary McAleese and playwright Brian Friel.

items.title: Iran government spokesperson confirms internet slowdown in the country
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

An Iranian government spokesperson on Tuesday confirmed a slowdown of internet connectivity in the country, saying "certain government agencies are occasionally compelled to reduce internet connectivity speed."
In recent weeks, users and various media outlets in Iran have repeatedly reported a noticeable slowdown in internet connections. VOA has also in the past reported some of the disruption.
At her weekly press conference Tuesday, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani, said the decision to slow down connectivity is due to wartime conditions.
Iran cut off access to the global internet when the conflict with the United States and Israel started at the end of February.

This outage lasted 88 days and over 2,000 hours. NetBlocks, a global internet watchdog, said it was the longest recorded nationwide internet blackout in the world. During the outage, NetBlocks reported that Iran's connectivity had dropped to approximately one percent of its pre-war levels.

On May 26, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ordered Communications Minister Seyyed-Sattar Hashemi to restore Iranian citizens' access to the global internet. The Cyberspace Headquarters, chaired by First Vice President Mohammad-Reza Aref, approved the order, which resulted in the restart of connectivity at speeds prior to anti-government protests.

The protests began well before the war did; in late December and January of 2025, during which the internet was not entirely shut off, but was severely slowed down and restricted. The total blackout began at the outset of the war in late February 2026.

Following the Iran’s May order to restore internet services, Deputy Minister of Communications Ehsan Chitsaz said, "Everyone will be connected to the global internet within the next 24 hours." Aref described the government's move as "the first step toward free and regulated access to cyberspace.”

Iran’s Court of Administrative Justice halted the implementation of the mandate. Instead, it established the "Special Committee for Organizing and Managing Cyberspace" after hearing complaints seeking its annulment.
Hardline factions and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) also opposed the order to restore internet access, citing "persistent security threats."
The restoration of access was incomplete, and users remarked that their connection experience fell far short of the government's promises.

The Iranian government has previously acknowledged that many online businesses could not survive for more than three weeks and that the national economy was suffering direct losses amounting to tens of millions of dollars daily in light of the blackout. Lifting internet restrictions had been a key campaign promise of the Pezeshkian administration.

items.title: Yes, the music is lovely, but cathedrals are crumbling | Letter
paragraphs: Jonathan Davies’ article (Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it, 7 October) speaks beautifully to the contribution of English choral music to our living cultural heritage, highlighting the importance of cathedral choirs in particular, in giving children access to “world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach”.
What he misses however, is just how under threat these bastions of England’s religious, cultural and spiritual heritage actually are.

Despite recent research from the Theos thinktank suggesting 74% of adults in England have visited a cathedral over the last three years, 80% of cathedrals in England are now in structural deficit. Several have recently reached crisis point, including those in Peterborough and St Davids. One in four cathedrals in England is now charging for entry, and even after significantly diversifying their income portfolios (including through controversial silent discos), they continue to struggle.

More than 90% of visitors surveyed by Theos (including 94% of non-religious visitors) thought of cathedrals as a hub for community life, and the same number see them as a symbol of local identity and a way to connect with history and tradition. Despite their significant social and cultural contributions to communities, and being some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings (two are Unesco world heritage sites and many are almost 1,000 years old), cathedrals receive no secure state funding and limited contributions from central church authorities. Unlike museums and galleries offering free admission, cathedrals are also not subject to the same VAT exemptions on repairs or maintenance.

This has left many cathedrals crumbling, and their finances with them. Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist. If more is not done to protect them, that reality could be closer than we think.Dr Coco Parkinson-HugginsResearcher, Theos

items.title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
paragraphs: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.
The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral.
"The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.
The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.
He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.
The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.
For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.
He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.

Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.

Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.

Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".
Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed.
These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.
The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.

For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.

That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.
In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips.

"The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".
