items.title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
paragraphs: No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.
Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.
As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.
She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.
He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.
In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.
On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.
"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.
"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."
As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.
Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.
It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.
"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.
"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."
What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?
"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"
Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify.
On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships.
"I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity.
"It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system."
The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether.
A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.
It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.
After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.
She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.
The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.
"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.
"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."
It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.
Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.
When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.
"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.
"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."
In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.
"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."
For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing.

She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records.
Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently.
"You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom.
The same can't be said for her new album, The Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top.
Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.
"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.
Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.
It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.
"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.
"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."
The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.
"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.
Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.
And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.
Ashe's album, The Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.

items.title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
paragraphs: Romesh Ranganathan lets out a scream while holding a dead woman's wedding dress in a haunted cabin
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.
Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.
The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).
When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.
Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players
Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses
Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?
"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."
Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."
Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."
On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.
"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.
"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.
"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."
Bella Ramsey was considered to be the Traitors' "biggest threat" and so had to go
Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.
The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.
The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her too as the day rolled on.
"I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."

Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.
Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true.
The group conversing with the grateful dead
Friday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way.
It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about matters unresolved.
"It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted Barbie actress Sharon Rooney on arrival.
Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the the group gathered in a graveside chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen.

The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
"Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you."
Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he fairly noted.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked
James Blunt led the charge against faithful Julie Hesmondhalgh and has seemingly now put himself in the frame as a result

The group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a child's toys and a woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.
"Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed.
Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet.

On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry having allowed him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls.
Traitor Jama smartly deflected attention away from herself by latching on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh.
Hesmondhalgh bade farewell to her fellow faithfuls, describing the show's reveal as "iconic"
Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful.
Once discussions were under way, she played the sympathy card, claiming she had been left feeling "vulnerable" as she knew her reputation as a brain box would make her a target.
Miss Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed Myha'la.

In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and pointedly, Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."
Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause.
"It would be a cruel move taking the most trusted member of our group," noted Sheen.
Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."
Newfound Traitor Hannah Fry survived a stressful episode
The conclusion was to banish Hesmondhalgh, who, in her parting words, said it had been an "immense experience".
"Alas," she continued, confirming her fidelity as tears appeared in eyes around the table: "It may mean I am not a phenomenal actor."
Singer Blunt, who had led the charge against her, appears to have now put himself in the frame. He told the group: "I'm so sorry, that's my fault."
"He's been wrong about every theory he's came up with," said Rooney.
Hart declared that "everything is up in the air" now, following Hesmondhalgh's eviction, which King Kenny called the team's "biggest loss" so far.
First recruit, Acaster's strategy is to continue playing the game as if he is a faithful, he said. Jama is clearly loving life on the dark side while Fry, it's fair to say, is not.
"You two saved me," Fry told the other two of her stressful day, while back in the turret in their cloaks.
The episode ended not with a murder but a fresh twist - the promise of a deathly game of hide-and-seek for four chosen contestants.
Ross Kemp, Rob Beckett, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Romesh Ranganathan looking delighted to have been chosen for a game of killer hide-and-seek
The traitors opted to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock.
"I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.
Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night.
"If only it was that easy Romesh," replied the host, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be in for a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.
Only Pinnock, it was decided, will be immune from murder in the game within a game, though the Traitors aren't to know that.
This much terror and mischief and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.
Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.
Have you played a version of the Traitors or another social deduction game at home or socially? Share your experience.

items.title: Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
paragraphs: Sean Fern, a former FBI agent, is joining the prediction market platform Kalshi to lead the company's efforts in fighting money laundering. Provided by Kalshi hide caption

Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.

Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement and regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity on the platform, which has exploded in growth in the past year.
According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.

In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn before his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.

"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."

The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.
Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.

At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.
Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.

Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.

Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.
The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.

During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

items.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
paragraphs: A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

items.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
paragraphs: Three employees recently fired by OpenAI allege the company punished them for being outspoken about safety. OpenAI disputes the claims and says they were dismissed for mishandling sensitive information. Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.
OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.
In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.
"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.
In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."
OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.
OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.
In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.
"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

items.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
paragraphs: The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.
The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

items.title: OpenAI caught Russians and Iranians using ChatGPT for influence campaigns
paragraphs: OpenAI says Russian operatives used its AI chatbot to update their bosses, shedding light on influence campaigns previously not attributed to Russia. Jeff Chiu/AP hide caption

OpenAI said in a blog post on Thursday that it banned Russian and Iranian accounts that were using the company's artificial intelligence tools to help with influence operations in multiple countries. The operatives said they managed to get their false narratives picked up by news outlets, and in once case, prompted a response from a member of the European Parliament, according to internal reports the operations produced using OpenAI's chatbot, ChatGPT.

OpenAI investigated the impact of the different campaigns the accounts mentioned and found that those focused on placing false narratives in established media outlets appeared to have reached a wider audience than campaigns that focused on using fake social media accounts to spread their message.

The Russian operations targeted countries in Latin America and appeared aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and influencing local politics, OpenAI said. The accounts appeared to be mostly using ChatGPT to write reports detailing their work to unspecified higher ups, OpenAI said. The company said one of these reports appeared to describe the widest-reaching influence operation OpenAI has come across so far, because it led to public response from a political figure.

In this campaign, the Russian operatives said they impersonated a regional educational authority in Peru and tricked some schools into organizing activities about Ukraine that featured Stepan Bandera. Bandera is a controversial figure, admired by nationalists for leading a drive for Ukrainian independence before and during World War II. He is reviled by others, including in Poland, because his movement sided with the Nazis and killed Poles and Jews. Peruvian outlet Extra reported that one such event did take place at a Peruvian school.
A Polish news report about the school event prompted a far-right Polish member of the European Parliament to suggest banning the entry of people who professed support for Bandera.
"The Russian fake thus both fed on, and fed into, historical tensions between Ukrainians and Poles," OpenAI wrote in its report.

"Russians are constantly engaging in these sorts of active measures," said Darren Linvill, a co-director of Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub who studies online influence operations. "Trying to engage in narrative laundering, creating fake stories, fake persona to either create or spread propaganda that aligns with Russia's worldview and Russia's political agenda."

The Russian internal memos created with ChatGPT also claimed that the operatives ran a fake think tank in Latin America and recruited unwitting researchers to interview experts and compose reports. OpenAI said that effort was similar to a 2020 Russian operation posing as an independent news outlet linked to the late oligarch Yevgeny Prigozhin's Internet Research Agency, which was involved in efforts to influence the 2016 U.S. election.

In other instances, OpenAI said, the Russian operatives took credit for events they were not responsible for. The Russians did use AI to generate fake material, OpenAI said, but it was a minority of the workload.
"These Russian underlings were trying to use AI to create a shortcut and do less work in the same way that a lot of us use AI, but in this case it helped get them caught," Linvill said.

While the Russian operatives primarily used AI to update their superiors, Iranian operatives used AI to help them push out content in Persian and English. The campaign mainly focused on the U.S.-Iran war and, to a lesser degree, American politics. OpenAI said the operation's activity "appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign" but that it was unable to identify who that was.
According to OpenAI, Iranian accounts made up seven fake authors to pitch and polish long articles to small media outlets around the world. They published almost 100 articles in this way.

The fake authors published articles in outlets including the progressive U.S. news site Daily Kos and the U.K.-based Middle East Monitor. According to NBC News, the Middle East Monitor published at least 21 articles by four fake authors. The outlet, which didn't respond to a request for comment, has since taken down the author pages.

The Daily Kos wrote in response to NPR's request for comment that its community section, where one of the fake personas posted, is separate from staff reports. Anyone can sign up to post in the community section and posts are "not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication," according to a disclaimer on the site. The community section does have rules for posting, including prohibiting "Pretending to be someone you're not." The posts by the persona are still up.

"AI was valuable to them above and beyond just being a shortcut," Linvill said. "It helped them create language that ... looked and felt and read authentic to the point where it was being published by legitimate outlets. And I think that is something that a few years ago, an Iranian operation like this would have struggled a lot more with."

items.title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
paragraphs: Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film Wicker
Culture correspondent at London Film Festival
It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external.
And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.
Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction.
"No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said.
"But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."
The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village.
Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.
Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.
As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.
And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.
The film has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.

Since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz online around the film - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.
Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.
When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for.
"And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"
She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.
"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.
Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet.
"I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."
But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.
He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot.
"We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said.
"But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."
The steamy new rom-com has been causing a stir at film festivals
The film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones.

After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it, external two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire".
But The Hollywood Reporter, external was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure".
Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules.
"It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki.
"It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch."
"It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman.
"I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot."
Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30.

paragraphs: What is a supercomputer for? How does it work? And who gets to use it? We explain all

items.title: OpenAI’s Jason Kwon gave even-toned, reassuring answers to the Australian government. Did … ChatGPT write this?
paragraphs: Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare.

Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey parliamentary committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.
Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend.

Asked by the senator David Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?”, Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting.” Asked why Open AI’s CEO Sam Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Australia’s deputy prime minister Richard Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”.
One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.”

In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI, which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting.

Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics, but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service.
Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?”

There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why Altman didn’t inform Marles about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After Tuesday’s committee hearing, it’s still unclear why.

It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window.
At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write it – even if it went to an obscure inbox.

But with Australia striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical.

Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data.
A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1m gigabytes.
Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand.
The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there.

items.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
paragraphs: Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.
It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon.

Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.

Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.

Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.
Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.
The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.

The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.

The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.

Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.

It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.

The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.
That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.

The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.

The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.

But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.

The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.

Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.

The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.
The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359.
The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.

The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.
The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.

All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.
Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

items.title: ‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creations
paragraphs: With nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.

Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan, who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.

In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.

In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.

“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”

Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.

Death row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.

Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.

While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”

As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”

Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.

One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”

The Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.

While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”

Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.

Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.

“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”

Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand Rapids Art Museum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)

items.title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
paragraphs: Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.

The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.

Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since the M2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIY iMac.

The machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.
It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.

The mini runs the latest macOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design that was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.

Siri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.

Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.
Ports back: 3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb Ethernet
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread
The Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.

For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.
The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.

The Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The Mac mini M6 costs from £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
For comparison, the A18 Pro MacBook Neo costs from £699, the M5 MacBook Air starts at £1,299, the M4 iMac starts at £1,499 and the Mac Studio costs from £2,499.

The Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.

The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.

The only downside is the RAMageddon-linked price hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.
Pros: very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.

items.title: K-art, William Kentridge and a Turner prize worth getting excited for – the week in art
paragraphs: Turner prize Kira Freije creates a waste land peopled by Rodinesque ghosts in the machine, Simeon Barclay meditates on masculinity, Tanoa Sasraku takes on big oil and Marguerite Humeau gets lost in wonderland in the most exciting Turner prize in years. MIMA, Middlesbrough, from26 September until 29 March
KoreaA survey of 2,000 years of Korean art, belief and philosophy – but will it be as big as Bayeux? British Museum, London, from 1 October until 31 January

Fail We May, Sail We MustArtists from Salvador Dalí to the 18th-century British painter George Romney star in another eclectic dip into artist Glenn Brown’s impressive collection. Brown Collection, London, until 7 August

Mark Wallinger: Circling the SquarePaintings and a film from the Turner prize winner, that explore abstraction and the vitality of nature with a nod to Dylan Thomas. Paul Stolper Gallery, London, until 24 October
William Kentridge: A Nicely Built CityA new animated film by this artist who takes drawing into new dimensions gets its world premiere. Goodman Gallery, London, until 7 November

Goons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents ride around in a clown car – a pretty clear comment on contemporary US. Elsewhere a solitary figure amid the ruins of Stonehenge is overwhelmed by the universe – are we now lost in in cosmic speculation? Welcome to the abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling world of Nicole Eisenman. Read our review here.
101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser has had an amazing life
Sophie Calle has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms and filmed her mother’s last breath in the name of art, but she has no regrets
Dutch sculptor Magali Reus reimagines rubbish into vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures
A new Magritte exhibition showcases his surrealist brilliance and his occasional trash
The Greek PM has said a deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached
Beverly Buchanan’s ramshackle mini barns memorialise the survival of enslaved people
Rachel Kneebone’s porcelain sculptures are edgy and marvellous
An Elderly Man as Saint Paul by Rembrandt, probably 1659

You can see he’s wearing archaic garments and has religious trappings that identify him as the early Christian Paul, but all that slips your mind compared with this man’s incredibly real, suffering face. Paul, who set out some of the Church’s most severe views on matters including sexuality, doesn’t usually come across as anything like as doubtful or hesitant as this pensive soul. He is surrounded by the shadows of evening, or night, or death, and in his eyes you see a world of cares and regrets. Rembrandt has no respect for the conventions of art or storytelling that would make this a picture of Paul and allow us to move on after recognising that: instead he wants you to be shocked into recognition of the human predicament. You are held by this face, dragged behind the painting, into the man’s mind or soul or whatever we call the essence of the human. Nothing else, for Rembrandt, is worth making art about. National Gallery, London
